How many classical bits can “really” be
encoded into {{formula:d9a4b1ac-1875-4bec-960e-7b8630e5d7cf}}  qubits?  Is it {{formula:382bcb8d-a3c4-41f7-9371-3f6df0d44886}} , because of Holevo's Theorem
{{cite:bbc40913850903434b00cdf12a0be49947fcbe08}}; {{formula:b3ee3905-c7cf-4d54-a729-0d9e5949ea2d}} , because of dense quantum coding {{cite:44b3fa52d28581c677b30edaa119036adc811c1d}} and quantum
teleportation {{cite:6c5e85f1be30ffdb808acd0f551ddbff0f97d76c}}; exponentially many, because of quantum
fingerprinting {{cite:ee5fc12c88c8cd05c97cf9c784b08f7e26c07335}}; or infinitely many, because amplitudes are
continuous?  The best general answer to this question is probably
mu, the Zen word that “unasks” a
question.Another mu-worthy question is, “Where does the power of quantum computing come from?  Superposition?
 Interference?  The large size of Hilbert space?”

To a computer scientist, however, it is natural to formalize the question in
terms of quantum one-way communication complexity
{{cite:f09da469e735106212608910cb08a0bab844a6a8}}, {{cite:ee5fc12c88c8cd05c97cf9c784b08f7e26c07335}}, {{cite:a1be961da522bcf1b98ba72bca24af931f00e195}}, {{cite:a29a32d0e97cd2f5854437f5e6cf604bdd23a206}}.  The setting is as follows: Alice has an
{{formula:3ecad0f5-b2b7-413b-a2d5-2d96ca21d46d}} -bit string {{formula:250a2685-8bd1-4926-8503-9ebfc002d593}} , Bob has an {{formula:9fa18140-e02d-4466-9a0e-f89c5d482a1d}} -bit string {{formula:2518b2e4-aa95-47a7-aa18-d0fe7139b839}} , and together they wish to
evaluate {{formula:d96a0b9a-b680-4092-a8f5-bb57ccee4e24}}  where {{formula:0b481e9f-7757-44d3-90bf-d53a02f46e92}}  is a
Boolean function.  After examining her input {{formula:9b40c029-24b7-49cc-a854-3ea0071a961e}} , Alice can
send a single quantum message {{formula:29b9b332-d2eb-4dd5-b1a5-8a5be0566301}}  to Bob, whereupon Bob, after
examining his input {{formula:4c8bba10-fbd9-4636-b81f-6d6c736b84f4}} , can choose some basis in which to
measure {{formula:62bfcb80-5bd4-4b10-8d11-b376863ab10c}} .  He must then output a claimed value for {{formula:fd877730-b799-43c3-9e33-2ee98d09b0d4}} .  We are interested in how long Alice's message needs to be,
for Bob to succeed with high probability on any {{formula:80aa0f12-fda1-412f-8c68-a55faca20399}}  pair.  Ideally the
length will be much smaller than if Alice had to send a classical message.

Communication complexity questions have been intensively studied in
theoretical computer science (see the book of Kushilevitz and Nisan
{{cite:9c79649b3cc79c1e619bfed2c7b56d2f045f7ba0}} for example).  In both the classical and quantum cases, though,
most attention has focused on two-way communication, meaning that
Alice and Bob get to send messages back and forth.  We believe that the study
of one-way quantum communication presents two main advantages.  First, many
open problems about two-way communication look gruesomely difficult—for
example, are the randomized and quantum communication complexities of every
total Boolean function polynomially related?  We might gain insight into
these problems by tackling their one-way analogues first.  And second,
because of its greater simplicity, the one-way model more directly addresses
our opening question: how much “useful
stuff” can be packed into a quantum state?  Thus, results
on one-way communication fall into the quantum information theory tradition
initiated by Holevo {{cite:bbc40913850903434b00cdf12a0be49947fcbe08}} and others, as much as the communication
complexity tradition initiated by Yao {{cite:e811a0746e8f56f4d080ef0149d1893775bbee25}}.

Related to quantum one-way communication is the notion of quantum
advice.  As pointed out by Nielsen and Chuang {{cite:aebe41a4488f0909c5c4740cd3eb7db86e831da7}}, there is no
compelling physical reason to assume that the starting state of a quantum
computer is a computational basis state:One might object that the
starting state is itself the outcome of some computational process, which
began no earlier than the Big Bang.  However, (1) for all we know highly
entangled states were created in the Big Bang, and (2) 14 billion years is a
long time.

[W]e know that many systems in Nature `prefer' to sit in highly entangled
states of many systems; might it be possible to exploit this preference to
obtain extra computational power?  It might be that having access to certain
states allows particular computations to be done much more easily than if we
are constrained to start in the computational basis.

One way to interpret Nielsen and Chuang's provocative question is as follows.
 Suppose we could request the best possible starting state for a
quantum computer, knowing the language to be decided and the input length {{formula:951be317-568b-47ef-a582-6814d7ccaecd}} 
but not knowing the input itself.If we knew the input, we would
simply request a starting state that contains the right answer!  Denote the
class of languages that we could then decide by {{formula:457fcf53-152e-416c-946f-c881ad4b164e}} —meaning
quantum polynomial time, given an arbitrarily-entangled but polynomial-size
quantum advice state.{{formula:2b7c2d7d-476e-48e2-929b-c66ac6f6acd7}}  might remind readers of a
better-studied class called {{formula:e7ae1254-7a2f-4656-a506-03e7f602e7b9}}  (Quantum Merlin-Arthur).  But
there are two key differences: first, advice can be trusted while proofs
cannot; second, proofs can be tailored to a particular input while advice
cannot.  How powerful is this class?  If {{formula:de2486ff-8049-481a-a30d-1514f9e44bf3}}  contained
(for example) the {{formula:7cc2bdcc-73c4-40df-8703-08893f630d55}} -complete problems, then we would need to
rethink our most basic assumptions about the power of quantum computing.  We
will see later that quantum advice is closely related to quantum one-way
communication, since we can think of an advice state as a one-way message sent
to an algorithm by a benevolent “advisor.”

This paper is about the limitations of quantum advice and one-way
communication.  It presents three contributions which are basically
independent of one another.

First, Section  shows that {{formula:588ebba3-ae9a-4b98-84cd-48102131ba4f}}  for
any Boolean function {{formula:588e6507-7251-47ab-9e49-fa8fed281ff6}} , partial or total.  Here {{formula:2c7d996e-1cd7-4d80-9846-cf169f367573}}  is deterministic one-way communication complexity, {{formula:a6c74321-6229-42ed-b8d2-458783efc977}}  is bounded-error one-way quantum communication complexity, and
{{formula:7b7a4ba0-c371-489f-ba01-6f289cc8c5a0}}  is the length of Bob's input.  Intuitively, whenever the set of Bob's
possible inputs is not too large, Alice can send him a short classical message
that lets him learn the outcome of any measurement he would have wanted to
make on the quantum message {{formula:c213745c-8bdd-4bb2-b2d7-166ace6238c8}} .  It is interesting that a slightly
tighter bound for total functions—{{formula:e0278ede-e768-4e77-892b-32981970fcf2}} —follows easily from a result of
Klauck {{cite:a1be961da522bcf1b98ba72bca24af931f00e195}} together with a lemma of Sauer {{cite:aa4f8ea4852e2bfa8cfaceb820b6acd674630e09}} about
VC-dimension.  However, the proof of the latter bound is highly
nonconstructive, and seems to fail for partial {{formula:97f4200a-83ba-4f30-b320-7257bc0064f3}} .

Using our communication complexity result, in Section REF  we show
that {{formula:13522361-abab-4247-8de4-2dfb98ea92ac}} —in other words,
{{formula:0dc7fab8-a035-4643-b144-b722f3de037e}}  with polynomial-size quantum advice can be simulated in
{{formula:c552e77d-ac7f-4388-a8d6-4a951910ae4b}}  with polynomial-size classical advice.Here
{{formula:ff9b7427-0386-42dd-b0b5-487d3972f1da}}  is Probabilistic Polynomial-Time, or the class of languages for
which there exists a polynomial-time classical randomized algorithm that
accepts with probability greater than {{formula:f510b9f7-3f28-44e5-aea6-7c308b60a1bd}}  if and only if an input {{formula:e9fac730-2240-4191-835b-f4c4aa03099d}}  is
in the language.  Also, given a complexity class {{formula:6b598932-5a9b-4c41-bbb3-253926883f36}} , the class
{{formula:e20faace-1dd1-4c13-8da0-c8f11e68c73a}}  consists of all languages decidable by a {{formula:88f7d64a-ea5c-49e2-ad29-2fe56d9e9689}}  machine, given a polynomial-size classical advice string that depends only
on the input length.  See www.complexityzoo.com for more information about
standard complexity classes mentioned in this paper.  This resolves a
question of Harry Buhrman (personal communication), who asked whether quantum
advice can be simulated in any classical complexity class with short
classical advice.  A corollary of our containment is that we cannot hope to
show an unrelativized separation between quantum and classical advice (that
is, that {{formula:495b394a-97ab-49cd-8cef-776441bcf5b1}} ), without also showing that
{{formula:24403727-7a67-4c51-a4c5-828ffeb18080}}  does not have polynomial-size circuits.

What makes this result surprising is that, in the minds of many computer
scientists, a quantum state is basically an exponentially long vector.
 Indeed, this belief seems to fuel skepticism of quantum computing (see
Goldreich {{cite:dc3eddec57cc60af4219d3a1c1c29849cd9e0a23}} for example).  But given an exponentially long
advice string, even a classical computer could decide any language whatsoever.
 So one might imagine naïvely that quantum advice would let us solve
problems that are not even recursively enumerable given classical advice of a
similar size!  The failure of this naïve intuition supports the view
that a quantum superposition over {{formula:9887cc3f-56b6-4daa-adfa-1df521f7304b}} -bit strings is “more
similar” to a probability distribution over {{formula:55a9b4a8-9991-4214-8a26-31c188d776dd}} -bit strings
than to a {{formula:c91c3c3e-e818-493b-8787-c690e9a5e584}} -bit string.

Our second contribution, in Section , is an oracle relative to
which {{formula:ef9cf0e9-c2a2-409a-90ca-b79ea3e6ddb9}}  is not contained in {{formula:7564185d-3954-48c7-8550-80836848cf21}} .  Underlying
this oracle separation is the first correct proof of a direct product
theorem for quantum search.  Given an {{formula:c44ff497-6399-4315-9a64-220073b16e5e}} -item database with {{formula:560735f3-b301-4370-b2cb-34030672848c}}  marked
items, the direct product theorem says that if a quantum algorithm makes
{{formula:561b2787-8005-42b4-ad6a-146d1a22e1eb}}  queries, then the probability that the algorithm
finds all {{formula:7825d2b5-a910-475f-8cae-8af9ae92bd03}}  of the marked items decreases exponentially in {{formula:716f7947-03ca-4250-8a5c-11e1b8ea11e3}} .  Notice
that such a result does not follow from any existing quantum lower bound.
 Earlier Klauck {{cite:888d098e5e870361a39ad04d41f5d2d0cf41c5d0}} had claimed a weaker direct product
theorem, based on the hybrid method of Bennett et al. {{cite:5a0a45badcd919053d8a7a3922bd95e2fdb29e2d}}, in a paper
on quantum time-space tradeoffs for sorting.  Unfortunately, Klauck's proof
is incorrect.  Our proof uses the polynomial method of Beals et al.
{{cite:2ff31b7d2c85795fb7aa3a59f30e11016425df62}}, with the novel twist that we examine all higher
derivatives of a polynomial (not just the first derivative).  Our proof has
already been improved by Klauck, Špalek, and de Wolf {{cite:06463ca2447dbe41a8c68e403f92ac00ac00372c}}, who were
able to recover and even extend Klauck's original claims about quantum sorting.

Our final contribution, in Section , is a new trace
distance method for proving lower bounds on quantum one-way communication
complexity.  Previously there was only one basic lower bound technique: the
VC-dimension method of Klauck {{cite:a1be961da522bcf1b98ba72bca24af931f00e195}}, which relied on lower bounds
for quantum random access codes due to Ambainis et al. {{cite:7e767e622a04476fa32c358dc7942fdc0c9f10b7}} and Nayak
{{cite:dbbc5932a302e0ec1c5f4aee88425fe61ed73799}}.  Using VC-dimension one can show, for example, that {{formula:0c5a7485-db0b-474f-91a7-725546dc2a81}} , where the
disjointness function {{formula:54ec6c21-4e52-426a-be18-31f66b634782}}  is
defined by  {{formula:2b3e5c8b-29c5-48cb-949f-a34cce7d7fa5}}  if and only if
{{formula:77ba77b0-0a79-4b23-92c0-26b5321c5b01}}  for all {{formula:325ade6c-b8e7-4f6a-b516-eeea6c0e4c7c}} .

For some problems, however, the VC-dimension method yields no nontrivial
quantum lower bound.  Seeking to make this point vividly, Ambainis posed the
following problem.  Alice is given two elements {{formula:2ad5ae93-fa35-41a7-8b11-eb6dce7a1ef9}}  of a finite field
{{formula:ee9c657d-036b-42a8-a691-d357b39666fd}}  (where {{formula:bfb662df-f80f-46c6-b5e8-4c7ef141e2a0}}  is prime); Bob is given another two elements
{{formula:09d37a14-7769-418c-873e-be8f8a0d7519}} .  Bob's goal is to output 1 if {{formula:807f25c7-5ed8-47d2-a78b-716eb700de1b}}  and 0 otherwise.  For this problem, the
VC-dimension method yields no randomized or quantum lower bound
better than constant.  On the other hand, the well-known fingerprinting
protocol for the equality function {{cite:edac30fe9bc5b70ed117bc35548e9ac78e8ced11}} seems to fail for Ambainis'
problem, because of the interplay between addition and multiplication.  So it
is natural to conjecture that the randomized and even quantum one-way
complexities are {{formula:135105f8-be21-4df8-9407-7844b9f3025d}} —that is, that no nontrivial
protocol exists for this problem.

Ambainis posed a second problem in the same spirit.  Here Alice is given
{{formula:ff1069e9-af54-47ea-bddb-1a00362db9a5}} , Bob is given {{formula:4ae21bdf-764a-4463-9696-4c5ad3d65c20}} , and both players know a subset {{formula:5a70f0f4-3ec0-4e76-877e-cc61bfb3f844}} .  Bob's goal is to decide whether {{formula:69cad43a-37d2-4832-9dab-1363e43d090c}}  where subtraction
is modulo {{formula:75030ba8-ad23-4cb9-88fd-1a90d8ad3fc6}} .  The conjecture is that if {{formula:ce803096-1366-4a96-b7a6-f7de837f30ed}}  is chosen uniformly at random
with {{formula:17f0d0f3-6363-4447-9d80-e8cb4a49bc70}}  about {{formula:66048b7b-d9b4-4db0-ae2e-76b70e71a601}} , then with high probability
the randomized and quantum one-way complexities are both {{formula:eae9da75-1b98-4a54-8628-e6f678cc0ced}} .

Using our trace distance method, we are able to show optimal quantum lower
bounds for both of Ambainis' problems.  Previously, no nontrivial lower
bounds were known even for randomized protocols.  The key idea is to consider
two probability distributions over Alice's quantum message {{formula:98057f4e-8455-44c3-802c-06a19adf2cd7}} .  The
first distribution corresponds to {{formula:df415dc9-98c0-42a8-9dfb-47b83cc466ba}}  chosen uniformly at random; the second
corresponds to {{formula:de5990ec-43f1-4f8d-9453-ecc1bb4284af}}  chosen uniformly conditioned on {{formula:6a5a4986-3cd8-473d-b27d-809be2e6d181}} .
 These distributions give rise to two mixed states {{formula:dae6b34e-08c2-4a57-bd57-7cde45ecd671}}  and {{formula:0775cf99-4292-4112-bd68-3c8e42a18a25}} ,
which Bob must be able to distinguish with non-negligible bias assuming he can
evaluate {{formula:554db61d-db1d-4c62-a608-02dbcfce26ae}} .  We then show an upper bound on the trace
distance {{formula:d8dcf234-9302-46f7-8d43-9d143f8e93e9}} , which
implies that Bob cannot distinguish the distributions.

Theorem REF  gives a very general condition under which our trace
distance method works; Corollaries REF  and REF  then show
that the condition is satisfied for Ambainis' two problems.  Besides showing
a significant limitation of the VC-dimension method, we hope our new method is
a non-negligible step towards proving that {{formula:2fa8e1ce-ea9b-4dd8-9468-31d94b47327c}}  for all total Boolean
functions {{formula:18853646-a44c-4be0-bd58-577797f6495f}} , where {{formula:16412b16-8f94-40de-86a8-6abf80fe6e8a}}  is randomized one-way complexity.

We conclude in Section  with some open problems.

Can quantum computers solve {{formula:2de743ab-f30f-4f20-85d1-cba9cc2299f0}} -complete problems in polynomial
time?  In the early days of quantum computing, Bennett et al. {{cite:5a0a45badcd919053d8a7a3922bd95e2fdb29e2d}} gave an oracle relative to which {{formula:a65f7339-f8b9-49d2-b9ed-ff373112a988}} ,
providing what is still the best evidence we have that the answer is no.  It
is easy to extend Bennett et al.'s result to give an oracle relative to which
{{formula:7de710c4-f088-4bbe-94bc-3393b935d9d6}} ; that is, {{formula:0feaf9aa-32ae-404f-8389-b73f910adf64}}  is hard
even for nonuniform quantum algorithms.  But when we try to show
{{formula:9e42b679-736c-4860-8a4a-a21221c28022}}  relative to an oracle, a new
difficulty arises: even if the oracle encodes {{formula:408e632b-a4bb-4177-9eb9-213f2f60a6c8}}  exponentially hard
search problems for each input length {{formula:e96c9337-84d0-448b-9d47-366ce5b41a60}} , the quantum advice, being an
“exponentially large object” itself, might
somehow encode information about all {{formula:5d9acaa0-a933-44cf-8bd8-aab0b7b2cc3d}}  problems.  We need to argue that
even if so, only a miniscule fraction of that information can be extracted by
measuring the advice.

How does one prove such a statement?  As it turns out, the task can be
reduced to proving a direct product theorem for quantum search.
 This is a theorem that in its weakest form says the following: given {{formula:c37bfeab-2a71-42c3-8f97-cc4f823b890b}} 
items, {{formula:1467963e-0e68-4009-b1c0-9f0441ba0340}}  of which are marked, if we lack enough time to find even
one marked item, then the probability of finding all {{formula:c2998e87-2e90-451c-9291-f66c990a603e}}  items
decreases exponentially in {{formula:4c8dea66-959c-423d-a6cf-3c7cec8bd41a}} .  For intuitively, suppose there were a
quantum advice state that let us efficiently find any one of {{formula:7fa376b9-b0b3-4d65-853a-15c8751f69ed}}  marked items.
 Then by “guessing” the advice (i.e.
replacing it by a maximally mixed state), and then using the guessed advice
multiple times, we could efficiently find all {{formula:df1649a1-4fe3-4589-8cd9-10d26f7ff23f}}  of the items with a success
probability that our direct product theorem shows is impossible.  This
reduction is formalized in Theorem REF .

But what about the direct product theorem itself?  It seems like it should be
trivial to prove—for surely there are no devious correlations by which
success in finding one marked item leads to success in finding all the others!
 So it is surprising that even a weak direct product theorem eluded proof for
years.  In 2001, Klauck {{cite:888d098e5e870361a39ad04d41f5d2d0cf41c5d0}} gave an attempted proof using the
hybrid method of Bennett et al. {{cite:5a0a45badcd919053d8a7a3922bd95e2fdb29e2d}}.  His motivation was to show a
limitation of space-bounded quantum sorting algorithms.  Unfortunately,
Klauck's proof is fallacious.Specifically, the last sentence in the
proof of Lemma 5 in {{cite:888d098e5e870361a39ad04d41f5d2d0cf41c5d0}} (“Clearly this
probability is at least {{formula:ec55e323-51e0-41ba-a80f-92031d5f9f3c}} ”) is not justified by what precedes it.

In this section we give the first correct proof of a direct product theorem,
based on the polynomial method of Beals et al. {{cite:2ff31b7d2c85795fb7aa3a59f30e11016425df62}}.  Besides showing
that {{formula:5917a3d5-d354-45bc-955c-79829cc2f6d3}}  relative to an oracle, our
result can be used to recover the conclusions in {{cite:888d098e5e870361a39ad04d41f5d2d0cf41c5d0}} about the

This section introduces a new method for proving lower bounds on quantum
one-way communication complexity.  Unlike in Section , here we
do not try to simulate quantum protocols using classical ones.  Instead we
prove lower bounds for quantum protocols directly, by reasoning about the
trace distance between two possible distributions over Alice's quantum message
(that is, between two mixed states).  The result is a method that works even
if Alice's and Bob's inputs are the same size.

In a data-driven world where permanent storage devices have an ever
growing capacity, I/O access becomes a bottleneck when read/write
performance does not increase as quickly as
capacity {{cite:6ae3558652e0ed58a1879fdc7eedcd5323bc68ad}}. As Gray put it: “we're able
to store more than we can access” {{cite:aeb227dbca36a9b49a95780e0125f34007284630}}. At the same
time, users of applications in OLAP {{cite:971a14abdf8a3fee2a4207ffb2bbe92e83be3efb}} or in
visualization {{cite:d9d48cc7d08d1d7e52a3fa8907276907225d0e08}} now expect online processing of
their data sets. A strategy to solve this problem is to use a
relatively small internal-memory buffer to precompute some of the
expected queries. For example, it might be reasonable to use a memory
buffer of one megabyte (1 MB)Throughout, we use the familiar units of kB, MB, GB and TB to
measure storage in
groups of {{formula:28645dac-2f4e-478b-89f3-2521cc7df241}} , {{formula:745933ff-bca0-4dce-a7b3-96914f077094}} , {{formula:5ffab6b1-e3c3-43a9-a760-06b89f5230af}}  and {{formula:e895999b-53b7-4455-a3d4-de30bfa03409}}  bytes.
Our units thus coincide with the new IEC
units KiB, MiB, GiB and TiB {{cite:80441cd728a19fa845bb0ed536799799cf92bf89}}.

Local moments are used widely, from pattern recognition and image
processing to multidimensional databases (OLAP). Among other things,
they have been proposed as a replacement for maximum likelihood
methods in statistics, to cope with the magnitude of the new
data sets {{cite:4068410bd2608a52576d857973ba9622e46d0d74}}.

As an example application, given the number of items in a store for
every possible price, the sum (moment 0) over a range of prices would
return how many items are available, the first moment would return the
total dollar value for items in the specified price range, and the
second moment would allow us to compute the standard deviation and variance
of the
price.

The PS, RPS, and PyRPS methods (and similar alternatives for other
queries) have a common inconvenience: each
type of range query is buffered separately: {{formula:4d08ffc3-7415-49b6-b516-307ff1f430fd}} , {{formula:12fcb205-0c85-40b1-966d-f8a703c6f40a}} , {{formula:68d00f80-7da1-429f-af1d-503b7dbbb6c6}} , {{formula:c005bc8f-4e22-4e80-b446-3ceb3f5b3127}}  An equivalent view is of a single
tuple-valued buffer, rather than several real-valued buffers.
The ProPolyne framework {{cite:02b263ec99a74822343d0ff348f8ccb053b6be31}} showed how to avoid tuple-valued
buffers by using wavelets. ProPolyne has both logarithmic
queries and updates at the cost of a buffer of size {{formula:f095815e-42c0-44dc-b9fa-3aa32edd9720}}  for
computing local moments (Polynomial Range Queries).
ProPolyne simultaneously buffers all local moments up to a given
degree. So, ProPolyne reduces storage when compared with
prefix-sum methods such as PyRPS, but at the expense of constant-time
queries.

various alternatives to buffer local moments.

In a wavelet framework such as ProPolyne,
we can keep only the most

The paper is organized as follows. We first
consider how bin buffers
can be used to speed up
many range queries over dynamic external
arrays (section ). For each bin or “range of indices,”
Bin Buffering {{cite:70d513ef7cb249b4de11cad8ec839f80eb125c99}} associates a
single buffer component.
However, its scalability is limited because very large buffers do not improve
performance and can even worsen it. In section , we present
the analysis of a variant,
Hierarchical Bin Buffering, which supports logarithmic queries and updates
even for modest buffers. These results are novel, but have been alluded
to in the concluding section of a paper {{cite:70d513ef7cb249b4de11cad8ec839f80eb125c99}}.
In section , we present a novel buffering framework: Overlapped Bin Buffering.
In Overlapped Bin Buffering, each buffer component depends not only on one but a range
of bins. In this context, we present Lagrange Interpolation (section ) as a tool
to compute a useful buffer and establish an explicit link between buffering and interpolation.
The result is an Ola buffer and we show it can be hierarchical as well.
Section  presents precisely stated algorithms and experimental results.
We then proceed on some concluding remarks. We elaborate on the
differences between Ola and Bin Buffering (section )
and show how Ola can support efficient progressive approximate queries (section ).

This section puts the ideas of the previous section into practice,
presenting more details of Ola and
presenting an experimental analysis of Ola
as an example of Hierarchical Bin Buffering.
There are three fundamental operations on Ola buffers:
building them initially, using them for fast queries, and finally, updating
them when the underlying data changes.
Each fundamental operation will, in turn, be described and its complexity
analyzed.
However, our complexity analysis
is typical and ignores system-specific factors including the relative costs
of various mathematical operators and the effects of the
memory-access patterns on a computer's memory hierarchy. To show that
the algorithm can be efficiently implemented, we
we
coded Ola in C++. The performance of our
implementation completes the discussion of each fundamental operation.

To enable replication of our results, we next provide some details
of our implementation and the test environment.
Our experiments were conducted with {{formula:58c20f8b-012b-4871-8b6f-69f65b202221}}  being even, and
we chose {{formula:217c2bbc-8543-4445-88fc-61a4ff862bbf}} ; these constraints were imposed
by our implementation. Our test platform was a
Pentium 3 Xeon server with 2 GB RAM running the Linux operating system
(kernel 2.4), and the software was compiled using the GNU compiler (GCC 3.2
with -O2).
For these experiments, we simulated arrays of any size by
“virtual arrays” defined by {{formula:c05e740c-8081-4808-8e4c-7fc55fb9a8d3}} : the function {{formula:8ba1e2f3-2951-4b4c-86a7-53f59becf99f}} 
is chosen arbitrarily and the intent is that the
access time to any one array element is a fixed cost (a calculation
rather than a memory or disk access). Results
are thus less dependent on current disk characteristics than
would be otherwise possible. See section REF  for disk-based
experiments.

For our experiments, array indices were always 64 bits, whereas stored values
are 32-bit floating-point values. Unless otherwise specified,
{{formula:8fcb20de-a6ee-4612-8551-ef4c0e05bda3}} , giving us about 4 GB of virtual-array data;
by “size”, we refer to {{formula:2ef63129-9663-4a76-a9e9-c9b5abfc88b5}} , the number of array elements.
As well, the buffer always fit within main memory
and no paging was observed. We considered several different
values of {{formula:3e64e62c-4219-458f-ab4b-bd6d95d32a94}} : 32, 128, 1024, {{formula:a284a41e-b15f-4f27-bba6-f75cb19a34dd}}  and {{formula:fadb3ff5-eb55-41ad-9ab9-cb4a86646dc5}} . The first three
values imply hierarchical Ola and can be justified
by the ratio of main memory to external memory on current
machines. The last two
values imply one-scale Ola and fit the introduction's
scenario that {{formula:7688d5b9-f881-4ff5-9c26-e324c829a230}}  would be an appropriate internal
buffer size ({{formula:6ee14361-3426-4e97-bc04-17ee3dcd9f73}} ), or fit a scenario where the user
wants whatever gains can be obtained from a tiny buffer.
We chose the value {{formula:3c7a6ea4-5d87-4c64-a1d9-814bc22a58a4}}  as the “typical” value when

quadratically as the number of moments buffered is increased.
For one-scale Ola, queries have two main sources of cost:
first, the cost from computing {{formula:4a274bb5-c2ff-4653-b916-6234d261b2d2}} , where {{formula:009ff456-cde1-4148-a283-94babcfbe674}}  is
piecewise 0 or an {{formula:cb20f462-a264-4622-a538-957ecc7d8d02}} 
degree polynomial, which we evaluate at a cost of {{formula:629ec0e1-ccfd-47da-b50d-2f2824647d08}}  per
point within the range of the query. The expected range of
our queries is long, so this cost is significant. The second
cost of our queries comes from a {{formula:9156bfb2-d7be-4f30-8d40-9d6b0072b76d}}  calculation done
around the range's endpoints. Therefore, for
our small values of {{formula:8280ae66-81fb-460b-bb51-6fee87245aaa}} , the total cost includes
both a large {{formula:9026f43a-adfd-4965-8037-55d311ccd9a4}}  as well as a large linear component. From
a theoretical point of view, however, the growth is {{formula:19d57864-1373-4ad2-b838-f591ba217cae}}  and
is dominated by the endpoint computations.
(See Figures REF  and REF ).
Hence, it might be detrimental to buffer many more moments than we require.
However, the number of moments has no effect on the space complexity,
unlike the bin size, {{formula:902679cf-09f6-4142-abb5-6997931d9e0a}} . Therefore, for large enough arrays, even if
we buffer many moments, the Ola approach will still be
several order of magnitude faster than unbuffered queries.
{{figure:91ebfd35-ee3a-408e-92f7-37c4b1f83ce6}}{{figure:26398709-ace3-493d-86b1-69d79984cab0}}

The Ola approach was not sensitive to the query:
range sums or first moments were measured to take
almost exactly (within 1%) the same time. Therefore,
these results are not plotted.

Based on the theoretical analysis, Ola can
permit huge query speedups, given extreme values for parameters such
as the relative speeds of internal versus external memory,
amount of memory allocated to the buffer, and so forth. However, we
need good speedups for “reasonable” parameters. From our
experiments, it is evident that buffered arrays were considerably
faster, and random queries that averaged about
71.6 s without buffering
could be answered in 0.390 s or
0.00605 s when the 4 GB dataset was
buffered with 128 kB or 32 MB (using N=4). This
corresponds to respective speedups of 184 and 11800. The construction
time of approximately 1500 s
means a total construction+query
break-even is achieved after about 
21 queries.

To update the buffer, we can consider how the buffer was originally
constructed: it was computed from the data source and then, in a
hierarchical manner, buffers were computed from the previous buffer
and stored in place. Recall, for instance, that in the Ola
buffer, values of the second-scale buffer are stored in indices {{formula:804c641a-91fe-465f-aa72-9dd99858e953}} 
whereas the values of the third-scale buffer are stored at {{formula:b15acb50-391a-4651-b203-cea9918ef430}}  and so forth. We define the cells
at scale {{formula:5b257ed9-4150-4f75-b96e-41bfe7d0a580}}  as those having an index divisible by {{formula:7b829a98-7842-4da9-92d4-4e6a5b1d3d81}} , with the
expository convention that “scale 0” refers to entries in the
external array. Our updates propagate changes from smaller scales to
larger scales. (See Algorithm REF .)

To understand the update algorithm acting upon this hierarchical
buffer with in-place storage, it is helpful to consider the
“is computed from” relation between cells, which forms a
directed acyclic graph (dag). Showing each cell at every scale
to which it belongs, coloring (black) the largest scale for each
cell, and focusing only on the
part of the dag that needs to be updated, we obtain
Figure REF .
The black vertices at scale {{formula:915c87a5-6fc3-4fbb-bcb4-4b531017fd8b}}  (for {{formula:c908cbe1-5832-41f6-aa0d-852931d207cb}} ) in the dag correspond to indices

The portion of the dag that is reachable from the changed cell (at

The use of “virtual arrays” in the previous section allowed us to abstract
away from the specific details of current memory-system hardware.
However, one might abuse such simplified models,
thus incorrectly predicting
good practical performance for algorithms that make
irregular and non-local accesses to disk. Nevertheless, our algorithms
for buffer construction and queries tend to have good locality.
For instance, with queries in One-Scale Ola, two consecutive groups of
indices (around either endpoint of the queried range) are accessed.
Experiments to support our claims were derived using memory-mapped
files. Unfortunately, due to our experimental setup (mainly a 32-bit address
space), we were forced to choose a smaller value of
{{formula:4c125912-c3c9-4721-89a0-c0fc012f714c}}  elements, or about
1 GB of data. These experiments were performed
on a computer with 512 MB of RAM, and since much I/O was
anticipated (and observed), we took wall-clock times while the system
ran in single-user mode.

We have seen that Ola can have a

internal buffer, and then adding bins one by one. Indeed, for a given
range query, the Ola algorithms involve many bins at both

This paper has considered bin-buffering algorithms and showed that using
a hierarchical approach, highly scalable algebraic queries were possible
even with a small buffer. Using overlapped bins, we have shown that
we could buffer several local moments simultaneously and use
much less storage than wavelet-based approaches while still supporting
progressive queries and very scalable queries and updates.

In short, we showed that {{formula:beb28896-8869-4852-86b6-6634bb8f6571}}  local moments could be buffered using
only a single real-valued buffer: using bins of a fixed size irrespective
of {{formula:da296d68-b55a-4f67-89d0-27f235a52e9c}} . Other
types of range queries could also be grouped and buffered
efficiently together {{cite:3ef5da4a02bb793893168133bd5a62bb433cc576}}.
By a direct product {{cite:aa49b595a8cf654ccc092582befe47263fd8efa8}}, Hierarchical Bin Buffering
and therefore the Ola approach
can be generalized to the multidimensional case.

Some implementation issues were not addressed. For example,
many forms of buffering using finite-accuracy floating-point numbers
are susceptible to significant numerical errors.

In these last years, consensus, coordination and synchronization problems have been popular subjects in systems and control, motivated by many applications in physics, biology, and engineering. These problems arise in multi-agent systems with the collective objective of reaching agreement about some variables of interest.

In the consensus literature, the emphasis is on the communication constraints rather than on the individual dynamics: the agents exchange information according to a communication graph that is not necessarily complete, nor even symmetric or time-invariant, but, in the absence of communication, the agreement variables usually have no dynamics. It is the exchange of information only that determines the time-evolution of the variables, aiming at asymptotic synchronization to a common value. The convergence of such consensus algorithms has attracted much attention in the recent years. It only requires a weak form of connectivity for the communication graph {{cite:0611b2b233fdc26e63788eca79cf783b27bc1c4b}}, {{cite:dffa2ea9c3c6665ef5522c572c54d2f0cecb647c}}, {{cite:3efacd2980bd04091680e3faf8df0579019de01b}}, {{cite:af976e19cdba38280449a63f2da95808858035c3}}, {{cite:b579dcdf8ffb560897f3d4db97eb65b04429a8a7}}.

In the synchronization literature, the emphasis is on the individual dynamics rather than on the communication limitations: the communication graph is often assumed to be complete (or all-to-all), but in the absence of communication, the time-evolution of the systems' variables can be oscillatory or even chaotic. The system dynamics can be modified through the information exchange, and, as in the consensus problem, the goal of the interconnection is to reach synchronization to a common solution of the individual dynamics {{cite:8e3157379ef855482fcaf37fe9405ef51457a194}}, {{cite:684dc66e7d4a0631af50bd0baaeacb3bded11a07}}, {{cite:f2645858041eedb262e8cf7c96110637549c6792}}, {{cite:a21a35419d06741d5fa243f5c23f57f052b23620}}.

Coordination problems encountered in the engineering world can often be rephrased as consensus or synchronization problems in which both the individual dynamics and the limited communication aspects play an important role. Designing interconnection control laws that can ensure synchronization of relevant variables is therefore a control problem that has attracted quite some attention in the recent years {{cite:3377176d8288814ff87c2dcfec20886d46780b65}}, {{cite:eb37f7114d6e7372c9c8d3c28bb100b08549eba5}}, {{cite:ae1621740a416c2873da35e86d33235d86024dc4}}, {{cite:032e7777248339fbdefded6f736f9ef54ceaf1f0}}, {{cite:fddc190ba04b15335e89d3e7f9f53df5b14d3eec}}.

The present paper deals with a fairly general solution of the synchronization problem in the linear case. Assuming {{formula:736e8374-8f6f-4274-9cc6-d310fe71f3fa}}  identical individual agents dynamics each described by the linear state-space model {{formula:2e1c1824-d387-447b-98b6-5f6625e21191}} , the main result is the construction of a dynamic output feedback controller that ensures exponential synchronization to a solution of the linear system {{formula:11890e3c-ed7f-4568-907c-9bbb4a824b68}}  under the following assumptions: (i) {{formula:7a4cf05b-7fe9-4241-bd9f-c1b2f0d07340}}  has no exponentially unstable mode, (ii) {{formula:69adb29b-ffa1-4408-889e-ae47c6506ba6}}  is stabilizable and {{formula:7ada616a-9eb7-4725-9f61-896962265488}}  is detectable, and (iii) the communication graph is uniformly connected. The result can be interpreted as a generalization of classical consensus algorithms, studied recently, corresponding to the particular case {{formula:b2c34407-09b6-4eb9-8873-58057cc5291b}}  {{cite:0611b2b233fdc26e63788eca79cf783b27bc1c4b}}, {{cite:dffa2ea9c3c6665ef5522c572c54d2f0cecb647c}}. The generalization includes the non-trivial examples of synchronizing harmonic oscillators or chains of integrators.

The proposed dynamic controller structure proposed in this paper differs from the static diffusive coupling often considered in the synchronization literature, which requires more stringent assumptions on the communication graph. For instance, the results in the recent paper {{cite:c1e1ffa3ebab1a8473177d4fd4cce2b7b0e7b4ff}} assume a time-invariant topology.
The paper also provides sufficient conditions for synchronization by static diffusive coupling and illustrates on simple examples that synchronization may fail under diffusive coupling when the stronger assumptions on the communication graph are not satisfied.

The paper is organized as follows. In Section  the
notation used throughout the paper is summarized, some preliminary results are reviewed and the
synchronization problem is introduced and defined. In Section  the linear case is studied when state coupling among the systems is allowed while in Section  the output coupling case is considered. In Section  we extend the main results to discrete-time linear systems and to periodic time-varying linear systems. Finally, in Section , two-dimensional examples are reported to illustrate the role of the proposed dynamic controller in situations where static diffusive coupling fails to achieve synchronization.

For the systems to be synchronized, the control action (that will depend on the coupling) must vanish asymptotically and must force the solutions of the closed-loop systems to asymptotically converge to a common solution of the individual systems. This leads to the formulation of the following problem:

Periodic linear systems, naturally arise in a number of contexts in engineering, physics, and biology {{cite:1acdfe19eab024bdf79bcd595be2be6a379a1598}}. Periodic models are
of large interest also in time-series analysis, economy and
finance, and in all other cases when seasonal phenomena has to
be taken in account.
Furthermore they arise when linearization of a nonlinear system along a periodic solution is analyzed. Therefore it is not difficult to figure out possible applications when synchronization of such models can be of interest.
The results presented in this section follow from the well-known Floquet theory, where the properties of linear periodically time-varying systems are studied via a state transformation into a new coordinate system in which the system matrix becomes time-invariant. The eigenvalues of this matrix are called the characteristic exponents of the original time-varying system matrix. In the following the continuous-time case is analyzed, the discrete-time case follows the same lines and is omitted for the sake of brevity.

In this paper the problem of synchronizing a network of identical linear systems described by the state-space model {{formula:a7e02dba-0c59-4950-b1eb-3578a5ae1f0b}}  under general interconnection topologies has been addressed. A dynamic controller ensuring exponential convergence of the solutions to a synchronized solution of the decoupled systems is provided assuming that (i) {{formula:f8589f9c-0c74-4e77-bd76-f907131ea839}}  has no exponentially unstable mode, (ii) {{formula:3ffec993-9346-4607-a733-ad410a92ac39}}  is stabilizable and {{formula:7d289923-8c74-497a-81af-4b66f95f6eb7}}  is detectable, and (iii) the communication graph is uniformly connected. Stronger conditions are shown to be sufficient (and, to some extent, also necessary) to ensure synchronization with the often considered static diffusive output coupling. The extension of the proposed technique for synchronization of nonlinear systems is the subject of ongoing work.

It is commonly accepted that confinement is due to
condensation of magnetic degrees of freedom. Such a mechanism is
established, both theoretically and via lattice measurements in the
Abelian cases of a pure gauge field in the compact version of the
theory and {{formula:7de494a9-6f29-42f9-9564-0d7fc1eb2f08}}  gauge theory, for an early review
see {{cite:a8427c57dcc17f3ba380152a7ea34d8beb8c0e9a}}. In this case the magnetic degrees of freedom
are in fact the Dirac monopoles.

Moreover on the lattice one observes monopole trajectories
and has to use the polymer approach to field theory, see, e.g. {{cite:6c904e4d8b9ed16df24a2a3bebf030d85d1a5421}},
to describe the monopole properties in the language of the quantum geometry.
In the geometrical language the confining
field configurations are
identified as infinite clusters of 1d defects, or trajectories.
Another Abelian example is the {{formula:561af0a1-bb4e-47f8-bc09-1ec99a5be6bf}}  gauge theory.
In this case the confining configuration is a percolating cluster of surfaces, or vortices.

In the non-Abelian
case For simplicity we consider pure SU(2)
gauge theory, without matter. there is no consensus yet
on the particular choice of the magnetic degrees of freedom.
The general idea is to reduce the non-Abelian degrees of freedom
to the pattern of Abelian theories where the mechanism of confinement is
well understood.
For this purpose one introduces the
so called projected fields:
{{formula:7a67639f-a35c-4ad7-802c-522c192b195b}}

where {{formula:98885a27-a089-4c17-b71a-6f5d8e95796f}}  is an Abelian gauge field, and {{formula:fde84e29-31cb-4ef9-850c-2ff6d9ed80c0}} 
is a {{formula:52c94282-5788-430b-96bd-0e5c0cc0500a}}  gauge field ({{formula:d68a0f22-7050-4b62-9c86-b1d7114de720}}  for links).
The U(1) projections emphasize the role of the monopole trajectories
or 1d defects while {{formula:696e8bd8-96e3-408e-a4cc-c185668ac542}}  projections allow to find center vortices,
or 2d defects The literature on the confinement is vast.
For the purpose of orientation and further references we can mention
reviews in Ref. {{cite:159c892c3d259e3addef7b29d7442a66f3949c31}} and in Ref. {{cite:b10971800f460463446d7990fb0f27b1d5e115f6}} exposing in detail
the {{formula:6da8284f-673a-400c-b667-bbfbe79ae362}}  and {{formula:1ea4e481-05ba-45b9-b5be-cd8704b46c9f}}  projections, respectively..

The projected fields (REF ) are related to the original
Yang-Mills fields in a nonlocal way and
theoretical interpretation of the lattice data is obscured by their use.
It turns impossible to reconstruct configurations
of the original non-Abelian fields {{formula:eb71c80d-8d3e-4cb3-b665-545ab7578d43}} 
which correspond to the monopoles or vortices.
However, it seems indisputable that effectively
Abelian degrees of freedom
are responsible for the confinement.

In this note we will reverse the problem and instead of trying to directly
interpret the lattice data consider classification of
non-Abelian singular fields in the continuum which could be
responsible for violations of the Bianchi identities while not
inducing violations of the color conservation. We argue that a
natural candidate for such defects are singular fields living on
two-dimensional surfaces. The central point is that such fields are
Abelian in nature and, therefore, violations of the Bianchi
identities and of the equations of motion are disentangled.

As far as the mathematical tools are concerned,
we utilize
the so called surface
operators {{cite:c5aa06e43ea80edae0ed2b80599f26c1330c658a}} which describe four-dimensional (4d)
non-Abelian fields living on 2d surfaces.
It is interesting that from the phenomenological
point of view the use of the surface operators suggests a unification
of the two alternative Abelian pictures mentioned above. Namely,
the defects are 2d, as emphasized by the center projections, while
the fields living on them are Abelian, as
commonly emphasized by the {{formula:6b397966-cc25-4b8f-ba32-240d00c2d383}}  projections.

In this paper we are going to make the next step and assume that
surfaces become dynamical and condense in the vacuum in the
confining phase so that there is a net of surfaces endowed with fields living
on them. The picture is similar to condensation of the
Polyakov's lines in
the deconfinement phase.

It is a strong assumption concerning the dynamics of non-Abelian theories
which in no way can be derived from first principles.
Our assumption is motivated by the lattice data
that do demonstrate existence of 2d surfaces
percolating through the vacuum
{{cite:b10971800f460463446d7990fb0f27b1d5e115f6}}, {{cite:52306a6f3f8d2b4ad6d3684e31ae66036b171545}}. For a more theoretically oriented reader
let us mention that holographic models predict
both percolation of the Polyakov's lines in the deconfining phase
and percolation of magnetic strings in the confining phase
{{cite:3dd807e682855f5073210076196a2bf29e5bd9b8}}.

In more detail, we will rely on the Sakai-Sugimoto
holographic model {{cite:031a9b76595f9cc8446145be6afcf324614b2a5b}} which is most successful in describing low-energy QCD.
The metrics of this model is formulated in terms of the ordinary 4d space
{{formula:abaa6c9a-c6d1-4423-983f-e70653979f8a}} , extra fifth dimension {{formula:729ffbf0-365e-4acc-840b-3f29c90696f3}}  with horizon at {{formula:0e4ca899-99e1-40fd-a0e4-e8969e361137}} ,
one more extra compact dimension {{formula:c242ef25-420d-4795-bb6e-e02de4f7fd27}}  and compact sphere {{formula:f6961b18-7cc2-4008-b428-7ba0dc6310c0}} :
{{formula:1e464e2b-3611-463a-9da5-044c9f53fa68}}

It is also crucial that the defects wrapped on the compact dimension {{formula:32e57b61-dc35-4869-bf45-d8bf6657ed71}} 
have non-trivial {{formula:b3b0c40a-fb03-4a47-a21e-3938c13c58b9}} -angle dependence.
Note that the metric in dimensions {{formula:73422054-d901-411f-a3d5-72bc15517e80}}  has a cigar form so that
the radius of the {{formula:22a8c88e-0690-47f0-a3c2-294a1127df9b}}  compact dimension tends to zero at the horizon {{formula:a3c6f7e1-5bd5-4189-a57d-57601a289ecb}} .
Which means that the defects wrapped around this dimension have tension
vanishing at the horizon. In particular, the magnetic strings are defined
as D2 branes wrapped around the {{formula:5a2c8a50-854d-45d1-bd11-b6148aa348ae}}  dimension. They look as strings, or 2d surfaces in
the ordinary 4d space and, in case of large enough area, have vanishing (classically) tension.
Because the D2 branes are wrapped on the compact {{formula:deb551ef-cc20-4888-b201-a4226bd3e739}}  dimension
one expects that they carry density of the topological charge.

The metrics (REF ) refers to the case of zero temperature {{formula:bc01f51f-199b-4bc2-897f-4a17ff79341c}} 
which we are mostly interested in. At finite T it is convenient to
use Euclidean space, with a compact time direction
{{formula:a3c548b6-d6dd-4c50-8f37-1744c7c5c977}} . Thus, at {{formula:ff5e61c3-c07b-478f-8cac-00f3e65b82c8}}  there are two
compact coordinates, {{formula:3eca3bc5-672e-4889-9fe8-f9f5d8296784}}  and {{formula:3e995065-5532-40a5-9881-ffd399a13281}} . The deconfining phase transition
is then understood as change of geometries in two-dimensional {{formula:48d9bc86-c541-4cf9-a628-57bbd196891e}}  and {{formula:14ebe8d4-1250-412f-8c96-0536ecad0255}} 
subspaces. Namely, at {{formula:569ab94d-36f3-47d9-b660-70a9ad2717a0}}  the cigar-shape geometry sets in the {{formula:1ff628ef-8d7c-4de9-995a-13e2b1a5dc7f}} 
coordinates while in the {{formula:51ec74b9-d251-4b97-bb90-587bd4377120}}  coordinates the geometry becomes cylinder-like.
As a result, defects wrapped in (Euclidean) time direction
become tensionless and could condense.
As is argued in {{cite:3dd807e682855f5073210076196a2bf29e5bd9b8}} this is a general phenomenon within the
dual model: below {{formula:22b9e000-dbb0-4131-8bbd-8316ca617c72}}  defects condensed in the vacuum have nontrivial
{{formula:927ba941-4995-4a92-b594-3a703b140775}} -angle dependencies while at {{formula:8658b375-837c-43b7-a66c-8130e6380416}}  it is the defects wrapped on the
compact time direction which are tensionless. The Polyakov line is wrapped
around the time direction and becomes tensionless at {{formula:d195c851-549a-4c63-8eb8-a0f5f7a7e4b0}} 
according to the dual model. This fits well the phenomenological models
which postulate condensate of the Polyakov's lines.
The magnetic D2 branes are wrapped around the compact {{formula:d039201a-c57f-42d0-a6c9-4a586cc62bf1}} 
direction and are tensionless at small temperatures.
They are expected to condense at small T.

The hint which we get from the dual models is that in the Yang-Mills vacuum
there could exist magnetic strings, tensionless. We conclude that their tensionlessness is
to be
manifested as percolation of 2d surfaces, or existence of an infinite
cluster of such vortices. As usual in quantum geometry, the surfaces are to be endowed
with action. Moreover, the vanishing string tension implies action-entropy balance.
Another important prediction of the dual models is that the surfaces are
carrying topological charge density (since the D2 branes are wrapped
around the compact {{formula:38da549b-d1ad-459b-a03e-9d1faaa3c9d9}}  coordinate).

A crucial observation is that the surface operators are an adequate
mathematical tool to consider the magnetic strings because they also
describe 2d surfaces endowed both with action and topological charge.
In this section we will consider further phenomenological consequences
of such identification.

Thus, the center vortices on the lattice do have properties similar
to those inherent to the surfaces discussed in the preceding sections
and based on the surface operators. However, the reader might
feel uncomfortable to discuss confinement in terms of singular fields
(REF ).
Indeed, in the continuum theory one usually discusses non-perturbative physics in Yang-Mills theory in terms of soft fields. On the other hand, the lattice
data reveals that hard fields are associated
with the confinement and this cannot be disregarded. Thus, we have a
paradox.

It is worth emphasizing therefore that it
would be wrong to consider the infrared and ultraviolet sensitive
descriptions as mutually excluding each other.
It is much more adequate to think in terms
of a kind of duality, that the nonperturbative physics can be described
either in infrared or ultraviolet terms. Moreover, one description
probably smoothly goes into the other one as a functions
of resolution of measurements, or of the value of the lattice
spacing {{cite:f76b1a71e86b218ab9f457b8fab669d4c905d2a2}}. The term 'resolution' is used here because
generating each filed configuration on the lattice,

the gauge fields on the whole lattice with resolution of the lattice spacing {{formula:e17c4f4e-f58b-4d7f-a547-739055428efe}} .

Unfortunately,
there is no detailed understanding of the role of the resolution.
Probably, one deals with quite a general phenomenon which
can be called stabilization of classical solutions
with high-frequency oscillating fields. At this time the guess
can be substantiated, however, only by some analogies
and intuitive considerations.
It would be extremely interesting to clarify further these issues
Analytically, interplay between the infrared and ultraviolet sensitive

by the Coulomb-gas model. The constituents are point-like and possess
topological charge equal to {{formula:6edff2e7-240b-4fe3-99ab-a2142b739afd}}  fraction of that of the instanton..

The phenomenon of the shrinking of classical solutions was discovered by the ITEP
lattice group {{cite:9dc61f41e0e270ecbcab4a4cedc035413be7b715}}. However, the classical solutions relevant to this paper belong
to a dual formulation of the Yang-Mills theories and the status of these
solutions is rather vague. The idea to check this phenomenon on the case
of 'instantons', or chiral defects belongs to the
authors of the first paper in Ref. {{cite:2b26d5dd83c3c37cffcf329063cdf08d30fad668}}..

Let us specify the notion of the 'volume occupied by an instanton'.
The definition is provided actually by considering zero- or near-zero fermionic modes.
In the classical instanton case the topological modes are located in the same region of
the 4d space as the instanton itself:
{{formula:6085f135-4a08-409f-8bd7-115f46660c97}}

where {{formula:03f88416-a955-4729-a2f2-7a4a8b31cd1d}}  is a zero mode of the Dirac equation
for a quark in external gluon field:
{{formula:b342c946-3357-40dd-a774-792f7a19b971}}

and to derive (REF ) one substitutes the instanton field for
the external gluon field.

On the lattice, one can solve the Dirac equation numerically
substituting into the covariant derivative {{formula:92a38119-60a6-4839-bf5b-d7e8daab4684}} 
the gluon fields generated on the lattice for a particular
configuration {{formula:7926f893-d8ef-40a3-94d7-27f341439075}} .
Then the volume occupied by the
topological fermionic modes can be understood
as the volume occupied by `instanton modified by high-frequency
perturbative fields'. Lattice data rather support estimate (REF ).

Let us emphasize that the shrinking volume of the instanton
implies also singular fields inside the small region occupied
by the modified instanton.
Indeed, the average value of the topological charge squared,
or topological susceptibility,
{{formula:1d8e9515-6a3b-46cc-a291-115ead4e7645}}

represents a matrix element and its value cannot depend on details of the
measurements, in particular on the value of {{formula:bd22e6ee-90af-4583-a5ec-e3ba06631d14}} . On the other hand,
the value of {{formula:807025d8-a6d9-4864-bb59-ca1a3849140a}}  for each configuration is equal to the number
of exact zero modes of the quarks. Thus, the total topological charge
of configurations cannot depend on the shrinking of each particular
lump of the topological charge.
Hence, the topological fields become singular in the limit
of the vanishing volume of the lumps.

Assuming all this to be correct, what are implications for
interpretation of 2d surfaces? To answer the question
note that in terms of the dual model instantons are D0 branes.
These branes have one extended coordinate which is wrapped around
the {{formula:fdd74291-f191-4bd3-acfe-e74a95db83f5}}  circle. In the geometrical language of the dual models
(REF ) this wrapping is responsible for the non-trivial
topological charge of instantons. To summarize: the instantons
are points in ordinary 4d space, within the defects classification
of the dual models.

On the other hand, in the ordinary field theoretic language
the instantons are rather extended objects of the size of order
{{formula:45fdf7fe-aa86-4cf7-b011-31c5c8a3bdf6}} . Remarkably enough, the shrinking
caused by {{formula:acbd11cd-36ec-4ec7-8a9e-185e8ec58a47}}  just brings an instanton to a point:
{{formula:115696df-6d04-4cbc-8cbf-adc68593436d}}

Thus, one can speculate that in the limit of vanishing lattice
spacing the geometry of the classical solutions becomes
similar to the geometry of the classical solutions
in the dual formulation.

Coming back to our surfaces populated with singular non-Abelian
fields they could well be a high-frequency image of classical
solution of Yang-Mills theory in the dual representation.
This guess cannot be supported however
by any straightforward derivation.

As we have demonstrated above, different approaches to magnetic
degrees of freedom converge to a common and highly non-trivial
picture. In particular, the dual models {{cite:3dd807e682855f5073210076196a2bf29e5bd9b8}}
relate percolation of the magnetic strings to the prediction
that
they should carry density of the topological charge.
The surface operators {{cite:c5aa06e43ea80edae0ed2b80599f26c1330c658a}} provide us with an adequate
construct to describe such surfaces endowed with both gauge fields and their
duals. On the lattice, one does observe percolating surfaces, with tension
in physical units and endowed with topological charge.

In this note we emphasized that the monopole mechanism of
confinement, whatever it means in detail, assumes significant role
to be played by singular non-Abelian fields. Indeed, 'electric'
degrees of freedom are introduced directly in the Lagrangian, while
'magnetic degrees of freedom' are emerging through violations of
Bianchi identities. Hence magnetic degrees of freedom are associated
with singular fields.

The construction is well understood and known since long
{{cite:a44616aff4062335e39e1da9b50099b58cb9124f}} in the Abelian case. One can either start with a
gauge field plus a scalar, Higgs field, or one can start with pure
gauge field but admit singular field configurations, monopoles. Then
these singular fields, or defects can be traded for a scalar field
and one comes back to an effective Higgs-like formulation.

In the non-Abelian case monopoles, or 1d defects do not match the
group structure {{cite:e86ca0cbb7c1500de3def195457c9355a62458b7}}, {{cite:81d53e3a9ed3da25c04c6033b98a5270a6afb4f3}}. Instead, one should look for
classification of singular fields consistent with the non-Abelian
symmetry. As is argued in fact recently {{cite:c5aa06e43ea80edae0ed2b80599f26c1330c658a}} such defects
are 2d dimensional surfaces with non-Abelian fields living on
them. In other words, the surfaces are endowed with densities of
action and of topological charge. We argued that such surfaces can be
profiled by 1d defects, or non-Abelian monopoles, whose field is not
spherically symmetric but rather line-like.

For the defects to become dynamical degrees of freedom there should
be a fine tuning which allows infrared and ultraviolet scales to
coexist. Such fine tuning is well understood in the Abelian case,
(see Eq. (REF )). A central point: for the
dual-superconductor mechanism of confinement to be relevant, similar
fine tuning should be realized in the non-Abelian case as well. This
time, however, it is self-tuning between the action and entropy of
the 2d surfaces. No explicit form of the fine tuning is known
theoretically but coexistence of the two scale is seen in the
lattice simulations.

Also, there should be consistency between dynamics in four
dimensions, or of the original Yang-Mills fields and dynamics on the
defects world-sheet. Let us conclude with an example of such a
consistency check. For dynamics of a particle (or 1d defect) to be
in fact independent on the ultraviolet scale the action associated
with the 'monopoles' should be approximately
{{formula:91b95a3b-bc67-490e-b6cf-f6899af3b929}}

see Eq. (REF ). And this has been checked on the lattice
{{cite:413a26e8015522e476bfb548de5c35df3fa878d4}}. On the other hand, the radiative mass
(REF ) is associated now with the non-Abelian fields
which live not in the bulk but on the world-sheet (see discussion
above). Which seems to be also true on the lattice, for references
and review see {{cite:52306a6f3f8d2b4ad6d3684e31ae66036b171545}}. The condition (REF )
replaces the quantization condition for the magnetic field in case
of the non-Abelian monopoles living on the surfaces.

During the past 25 years, observations from IRAS, ISO,
and Spitzer have revealed substantial mid-infrared (mid-IR)
excesses associated with hundreds of normal main sequence stars
{{cite:cf43306a729232b383e7c9e12239cd3f9d45740f}}, {{cite:b79b5f21f14f75df28c22ae86e1d04c10cf91498}}, {{cite:7616a256c978424eae5a721ae7d84f39a1b29acd}}, {{cite:ec730dc89349d81494e3207e09e0c21833dd1c62}}, {{cite:dbf008377b567affa0c70fe45bee1ba91768a32b}}, {{cite:89cede9eecacb78d37fe78db71104c330a76cd5f}}.
Current samples include stars with spectral types A–M and ages
{{formula:dde1549a-db62-42fd-8a09-c9c56dc21172}}  5 Myr to {{formula:14283171-50e0-404d-9fac-95f25a2ce6d9}}  10 Gyr
{{cite:a7ab1fc600e8c982682ddcfae31274e730c78cf9}}, {{cite:87daa1dd87ac5ad6569201cc934747b38bf7c545}}, {{cite:7616a256c978424eae5a721ae7d84f39a1b29acd}}, {{cite:06b319a8251667a079b756b54b3a0187dc9c6602}}, {{cite:2525102115cb9dd43c3166d92e6bc0f1546c4f25}}, {{cite:a019f913be7084554f448629b81aac10c6a1e37c}}.
Although binary stars and single stars in dense clusters and in
the field are roughly equally likely to have IR excesses
{{cite:be90df349d7073c0fe1a35b13df86e711a90e00e}}, {{cite:2525102115cb9dd43c3166d92e6bc0f1546c4f25}}, {{cite:ec730dc89349d81494e3207e09e0c21833dd1c62}}, {{cite:f386261ca326c28d9edfdc53b6635363a1b69cd6}}, {{cite:4daced9e2431a75a6c0f3c70b4312ea64e4f85a7}}, {{cite:55289bde469aee30a3f039b81beeccf09e62aca3}}, {{cite:1262507c43052f98b618f7852922f316f9ab70c4}}, the frequency
of excess emission declines from {{formula:5856883e-a43d-484d-9a39-121fe3a19b6d}}  30%–40% for A-type stars
{{cite:2525102115cb9dd43c3166d92e6bc0f1546c4f25}} to {{formula:9db96e34-f65b-437b-a3ff-bfa5a78edeac}}  10%–20% for solar-type stars
{{cite:a205301a5c7c83383c1e6dc7ac1e4cd716dd2f75}}, {{cite:e51dbc9f2514de5ee5354ed875037c5d5ca135ba}}, {{cite:a0ee16eec770ec15449df7c87c3ed493097723e4}}. Thus, this phenomenon is common among
main sequence stars and may depend on stellar mass.

High quality images demonstrate that dust orbiting the central star
produces the excesses {{cite:5a84c91c2c6d88a0f3bf5e2c72352cf852586b70}}, {{cite:dcd8209c93902c516d0485e7369780a9e17f22f3}}, {{cite:d8dc66ac61c877c0dde12c89c2500eb4b8c904e9}}, {{cite:43408897f382a527727c3ac3c3a97ba71d60aff9}}, {{cite:40e1b050f3a5b2cf87eb4d45d8abe38bb64c9685}}. In
{{formula:b396624c-ec73-4d00-b2a3-69aa97288b88}}  Pic and AU Mic, the dust is in a geometrically thin, edge-on
disk with an outer radius of {{formula:9c9da195-156d-4bac-8a80-93d6cacb972e}}  200–1000 AU
{{cite:5a84c91c2c6d88a0f3bf5e2c72352cf852586b70}}, {{cite:70c60c72191e8937caa18063afae875ca49a3662}}, {{cite:15dbacdd379823b04b4a94153e404eed9c665bb8}}, {{cite:cbe1dd40ac26b05f794fda4b0660ef9a56310eff}}, {{cite:a1b5268e81eca2143550b45e5b90d1191c78cf59}}, {{cite:b69e9ba806e793decd9b32fd97a1f4a6a4903ef2}}.
In these disks, the small scale height of the dust, {{formula:2a9419af-14a2-4e4f-badf-6ef8cf7e4cf5}}  0.1,
is consistent with material in roughly circular orbits
{{cite:cf43306a729232b383e7c9e12239cd3f9d45740f}}, {{cite:cbe1dd40ac26b05f794fda4b0660ef9a56310eff}}. Although broad
tori of dust are visible in many other systems
{{cite:cfe294ceea3deb0327617079a139cf27e8242c19}}, {{cite:04617380d9a975a297effc04da8e29bde4fa788c}}, {{cite:1eed6f338828e27599061ba6a5db06d94e49a1ab}}, {{cite:6f9a347e5b0668385f5e06fec7af1485a8d2249b}}, {{cite:2525102115cb9dd43c3166d92e6bc0f1546c4f25}}, {{cite:0c9a6e2592ec88211418a707b0587224e481bf41}},
narrow rings of dust produce the emission in {{formula:5d0d340c-f3b9-4d6d-99fe-0f130327ab8c}}  PsA and HR 4796A
{{cite:461c441bdfd15bd1e3d5091da4d192147d956651}}, {{cite:07eb5197b38ad54ae4f666fbfd2dd824e041ee06}}, {{cite:9513cfe809d85e590199ff095584928177722651}}, {{cite:4993f4e11c4d9201abb4c1244784b2564afccc00}}, {{cite:5b3ef2d8d1006e49eb8f4fc5e7d1c0ff6ebe83a8}}.
For systems with face-on rings and tori, the total emission constrains
the scale height, {{formula:cd1e1c0e-f792-4a77-a42c-3c1c5ac8e047}}  0.1. Thus, the dust in these systems is
as highly flattened as the structures in {{formula:27b55cfd-0bf1-439d-97f5-2b873723935a}}  Pic and AU Mic.

Broadband spectral energy distributions constrain the luminosity, size,
temperature, and total mass of the dust {{cite:cf43306a729232b383e7c9e12239cd3f9d45740f}}, {{cite:653761372f88cf73944ba32b5464869e0e2056cd}}, {{cite:0676672210d173951979f430784f4e39f01be1c8}}, {{cite:0c7d188c569a0ed38083b372d37e81e3b648873d}}.
Some stars have excesses from grains plausibly associated with the
terrestrial zone
{{cite:2542f130b3b22d991ba9b5ada612d16aa350754a}}, {{cite:0c6012c7e5ba25800ca5dd6bb25b6680ba0b861b}}, {{cite:7a32c48dda872e4b7bd31f302f80676015fa0e44}}, {{cite:f7a94f0a4512cee1836423bcac3cde0ba380e9ae}}, {{cite:a0ee16eec770ec15449df7c87c3ed493097723e4}}, {{cite:9ccd95703ce60024cfa11a75b6be72664b6d2585}}.
Optically thin emission from cooler material with temperature {{formula:233cbba6-4e90-4284-8fd3-6b116db4a1a4}} 
20–150 K is more typical {{cite:2525102115cb9dd43c3166d92e6bc0f1546c4f25}}, {{cite:e51dbc9f2514de5ee5354ed875037c5d5ca135ba}}, {{cite:a019f913be7084554f448629b81aac10c6a1e37c}}.
For systems with submm observations, the measured fluxes suggest grains
with sizes {{formula:69984796-42d0-4c7a-af03-4c2de8bb845c}}  1 {{formula:4bf9f8b7-fed1-4083-af63-00cc17a951bd}} m–1 cm and total mass {{formula:ba1afa67-c5c7-47f8-a94d-4f51ae21501d}} 
0.01 M{{formula:9360a2d5-1414-40ca-a0cf-3383160866b8}}  {{cite:cc4b91b2785a8ffb94c4c9f8c5551f50623a9ee1}}, {{cite:3e3ce9fd27a3cbc320c08bd6f62f8b145a78b776}}, {{cite:6c6f9ed3cfc11aff1e1ac916314513a5c9ea6ce0}}, {{cite:df32538124c17492f62d6b012841d47463ac8342}}.
The grains have compositions similar to dust in the asteroid belt,
comets, or the trans-Neptunian region of the Solar System
{{cite:a710c434d9fcc212a88febcf4227c280e4c7eaac}}, {{cite:9b51b9820fbbb865cbfe55d9d2170126396996bf}}, {{cite:fde729a4970951c44a64a52fd0a60fb009efe459}}, {{cite:8522896f07d45aa7723acf2997ca1c25443099c7}}.
Because the dust mass in these systems lies between the initial mass
of solids in protostellar disks
{{cite:0b291d4f864487565fc846c94257cb8bacf2e9f3}}, {{cite:f83484ddf4cfa96e8bbff1ab0adf65002df10ffe}}
and the dust mass in the Solar System
{{cite:c42935dfd475bfdae76605035a209a9177a3c7b7}}, {{cite:e939516d1e5c6094b5cc6be7fc8090efbd8101f3}}, {{cite:202bf9b069d246193433a8a97e5b46112fbfcef2}}, the
dusty structures in these systems are often called `debris disks'
{{cite:cf43306a729232b383e7c9e12239cd3f9d45740f}}, {{cite:653761372f88cf73944ba32b5464869e0e2056cd}}.

In addition to the dust properties, several other observations suggest
plausible links between debris disks and the formation of planetary systems.
Observations of A-type stars suggest a `rise and fall' of debris disk
emission {{cite:94dc1f0f8296d6b81fc8ea5b7a3645f46ef6211e}}, with a clear increase in the typical 24 {{formula:b83bc6c5-2da0-4e7e-928f-cd3a300cd01f}} m
excess at 5–10 Myr, a peak at 10–20 Myr, and a decline for {{formula:414d455c-aa6b-4fa0-ae5a-dd1d2ea5bd3f}} 
20–30 Myr. The rise in debris disk emission roughly coincides with the
disappearance of optically thick emission from protostellar disks
{{cite:209cbcd1f3e796d4346f097af3b0d699dac69d38}}, {{cite:0143c8955dee99dac39dbd755ae3d883c1a6669e}}, {{cite:5b84bbf9066ac919d8f41845ccb2297efb9d916f}}, {{cite:4daced9e2431a75a6c0f3c70b4312ea64e4f85a7}}, {{cite:60029fd474aafdeae05123e93b65ad0e127389ab}}.
The broad plateau occurs at a time when radiometric dating
{{cite:41c52061870492aac0cf9ba698d081248a013899}} and theory {{cite:60c67b856b34cdf848c574092a156e8b98c44e3b}}, {{cite:b4821f61d8de2dc75d627ce0a966c0824b1fcb24}} suggest the Earth
contained {{formula:960ea19f-e5a6-4739-a060-61dd3ef214de}}  90% of its final mass. The decline of dusty debris
around A-type stars is at roughly the same time as a gradual decrease
in the cratering rate of objects in the Solar System
{{cite:4d6edd10589042a4d28122cdfc604b28f0fe1b79}}, {{cite:8ee43c0d8ad4ed20f04546e5ec1575c7ec872a55}}, {{cite:5884625556525a5ff720f2e2e6d6a237db8563fb}}, {{cite:add63f0b3279c51a85c99c05c811c2b30411c6fe}}. These results suggest that the evolution
of dust in debris disks parallels the evolution of larger solid objects
in the Solar System.

Simple physical arguments also link debris disks with the formation of
planetary systems. Because radiation removes 1–100 {{formula:b11b6283-d6b1-4cdc-b838-6e0f7563a0cc}} m grains on
timescales shorter than the stellar age, some process replenishes the dust.
To maintain the observed dust masses for long timescales, normal stars
must have a large reservoir, {{formula:77cf2868-6b38-4ac1-87e4-a128dfd98747}}  10–100 M{{formula:d15400fa-7572-4ab7-a590-35fbaa966115}} , of unseen objects
that continuously collide at large velocities and fragment into smaller
objects. Remnant material from planet formation satisfies both needs.
The growth of 1000 km or larger planets in a disk of small grains
naturally leaves behind an ensemble of `leftover' 1–10 km `planetesimals'
on eccentric orbits {{cite:fc5160291733ee42d370c4f84862f4754136455e}}. For a mass of {{formula:2ae474e7-0d13-477f-a901-7398fe489ab1}} 
10–100 M{{formula:fb15b5df-fc8c-4569-a91c-f63a4b92ed75}}  in leftovers, high velocity collisions produce enough
dust for most debris disks {{cite:cf43306a729232b383e7c9e12239cd3f9d45740f}}, {{cite:b79b5f21f14f75df28c22ae86e1d04c10cf91498}}, {{cite:34b2cc4693695ca9f2a682d190e35e7ab035e5d5}}. If this
interpretation is correct, debris disks provide conclusive evidence
for the formation of Pluto-mass or larger planets around many, if not
most, main sequence stars.

In addition to these considerations, numerical calculations suggest that
an evolving swarm of 1–10 km planetesimals explains several observed
trends in the properties of debris disks. Starting with an ensemble
of {{formula:acc9d488-e97a-4a51-8dd4-9bb625af7ee9}}  1 km-sized planetesimals, {{cite:14e2de5560d432886cdae8c099e6341d94636978}}
show that
collisions and mergers form 500–1000 km-sized objects in 1–50 Myr.
These protoplanets stir up leftover planetesimals along their orbits.
Destructive collisions among the leftovers then produce a collisional
cascade – where collisions gradually grind large objects into smaller
ones – along with copious amounts of dust
{{cite:e2ddcac6b5435c1ca57616223bb671c221740bc4}}, {{cite:e819702eaf9e03ebc91c84ec40a6ecf0b89fa575}}, {{cite:1b94d15f6b46fab1d22b618e6905e29327f07583}}. {{cite:01fd6baa67fcb49c44ae8a99c42c24013e2ef90e}}, {{cite:8ed7f500c297ec51416f49b25079f92e18831bf0}}, and
{{cite:076842c186f45f49d0bd121c08d4823fa7e728fa}} show that collisional evolution in a belt of high velocity
planetesimals naturally produces a dust luminosity that declines roughly
inversely with time {{cite:272f0f677d3f961d80f8ef8601d23741427a09ab}}, explaining
the observed time evolution – {{formula:9d750c1a-d981-40b4-b1d1-2e51dc2541ac}} , with {{formula:43f1de0d-77a3-46d1-af99-1cfda878776a}} 
0.5–1 – suggested by recent observations of A-type stars
{{cite:0f39f77a0288f92a281a7d5e9011f09e55a4bc3c}}, {{cite:b79b5f21f14f75df28c22ae86e1d04c10cf91498}}, {{cite:750aa339a832ad97d27ecbe47b1c8dced3f128db}}, {{cite:a205301a5c7c83383c1e6dc7ac1e4cd716dd2f75}}, {{cite:7616a256c978424eae5a721ae7d84f39a1b29acd}}, {{cite:89cede9eecacb78d37fe78db71104c330a76cd5f}}. To account for
the large observed range of IR excesses among stars of similar ages,
{{cite:8ed7f500c297ec51416f49b25079f92e18831bf0}} propose belts with a range of initial masses and semimajor
axes, as suggested from submm observations of protostellar disks
{{cite:f83484ddf4cfa96e8bbff1ab0adf65002df10ffe}}.

Here, we continue to explore the evolution of dusty debris arising from
planet formation in a disk of icy planetesimals. Our suite of calculations
for disks at 30–150 AU around 1–3 M{{formula:44339ba8-2b84-4acf-b7ba-988cf325ed91}}  stars yields robust predictions
for the maximum sizes of icy planets as a function of semimajor axis and
stellar age. Results for the long-term evolution of IR excesses account
for many fundamental aspects of the data. These calculations are the
first to explain the `rise and fall of debris disks' around A-type stars
{{cite:94dc1f0f8296d6b81fc8ea5b7a3645f46ef6211e}} and the apparent peak in the 70–160 {{formula:38ed5bd2-2c02-4f8e-aecb-27fe96257fb4}} m excesses of G-type
stars with ages of {{formula:d95574be-39a8-4f40-91c8-e514c11d693d}}  100 Myr {{cite:a019f913be7084554f448629b81aac10c6a1e37c}}. Comparisons between our
models and current observations suggest that the minimum stable grain size
and the slope of the IR emissivity law are critical parameters.

The models suggest a set of further critical observations. Spatially
resolved images of debris disks around A-type and solar-type stars can
improve our understanding of the minimum stable grain size. Larger
samples of debris disks with high quality submm data from ALMA, Herschel,
and SOFIA can place better constraints on the slope of the emissivity law.
Together, these data can test our predictions for the time evolution
of debris disk emission around 1–3 M{{formula:45d985ff-408a-4d68-9e53-88fd1a231e6b}}  stars and provide input for
more complete calculations that include the formation and dynamical
evolution of giant planets.

We outline our model in §2. We describe results for the formation of
icy planets in §3 and the evolution of debris disks in §4. After
discussing several applications of our calculations in §5, we conclude
with a brief summary in §6.

{{cite:8c63e70eaf872a2de8010a0826e05b4630c96625}} and {{cite:dbd08c168ea882680d2bf1375a891430f3b54119}} describe our hybrid
multiannulus numerical model for planetesimal growth. {{cite:2ee1f5fbb05af202d278638441fba201dd7de042}},
{{cite:8c63e70eaf872a2de8010a0826e05b4630c96625}}, and {{cite:dbd08c168ea882680d2bf1375a891430f3b54119}} compare results with analytical
and numerical calculations. We adopt the {{cite:23e7fce8a7372ed5199433fbed94cad2624ba261}} statistical

To follow the evolution of the most massive objects more accurately, our
code includes an {{formula:a0bf1a4d-ef66-49f7-8fe6-c079d9514c69}} -body algorithm. When objects have masses exceeding
a `promotion mass' {{formula:c188790c-a581-49bf-985c-0838cd45d041}} , we promote them into an {{formula:0d63834e-4b76-4dc6-8ee1-5fa521e7c884}} -body code that
directly solves their orbits. The {{formula:44680dca-a444-4eae-ad2a-1c1a70d2edf1}} -body code incorporates algorithms
to allow collisions among {{formula:b0717fb8-ce77-47bc-8ddb-ed542f5f9209}} -bodies and interactions between {{formula:04a445bd-c7eb-49a4-bd39-ca30cbfbcbed}} -bodies
and coagulation particles. {{cite:dbd08c168ea882680d2bf1375a891430f3b54119}} describe this code in detail.

We begin with a discussion of planet formation in disks at 30–150 AU
around a 1 {{formula:02d9d9f5-7245-4f06-a368-3ffe01e5cf18}}  star. For most disks around low mass stars, the
timescale for planet formation is shorter than the main sequence lifetime.
Thus, the growth of planetesimals into planets and the outcome of the
collisional cascade depend more on the physics of solid objects than on
stellar physics. Here, we review the stages in planet growth and describe
the outcome of the collisional cascade. For a suite of calculations of
planet formation in disks of different masses, we derive basic relations
for the growth time and the maximum planet mass as a function of initial
disk mass. We also show how the dust production rate and the mass in small
objects depend on initial disk mass and time.

The next section compares these results with calculations for
1.5–3 {{formula:1956e6eb-51d2-4242-b22a-62d56f689128}}  stars. For disks around more massive stars, the
planet formation timescale is comparable to the main sequence lifetime.
Thus, the central star evolves off the main sequence before planet
formation and the collisional cascade reach a natural end-state.
During post-main sequence evolution, the star brightens considerably
{{cite:85d9408e2887deb2c74d0b747f81c875fc9f6c1a}} and develops a powerful stellar wind
{{cite:6e32b5736bcdb301835aad81c8255c7f22b81747}},
melting icy objects in the inner disk and ejecting small grains
throughout the disk. Thus, we halt our calculations when the star
evolves off the main sequence. Here, we show how the physics of
main sequence stars changes the results derived for planet formation
around 1 M{{formula:12505ee0-25c8-4d40-9828-2fc6e3a54ba1}}  stars.

The formation of icy planets in the outer regions of a quiescent
planetesimal disk has three distinct stages {{cite:c54ec08340257a17e20f04f578bc10b62c37c958}}, {{cite:fc5160291733ee42d370c4f84862f4754136455e}}.
Planetesimals with {{formula:b1243f33-9d0a-44a0-a742-cdcd30172aef}}  1 km grow slowly. As they grow,
dynamical friction damps {{formula:676e525a-4ca5-4f8f-b7db-7e7a15f60315}}  for the largest objects; dynamical
friction and viscous stirring raise {{formula:555db44a-56ec-422f-846f-21491dbc3de4}}  for the smallest objects
{{cite:2c64bf6c69e65cb2071f345755326f7896f1aad9}}, {{cite:e05b94b0abb0e87284463403d1e211fddb97a564}}, {{cite:aef1150cb2f106ca20f550436c2678018f817763}}. After {{formula:47663270-8efe-4ffc-82e9-e78609e0f5e8}}  0.1–1 Myr,
gravitational focusing enhances the collision cross-sections by
factors of 10–100. Slow, orderly growth ends. Runaway growth begins.
At the inner edge of the disk, the largest objects take {{formula:522f3268-94ec-45c0-8eae-0885f79a613b}}  3 Myr
to grow to {{formula:48e0f3a0-4012-4c3f-bc82-f233e1793988}}  100 km and {{formula:9db14fd2-a64a-4a28-a476-345b853c0cdf}}  30 Myr to grow to {{formula:30cd1731-e719-4ccb-8f79-ebf481f5d89c}}  1000 km.
Throughout runaway growth, the gas disk dissipates. Thus, velocity
damping by gas drag ceases; dynamical friction and viscous stirring
increase {{formula:8949c388-50c9-4769-b13d-5c1df6e4e7a3}}  for the smallest objects. Stirring reduces gravitational
focusing factors, slowing the growth of the largest objects relative to
one another and relative to leftover planetesimals {{cite:73bbdc34943c9d5fef8a698d185f1ef84b96a7c9}}, {{cite:e05b94b0abb0e87284463403d1e211fddb97a564}}.
Runaway growth ends; oligarchic growth begins {{cite:396b02bf59366b0c9bb6df64dcb680dca0c3c04c}}, {{cite:39a0110e85e222f62f0ffbf1c3fb0dc9214e4abb}}, {{cite:c33cd75b4bafd04c8395a8e21ec3ef4fa5647814}}, {{cite:d2b55e89766dd979bb0087bbf11dc00aedfa27e6}}.
After 30–100 Myr, the largest objects – oligarchs – grow slowly
and contain an ever increasing fraction of the remaining mass in the
disk.

During the transition from runaway to oligarchic growth, collisions
start to produce copious amount of dust. Once oligarchs reach sizes
{{formula:70798835-c7e0-4386-b6ed-af2aad186963}}  500 km, collisions between 1–10 km objects produce debris
instead of mergers {{cite:eb5f3eac10b7d22cdae1be704bffa98b7dcbba6f}}. Once
fragmentation begins, continued stirring leads to a collisional
cascade, where leftover planetesimals are ground to dust. For dust
grains with sizes {{formula:a26f6367-64a2-4e91-bee9-b0ffd1b8ac78}}  10 {{formula:1591542e-7d79-4f56-984b-506c6ef66c30}} m,
the collision time is much shorter than the time to remove particles
by gas drag {{cite:1bcfe65f2f9d019c5d6bf5102194a1e2de4a9508}} or by Poynting-Robertson drag {{cite:8920662bb01f946d0044d471e1e44ca1679406ea}}.
Thus, the cascade proceeds to particle sizes {{formula:82cbbd61-257b-40d4-a3af-1151f1e28db0}}  1–10 {{formula:cb3d0ebb-9827-440a-98a1-d19102ff3713}} m,
where radiation pressure removes material on the dynamical time scale
{{cite:8920662bb01f946d0044d471e1e44ca1679406ea}}. Because runaway growth leaves most of the mass in 1–10 km
objects, the collisional cascade effectively removes a significant
fraction of the solid material in the disk.

In our calculations, the collisional cascade limits the size of the largest
objects. Once a few objects have radii {{formula:2e727ac1-a262-4fb3-a5fc-2f448a43c409}}  1000 km, they stir up leftover
planetesimals to the disruption velocity. When the collisional cascade
begins, the timescale for 1 km planetesimals to collide and fragment
into smaller objects is shorter than the timescale for oligarchs to
