stalls at {{formula:8899860d-b474-43a4-8185-5adb97edbac0}}  1000–2000 km ({{formula:1621fa87-3345-4ce2-9aea-393852aa312f}}  0.01–0.02 {{formula:894c9839-1b5a-47ac-b6d4-6a96086bb045}} ).

with {{formula:5fda0432-19fa-4b33-aa12-23e5542b8d5d}}  5000 km ({{formula:2c1a0e3b-f9fd-4b72-b8a4-fe14dc208b97}}  0.1 {{formula:8c352646-247f-479d-8c6b-846dfe1c1c7a}} ), but these objects form

semimajor axes and tend to form in more massive disks.

The large radial variation in the formation time produces dramatic differences
in the mass distribution as a function of semimajor axis (Fig. REF ).
In the inner disk, rapid growth leads to many objects with {{formula:ac0b9251-e23e-4614-b5df-98aca4070c6d}} 
1000 km (Table REF ). With many large objects stirring
the leftover planetesimals in the inner disk, the collisional cascade
removes most of the mass in small objects (Fig. REF , left panel).
In the outer disk, slow growth results in a handful of Pluto-mass
objects. A few large objects cannot stir leftover planetesimals
efficiently. Thus, the collisional cascade is weak and leaves a
substantial amount of mass in 1–10 km planetesimals

The growth of objects as a function of semimajor axis and time is not
sensitive to the size of the model grid (Fig. REF ).

the median radius of the largest object in each annulus is nearly

The results for Eqs.

At all semimajor axes, the collisional cascade converts a large fraction
of the initial mass in solids into small dust grains. Because oligarchs
and leftover planetesimals are unobservable with current techniques,
dust emission provides the sole observational diagnostic of the growth
of icy planets at 30–150 AU around other stars. Here, we describe the
evolution of these small particles and demonstrate that the collisional
cascade is observable.

Two physical processes set the visibility of dust grains in a debris
disk. Once significant fragmentation begins, collisions gradually grind
the fragments to dust. When dust grains are small enough, radiative
processes remove them from the disk. For disks at 30–150 AU, radiation
pressure dominates mass loss for {{formula:06eee8d4-3574-4809-9c44-4a1b8d8763b9}}  1–3 Gyr and removes 65%
to 70% of the total mass loss. Poynting-Robertson drag removes material
at late times and is responsible for 30% to 35% of the total mass loss.
Because the gas density is negligible once the collisional cascade begins,
gas drag is unimportant.

To describe our results, we divide dusty debris into
`large grains' with 1 mm {{formula:599bc23f-4c6c-4e61-a57e-f773ce4dc4fd}}  1 m,
`small grains' with 1 {{formula:a1d332b4-c6f5-4705-a93a-490d4af27dd1}} m {{formula:5af8ff04-7a7f-45ae-b297-d450952ba083}}  1 mm,
and `very small grains' with {{formula:6516576b-fa6d-4f3d-93e9-ffd94a32c28c}}  1 {{formula:6e40b8df-b446-49bf-a3d5-e7fd825f73a3}} m.
Collisions dominate the evolution of large grains at all times.
For {{formula:56773db6-5e53-4cd5-ba6a-a4e1f4e3de34}}  1–3 Gyr, collisions dominate the
evolution of small grains; Poynting-Robertson drag
then removes grains with radii of 1–100 {{formula:030d428c-d7c6-4bb6-95f2-d9d768f45300}} m on Gyr
timescales. Radiation pressure removes very small
grains on the local dynamical timescale. Thus,
radiation pressure produces a `wind' of very small grains
in the disk midplane.

Fig. REF  shows the time evolution of the dust production rate
for very small grains as a function of initial disk mass. At the start
of each calculation, dynamical friction and collisions damp orbital
eccentricities. Thus, collisions produce less and less debris; the
dust production rate declines with time. As oligarchs reach radii of
{{formula:24a2ea19-8e51-49bc-bdda-02237bd86479}}  500 km, they stir leftover planetesimals along their orbits.
Dust production increases. Because oligarchs continue to grow, they

energies rapidly exceed the critical disruption energy; the dust production
rate increases dramatically (Eq. REF –REF ). When oligarchs
start to reach their maximum radii in the inner disk (Eq. (REF )),
the dust production rate peaks. As oligarchs grow at larger and larger
disk radii, the dust production rate slowly declines.

Several features of the collisional cascade set these timescales. Early
in the evolution, the collision timescale for all particle sizes is
smaller than the timescale for Poynting-Robertson drag. Thus, the cascade
erodes small particles until radiation pressure ejects them. As planet
formation propagates out through the disk, collisions produce more and
more small grains. Because the mass in grains is set by a balance between
the collision time, which scales as {{formula:068d6917-ba98-46a8-8818-303f45087886}}  and the local dynamical
time, which scales as {{formula:6702d0ec-b60d-4a4f-9b45-3361eef67a63}} , the timescale to reach the maximum
grain mass is proportional to {{formula:12ece7a8-8483-4912-93b7-f3dbed9740d2}} . As the collision rate declines,
Poynting-Robertson drag starts to remove mass from the disk. This drag
removes smaller particles from the disk more effectively than it removes
large particles. Thus, the mass in small grains peaks before the mass in
larger grains.

These results suggest that the mass in collisional debris is large,
roughly a lunar mass in 0.001–1 mm grains, throughout the lifetime
of a 1 {{formula:0404bd79-c5c3-49cd-9d8e-fac8047ab647}}  star. Although the Solar System has much less dust
{{cite:e939516d1e5c6094b5cc6be7fc8090efbd8101f3}}, {{cite:202bf9b069d246193433a8a97e5b46112fbfcef2}}, these large disk
masses are comparable to the mass in dust grains detected in many
debris disks around other stars {{cite:06b319a8251667a079b756b54b3a0187dc9c6602}}, {{cite:e51dbc9f2514de5ee5354ed875037c5d5ca135ba}}, {{cite:38cab09cd8ea2cb2205789d7fcf4f214d6ae457e}}.
Because our dust production rates are observable, the large range in
dust masses as a function of initial disk mass and time implies a
correspondingly large range in the observable properties of debris
disks, such as the disk luminosity and the IR excess, at fixed
stellar age. Because the dust production rate declines with time,
we expect the disk luminosity and IR excesses to decline with
time. We derive detailed predictions for this evolution in §4
and compare these results with observations in §5.

Stellar evolution is an important feature of icy planet formation
at 30–150 AU. Because the main sequence lifetime
{{cite:7372c9ca185d52967402806b2f4b0507a51968ee}}, {{cite:85d9408e2887deb2c74d0b747f81c875fc9f6c1a}} is more sensitive to stellar mass than the
timescale to produce large icy planets
({{formula:2f3b15f9-490c-430d-af79-7cecd308f203}} ; see below), massive stars evolve off
the main sequence before oligarchic growth and the collisional cascade
remove solid material in the outer disk. After a 1–3 M{{formula:5e4cedc1-9d3a-4790-9067-2ff8828a5bdc}}  star
evolves off the main sequence, it becomes more luminous (as a red giant)
and hotter (as a post-AGB star). During this evolution, icy planetesimals
and planets melt, decreasing collision rates and changing the outcome of
the collisional cascadeWe assume that melting is accompanied
by a loss of volatiles and an increase in the mass density of leftover
planetesimals.. Short main sequence lifetimes of massive stars thus
lead to clear differences in the amount of solid material in large and
small objects in the outer disk.

The evolution of dusty debris in disks around 1.5–3 M{{formula:9c112e56-ae40-4ed2-947c-c28eadbf00d8}}  stars
generally follows the evolution for 1 M{{formula:7e0c8c2e-ffd0-473b-a29a-df5c7db83480}}  stars. As oligarchs
form, stirring leads to a collisional cascade that converts 10 km
and smaller objects into small dust grains. Because planets form
more rapidly around more massive stars, disks around massive stars
produce dust sooner than disks around lower mass stars. In our
calculations, the disk mass scales with the stellar mass. Thus,
disks around massive stars also produce more dust than disks around
lower mass stars. However, massive stars do not live as long as
lower mass stars, preventing the collisional cascade from removing
all of the small objects from the disk (Fig. REF ). Over
the lifetime of the star, disks around lower mass stars form more
dust than disks around more massive stars.

declines with time. As runaway growth ends, there are three distinct
phases in dust production: (i) an exponential rise when runaway

Because planets grow more rapidly around more massive stars, the
exponential growth in dust production occurs first around more
massive stars. The timescale for the onset of dust production
also scales inversely with disk mass; thus, more massive disks
produce dust faster than low mass disks.

Once oligarchs form in the outer disk, the dust production rate declines
rapidly. Stellar evolution sets the duration of this decline. In massive
stars, the short main sequence lifetime halts the evolution before the
collisional cascade depletes the disk of 1–10 km objects. Thus, the
dust production rate declines by roughly an order of magnitude before
the central star evolves off the main sequence. For lower mass stars,
the long main sequence lifetime allows the collisional cascade to
remove some material in the outer disk. Thus, the dust production
rate declines by {{formula:5c96dcb6-c18d-43e5-888a-c7f8c4aef05d}}  two orders of magnitude before the central
star evolves into a red giant. We show in §4 how the long-term
evolution of the dust production rate as a function of stellar mass
produces observable differences in the IR excesses of massive and
low mass stars.

In previous papers, we have described limitations to multiannulus
{{cite:dbd08c168ea882680d2bf1375a891430f3b54119}}, {{cite:8c63e70eaf872a2de8010a0826e05b4630c96625}} and single annulus
{{cite:2ee1f5fbb05af202d278638441fba201dd7de042}} coagulation calculations. Here, we review
how several of these limitations affect results for the simulations
described above.

As long as the statistical assumptions underlying the formalism are
met, coagulation calculations provide a reasonable representation of
real collision evolution
{{cite:5236f64017cd2f1c1db97fb6ec2df7ae8ea463d8}}, {{cite:2c64bf6c69e65cb2071f345755326f7896f1aad9}}, {{cite:dd0e5aa3e6d0aa096049e9843835c0f7712906ba}}, {{cite:a2ed2e2f74c181b1efd0087c9b099d945eb86008}}, {{cite:ef113e1b2a6ed7224b5a09878eac5b9dfb8ee795}}, {{cite:b093907d4a3cb5b9dff5174e7820be0800b942b5}}, {{cite:e05b94b0abb0e87284463403d1e211fddb97a564}}, {{cite:c46d22644756616786816ff8243f85a3ef116ca1}}, {{cite:ce9f8737a1f81a7e452b2d91c706364bba394ee4}}, {{cite:2ee1f5fbb05af202d278638441fba201dd7de042}}, {{cite:33dddbfee7450dac3fbefd374b8812b721c5c482}}.
For calculations at 30–150 AU around 1–3 M{{formula:bbc857ae-465e-439d-b410-ab04ee1aba90}}  stars, the spacing
of mass bins in an annulus and the spacing of annuli in the disk limit
the accuracy of the results. Our standard mass spacing, {{formula:70fc209f-d068-432c-b33c-7b139dface75}} ,
lengthens the evolution time by 10% to 20% relative to more accurate
calculations with {{formula:257ac13a-028c-45b4-bbfb-2acd3023d202}}  1.4 {{cite:2ee1f5fbb05af202d278638441fba201dd7de042}}. The radial resolution, {{formula:50ffe053-2d66-4894-b232-762e76852b57}}  = 0.025, also
lengthens the evolution time. Compared to calculations described in
{{cite:34b2cc4693695ca9f2a682d190e35e7ab035e5d5}}, improvements in our treatment of interactions among
particles in neighboring annuli reduce lags by a factor of two,
from {{formula:120b00dc-7c7d-489a-a616-7bc9090105e7}}  20% to {{formula:08a08372-60a3-413c-84e4-1c539fc1d85f}}  10%. Combining the lags for mass
spacing and radial resolution, our evolution timescales are {{formula:f02c34c8-781d-4e41-b7a2-cfc29235d6dd}} 
20% to 30% longer than the actual evolution times. This lag is
comparable to the dispersion in timescales derived from multiple
calculations with identical starting conditions. Thus, improvements
in resolution are unlikely to alter our results significantly.

The coagulation algorithm begins to break down when (i) a few large objects
contain most of mass in the grid and (ii) the gravity of these objects
dominates the stirring. For {{formula:de496972-ee20-48f7-b907-8c0a20861a01}}  500–1000 km, the largest
objects contain a small fraction of the mass in an annulus; individual
dynamical interactions are much smaller than the Fokker-Planck stirring
rates. Thus, kinetic theory yields good estimates for collisions and
stirring among small objects. As objects grow beyond {{formula:a1b3f2a4-743d-4440-acbd-934d9e415b4a}}  1000 km,
however, both assumptions of our statistical approach begin to fail:
(i) the collisional cascade removes leftover planetesimals, increasing
the fraction of mass in the largest objects and (ii) individual
interactions among the largest objects in an annulus can deflect large
objects into neighboring annuli, raising collision and stirring rates
significantly. With {{formula:ccb963e5-4015-4754-9e03-a9aa4af4e107}}  100–1000 Pluto-mass objects at 30–150 AU
(see Tables REF –REF ), interactions among
the largest objects could play a significant role in the late-time
evolution of our models.

when the radial spacing is {{formula:16f19d8f-e536-415f-b321-abfba3ddd9f7}} , where {{formula:b78121c0-1358-47f4-9bb7-9ab8538fd7c7}} 
is the Hill radius in Eq. (REF ). For planets with mass

0.001 {{formula:8c324fa4-d7b9-49a6-955f-b06c007e000b}} . Thus, dynamical interactions among the largest objects
are inevitable when {{formula:7ee6be6e-9da7-48ac-8c2c-d6a2e8d9940b}}  50–100 in a region with a radial
extent {{formula:5ccf59ee-a9d5-48b1-82ee-26c4823b8a05}}  0.2 {{cite:aef1150cb2f106ca20f550436c2678018f817763}}, {{cite:b4821f61d8de2dc75d627ce0a966c0824b1fcb24}}. Many of our

However, we can infer the outcome from scaling the results of

{{cite:60c67b856b34cdf848c574092a156e8b98c44e3b}}, {{cite:dbd08c168ea882680d2bf1375a891430f3b54119}}, {{cite:b4821f61d8de2dc75d627ce0a966c0824b1fcb24}}. At 0.4–2 AU, dynamical evolution of

This analysis suggests that dynamical interactions between large numbers
of Plutos at 30–150 AU are interesting only for low mass stars. For

needed for Plutos to interact, to collide, and to grow into Mars-mass

the escape velocity of Mars-mass planets exceeds the orbital velocity.
Although dynamical interactions among Mars-mass objects can produce
ejections in these circumstances {{cite:aef1150cb2f106ca20f550436c2678018f817763}}, damping by leftover
planetesimals limits ejections in our simulations.. Although this evolution
leads to some extra stirring of leftover low mass planetesimals, there
are only small changes in the dust production rate and the total mass
in small grains. Thus, dynamical interactions among Plutos have little
impact on our general results.

Fragmentation is another uncertainty in our calculations. We treat
destructive collisions with an energy-scaling algorithm that uses
(i) the ratio of the center of mass collision energy {{formula:a72c823f-0309-45d5-a712-a6d296db9c19}}  to the critical
disruption energy {{formula:a737ef39-54d1-4e42-ae60-af32c5432dd4}}  and (ii) a simple power-law size distribution
to apportion ejected material into lower mass bins. Although the
energy-scaling algorithm yields a reasonable treatment of collisions
in coagulation calculations, the disruption energy {{formula:7665fec6-febb-4530-9217-d7d5bbecb249}}  sets the
strength of the collisional cascade. Large {{formula:19d52339-8264-4ba5-819a-348e869515c9}}  leads to a weak
cascade with little debris; small {{formula:72405822-2093-4296-b25c-386829f7a0df}}  allows a strong cascade
with significant debris. Because {{formula:43c35226-55b1-4177-ac99-1489ea10d9c0}}  and the size distribution
of the ejecta set the amount of material in small grains, we now
discuss how our choices for these input parameters affect our results.

Detailed comparisons of various approaches suggest that the size
distribution of the ejected mass has little impact on our results. For
the large collision rates in our calculations, all methods for dividing
ejected mass among lower mass bins – including dividing the ejected
mass equally among 2–3 lower mass bins – leads to a power-law mass
distribution with a characteristic slope of {{formula:9ac273e5-9b08-4fa6-b0a6-99beba5c16ea}} 
{{cite:13124f594841c33cfad86acbbf44c5cefa2da777}}, {{cite:e2ddcac6b5435c1ca57616223bb671c221740bc4}}. Thus, the adopted mass distribution for the ejecta
is relatively unimportant.

{{formula:987b2e5f-7f0f-488c-ab28-26bb853d84ba}}  erg g{{formula:d7399c1e-2816-4c27-84ea-56eaa0dbea9f}} , the dispersion in dust production rates
near the time of maximum dust production is {{formula:8c871217-41ef-4849-b83b-b4421fb1cc35}}  5% or less for all
disks around 1–3 M{{formula:a5d5f4c3-b66c-4fe5-a136-9169ae7dcef4}}  stars. Although the dispersion in the total mass
in large and small grains is a factor of {{formula:c614b988-0bef-4435-aa76-1b4683e428dc}}  3 during the early
stages of oligarchic growth, the dispersion in dust masses declines
to 10% or less at late times when the dust masses reach their
maximum values {{cite:34b2cc4693695ca9f2a682d190e35e7ab035e5d5}}.

The time variation in dust production rate and total dust mass as a
function of {{formula:14aca404-86c9-4067-b0f9-92ac9708babc}}  has a simple physical origin {{cite:eb5f3eac10b7d22cdae1be704bffa98b7dcbba6f}}.
During runaway and oligarchic growth, the collision energies of small
objects scale with the mass of the largest objects in the grid
{{cite:aef1150cb2f106ca20f550436c2678018f817763}}. Thus, small objects have larger and larger
collision energies {{formula:154a12b1-4a5e-453e-a09c-3eadabc3adf7}}  at later and later evolution times. Because
this feature of the evolution depends only on gravitational stirring,
it is independent of {{formula:4e483782-c75f-4cdd-b832-4d64fdcefff7}} . Throughout the evolution, the mass ejected
in a collision scales with {{formula:644e33e6-9a20-431e-8c05-bb3610233546}}  (Eq. (REF )). Thus,
calculations with small {{formula:6a005558-635a-44ae-9df7-ff29025c2595}}  eject more material at early times
compared to models with large {{formula:78490f8f-6f83-4a4a-833c-ef58d92eae9d}} , leading to a large dispersion
in the dust production rate and total dust masses early in the evolution.
At late times, all calculations produce objects with {{formula:79624fc4-1c3d-4fb6-b01b-eae0f9bd43b8}} 
1500–2000 km. These large objects stir all leftover small planetesimals
to large random velocities, where the collision energies {{formula:22a0f8f5-6029-4b70-9837-683e04d74dd7}} 
for all {{formula:6be33ef1-464f-4a37-bd8d-894e29468815}} . All collisions then lead to copious mass loss, which
eliminates the dispersion in dust production rates and total dust
masses at late times {{cite:34b2cc4693695ca9f2a682d190e35e7ab035e5d5}}.

In addition to the small late-time dispersion in dust production rates
and total dust masses, our results yield negligible differences in the
late-time fractions of mass in large objects ({{formula:89c7bdc7-4ab3-440f-b22e-2fab2fa6427c}}  100 km) as
a function of {{formula:e7a3d338-937b-4d5d-ab92-3f39aec46bd3}} . The median radius of the largest object and the
median number of Pluto mass objects are also independent of {{formula:76926f16-2f6a-4701-beb8-6f19b5c370ec}} .
Thus, our analysis suggests that the fragmentation parameters have a
small impact on observable quantities. For low mass disks at {{formula:e5cb3447-6762-4029-a2fd-08dc948197ea}} 
10 Myr, destructive collisions between planetesimals with small {{formula:14cc662e-49ef-437a-af19-84f1c0418cb7}} 
produce more dust than objects with large {{formula:26eb7ffe-6b26-4ac2-897e-337902331e25}} . Although these
differences are probably large enough to be observable, they disappear
at late times when planets reach their maximum sizes.

Our algorithm for deriving the evolution of small particles with
{{formula:b024f037-799c-48d7-a045-bdf79af75893}}  1 m is a final uncertainty in our calculations. To follow
the evolution of sizes and orbits for large objects in a reasonable amount
of computer time, we do not calculate the evolution of small particles
directly. Instead, we use the known production rate of small particles
from the detailed calculation {{formula:dbaea723-9c31-499e-894d-eb2c0effe6e1}} , an adopted power-law size
distribution, and a simple collision algorithm to evolve the small
particle size distribution with time.

Because we include radiation pressure and Poynting-Robertson drag in this
simple treatment of collisional evolution, our predicted size distributions
consist of three distinct pieces. For particle sizes where the collisional
timescale is shorter than the timescale for Poynting-Robertson drag,
{{formula:c888fc93-ba74-4963-80a3-e1f3f8a13405}} . For very small sizes where radiation pressure ejects
grains, we adopt {{formula:5e3f451f-ee43-41cd-8339-0503dee64d19}}  for grains in a constant velocity
outflowing wind (see the Appendix). For intermediate sizes,
Poynting-Robertson drag can remove grains faster than collisions replenish
them. Thus, the particle number {{formula:7c7c6725-fcd9-4b5b-92d7-591a192438b0}}  0. To conserve mass,
we solve a continuity equation to derive the number density of grains
dominated by Poynting-Robertson drag.

Although our solution for the evolution of small particles is efficient,
it does not consider how fluctuations in the collision and fragmentation
rates might modify the size distribution. {{cite:508f8c1b8f61ed187e32c190898ffa73fc3d4ffb}} note that
size-dependent fluctuations can produce wavy size distributions for
0.1–10 mm particles. In their simulations of the {{formula:f10f1d6a-1c82-45c7-b100-dd0017851236}}  Pic disk,
{{cite:8cf71618f926f5bdc6257a84e6f17f9def7bd376}} derive steady-state size distributions with substantial
deficits of 0.1–10 mm particles compared to a standard {{formula:5d6591d8-c50e-4ec6-b92f-7f952a5d3eac}} 
power-law {{cite:f1a6aad29dc2ee19376a60ceb8b95974b65de4d9}}, {{cite:074ad0d1a62f64edabe5c5d5f60966d9b22249e2}}, {{cite:076842c186f45f49d0bd121c08d4823fa7e728fa}}. If these deficits are
typical, then our algorithm seriously overestimates the mass in small
dust grains and thus the infrared fluxes of debris disks.

To check for this possibility, we computed several models with a simple
version of our multiannulus coagulation code. In these tests, we
extracted a complete disk model near the peak of the collisional cascade,
extended the lower end of the size distribution from {{formula:88df6ce8-3e47-47ae-9eb6-f4caf19c211c}}  = 1 m to
1 {{formula:c268fca8-3323-428b-9d01-05519bc043e3}} m using a power law {{formula:cbb2a2b5-aa16-4ae8-86f3-83ac909efffe}} , and continued the
calculation for {{formula:9b697ef6-c9dc-45d9-ab06-0978a12f1f74}}  100 Myr with collisions and Poynting-Robertson
drag but without our Fokker-Planck velocity evolution. To estimate the
range of errors in our simple algorithm, we varied the power law exponent
for the size distribution, {{formula:4d17264c-1b95-47db-bab7-073d6468015e}}  0.6–1, the power law exponent
for the fragmentation law, {{formula:419c5d5a-52b2-4eb1-97ab-deea820943e6}}  -0.5–0, and the magnitude of
the bulk strength {{formula:b782d25e-59f4-4abd-96a0-d246e8c7c197}}  = 1–{{formula:f53441de-49c9-4d94-8fd7-43bd9d354498}}  erg g{{formula:f57f2fe4-bb13-4954-b2d2-05537958950d}} . For a range of disk
masses around a 2 M{{formula:ddcc394e-5e46-4b7f-8eca-9528e99bf17b}}  star, this approach provides a straightforward
estimate for the accuracy of our results for small particles.

These tests confirm that the simple collision algorithm yields results
reasonably close to more detailed coagulation calculations. For models
with {{formula:fc2f165b-7062-4f19-9761-4f8efa2385f8}}  0, {{formula:7241bf46-1dd8-400f-920a-3c472dba6390}}  {{formula:730afc05-862c-421f-bcad-f070fdc1147f}}  erg g{{formula:752bec52-7be9-43fc-bcb1-d7c745aaf5d8}} , and
{{formula:85348f4d-402d-4b5b-9961-b2fbac1c6b77}}  0.6–1, the derived size distributions are within

with {{formula:8bf4b05d-d9cd-467d-8272-b12a845b85a6}}  0.01–100 mm. Although calculations with

{{formula:cda16d6a-dd64-4584-9895-2b019fb95662}} .

Several features of our calculations combine to minimize wavy size
distributions for small particles in disks at 30–150 AU. Because
icy planet formation is inefficient, the collisional cascade begins
when most of the initial disk mass is in 1–10 km planetesimals.
Fragmentation of the leftovers leads to a very large production
rate of 1 m and smaller objects. Continued fragmentation of these
objects tends to wash out wavy size distributions produced by a
low mass cutoff {{cite:508f8c1b8f61ed187e32c190898ffa73fc3d4ffb}}, {{cite:8cf71618f926f5bdc6257a84e6f17f9def7bd376}}. In our Fokker-Planck treatment
of velocity evolution, leftover planetesimals are also in dynamical
equilibrium with larger protoplanets that are `safe' from fragmentation.
Thus, the dust production rate from the collisional cascade is
well-matched to the dynamical state of the system and tends to
sustain a power-law size distribution for the smallest objects.

Starting with a disk of 1 km planetesimals, icy planet formation at
30–150 AU follows the same path for all 1–3 M{{formula:fc3ada0f-22ae-42f3-b017-0ecf944e2265}}  stars. This
evolution has six main features.

It takes 5–30 Myr for runaway growth to produce an ensemble
of oligarchs with radii of 500–1000 km. Throughout runaway growth,
oligarchs stir up the orbits of leftover planetesimals. Collisions
between leftover planetesimals produce more and more debris.

From {{formula:5564c44b-cec2-416c-b375-f5d2415924c8}}  10 Myr to the main sequence turnoff, planets slowly
grow to a characteristic radius. For a broad range of input parameters,
the maximum size of an icy planet is {{formula:bd85ae24-5109-4b7f-8c86-461f9ea63996}}  1750 km at 30–150 AU.
Because the timescale for planet formation at 100–150 AU is
similar to the main sequence lifetime of a 1–3 M{{formula:05a16ed1-512d-4842-b7d0-628ea51998a7}}  star, the
inner disk contains more 1500–2000 km planets than the outer disk.

As planets grow slowly, a collisional cascade grinds leftover
planetesimals to dust. Early on, radiation pressure ejects the
smallest grains in an outflowing wind. Later, Poynting-Robertson
drag also removes larger grains from the disk. In our calculations,
radiation pressure removes roughly twice as much mass from the
disk as Poynting-Robertson drag. The timescale for the collisional
cascade to remove leftover planetesimals is close to the main sequence
lifetime of the central star. Thus, the cascade removes more material
from the inner disk than from the outer disk.

Icy planet formation is inefficient. In our calculations,
icy planets with radii exceeding 1000 km contain {{formula:511d1208-acf9-4204-bd94-d855433d0302}}  3–4%
of the initial mass in solid material. Objects with radii {{formula:0bccc439-3932-47db-b7eb-f5ccc1a42a37}} 
100–1000 km contain {{formula:35a49d0e-fb99-4c8d-af82-2543877bee45}}  2–3% of the initial mass. Because
short stellar lifetimes limit the growth of planets in the outer
disk, the mass in large objects declines linearly with increasing
distance from the central star. Thus, the inner region of the disk
contains many more Pluto-mass objects than the outer region.

The dust produced by the collisional cascade is observable.
For disks around 1–3 M{{formula:80295743-d8ba-4d36-bf2c-97def046e98c}}  stars, the maximum mass in small dust
grains with radii of 1 {{formula:5e278f59-6e9d-458e-8b41-487f9ed6d8f2}} m to 1 mm is {{formula:e2756beb-2ee7-47c3-9a0e-b43d38e55ff6}}  1–2 lunar masses.
This mass is comparable to the masses derived for the most luminous
debris disks around A-type and G-type stars. The time evolution of
the dust production rate and the mass in small dust grains suggest
the dust luminosity declines with time.

Dusty debris is a signature of the formation of a planetary
system. This debris is present throughout the lifetime of the
central star.

To convert our derived size distributions into observable quantities,
we perform a radiative transfer calculation. For each evolution time
{{formula:d0b7d41f-a1d5-4ae1-8043-1ca0fccfa9d2}} , we derive the luminosity {{formula:3524b852-351d-499b-85ce-bd7d80a461c4}}  and effective temperature
{{formula:26f63e34-3c91-4aad-9ffa-64867ad6914b}}  of the central star from the {{formula:804b21f4-ff00-4911-9ad7-837c35286f98}}  stellar evolution models
{{cite:85d9408e2887deb2c74d0b747f81c875fc9f6c1a}}. We then compute the optical depth {{formula:dcf4745f-9a15-45c0-8adb-c887baccde40}}  of each
annulus in our model grid. The optical depth allows us to derive the
fraction of the stellar luminosity {{formula:8afd12e1-14d2-4722-a6ff-b9c60437b924}}  absorbed by each annulus.
For each grain size in each annulus, we derive an equilibrium grain
temperature {{formula:6cfef060-8bbf-4e5b-823d-53abadac1c8f}}  and an emitted spectrum. Summing the emitted
spectra over {{formula:0ff50d5d-05bc-44f2-8870-a57ab02bcf07}}  and {{formula:9b78a818-757f-4d25-b21a-8bf17d9af1d2}}  yields the predicted spectral energy
distribution (SED) and the total dust luminosity {{formula:aba856cf-a152-4ff3-9244-ffbd37ee1b0a}}  as a function
of time. The Appendix describes this calculation in more detail
{{cite:34b2cc4693695ca9f2a682d190e35e7ab035e5d5}}.

In our calculation of observable quantities, the most important input
parameters are the smallest stable grain size {{formula:4aae1a60-1222-4825-9dad-293daf220591}}  (also known as the
`blowout' radius; see Backman & Paresce 1993) and the slope {{formula:de12a515-78e5-40de-ab02-5af3ffe0adb7}}  of the
emissivity law for small grains. Although several estimates for the
minimum grain size suggest {{formula:10a97eab-c177-4aa0-a9e6-45107f80617d}}  {{formula:6830377e-f4c6-40b7-b539-822e22be5e43}} m
for 1–3 M{{formula:8294f987-16a3-45c8-9e56-1cf811fde033}}  stars {{cite:8920662bb01f946d0044d471e1e44ca1679406ea}}, {{cite:f1b6a33095f1cbb469ed913b1ae77430c8f89476}}, {{cite:cf43306a729232b383e7c9e12239cd3f9d45740f}}, {{cite:598e56bec3054f3b1afdbe9893d0a452809dc46d}}, the
coefficient and the scaling relation are sensitive to the composition,
internal structure, and radiative properties of the grains. Because
observations allow few tests of this relation, we adopt {{formula:109198e7-01b4-457b-82b5-5b8f881eeefb}}  = 1 {{formula:2f25db38-8f06-4704-abc9-cff9d0bffc6e}} m
for all stars. If more luminous stars have larger {{formula:5339962c-5ed5-434d-8322-a726f7a1a9d2}} , our calculations
overestimate the optical depth in small grains. Thus, we overestimate
the mid-IR and submm excesses. For the emissivity, submm data suggest
{{formula:5e505dac-6fa8-4ed0-86de-c8f26eca1467}}  0.6–1 from a handful of debris disks {{cite:3e3ce9fd27a3cbc320c08bd6f62f8b145a78b776}}, {{cite:df32538124c17492f62d6b012841d47463ac8342}}.
To provide some balance for our likely underestimate of {{formula:84614861-f2bf-439d-8b53-3a4381a512aa}} , we adopt
{{formula:81636f0e-2b51-4c62-ae64-d8cd70aa627c}}  = 1. Grains with smaller {{formula:e19c050c-725e-4bdf-8260-e32c3779500e}}  emit more efficiently at longer
wavelengths; our models then underestimate mid-IR and submm excesses.

To describe the evolution of observable quantities with time, we focus on
the dust luminosity {{formula:1110a41c-6aa0-4c5e-8d82-2e443190fc74}}  and the excesses at IR and submm wavelengths.
The fractional dust luminosity {{formula:0718c10c-e805-42f2-8a90-777c57c9fd1e}}  provides a clear measure
of the relative luminosity of the debris disk. For excesses at specific
wavelengths, we quote the total emission of the disk and the central
star relative to the emission from the stellar photosphere,
{{formula:accc5fc9-8ea0-4884-81e3-9f6a2ce13100}} . With this definition, disks that produce
no excess have {{formula:32681082-37f2-4289-aa23-d49d87f2d1ae}}  = 1; disks where the excess
emission is comparable to the emission from the central star have
{{formula:8896c00a-e1f8-4ab1-8eab-f340b43c46c5}}  = 2.

To test whether our predictions provide a reasonable match to observations,
we now consider several applications of our models to real systems. For
these calculations, the broad trends in the evolution of IR excesses and
colors are sensitive to the physics of planet formation and the collisional
cascade. Thus, our main goal is to compare our results with observed trends
of excesses and colors for large samples of main sequence stars observed
with the IRAS, ISO, and Spitzer satellites. In addition
to long-term trends, the absolute level of the excesses depends on {{formula:ddc29f4d-a0aa-4dca-8df7-d2c37ff75892}} 
and {{formula:7bf1dbca-179f-4026-a52d-c258a0712705}} . Thus, our second goal is to learn whether our assumptions yield
mid-IR and submm excesses similar to those observed.

We begin with an analysis of Spitzer data for the prototypical
debris disk, Vega. After demonstrating that our models can explain
the mid-IR fluxes and morphology of Spitzer images for this system,
we show that our predictions provide a good match to observations of
mid-IR excesses for a sample of A-type stars {{cite:7616a256c978424eae5a721ae7d84f39a1b29acd}}, {{cite:2525102115cb9dd43c3166d92e6bc0f1546c4f25}} and
a sample of solar-type stars {{cite:06b319a8251667a079b756b54b3a0187dc9c6602}}, {{cite:a019f913be7084554f448629b81aac10c6a1e37c}}.

Observations of Vega with IRAS first revealed a large excess of
emission above the A-type photosphere for wavelengths exceeding
12 {{formula:379006b2-4d82-4f6f-87ff-acbbc5453b30}} m {{cite:dbb3211ad2094d6064b15564568d67f3f2d4af06}}. The best-fitting single temperature blackbody
to the IRAS data yields a temperature of {{formula:a467142d-f876-46d4-af6d-5610decb2035}}  85 K, a fractional
luminosity of {{formula:6cec5b9a-4d2a-4c4f-8a6f-06ca34a7e9da}}  relative to the central star,
and a radius of {{formula:57bf16ce-6bbe-4d31-9575-8fc2d8dece17}}  150–200 AU for the emitting material. Because
the lifetime for small grains at 150–200 AU is much shorter than the
age of Vega, {{cite:dbb3211ad2094d6064b15564568d67f3f2d4af06}} concluded that the grains have sizes larger
than 1 mm. Thus, Vega provided the first direct evidence for grain
growth outside the Solar System.

Since the {{cite:dbb3211ad2094d6064b15564568d67f3f2d4af06}} discovery, Vega has become the prototypical
debris disk {{cite:cf43306a729232b383e7c9e12239cd3f9d45740f}}, {{cite:91426b5f7cb653a3bdeedae057ae7e7591f7a807}}, {{cite:653761372f88cf73944ba32b5464869e0e2056cd}}. The debris consists of a
bright torus with small-scale clumps at 80–1000 AU from the central star
{{cite:1dd5721d55098821f4312617ecdde86e0e89761c}}, {{cite:a700d67460fa2da1387aff4069c0a49d576ed60c}}, {{cite:a1e8a027d81ad0b5dd45f05ce3d64e46feade213}}, {{cite:f315b3e9036d2b875754223ce57a67f271245c4f}} and a smaller disk of debris at {{formula:979d9972-3760-4d62-94e8-264808dfb25f}} 
1 AU from the central star {{cite:0c6012c7e5ba25800ca5dd6bb25b6680ba0b861b}}. Dust in the small disk is
hot ({{formula:da36443a-7113-4574-8acd-ff2da5350b6f}}  1500 K), luminous ({{formula:62adb6ff-a185-4bfb-af71-6bc223df82eb}}  {{formula:7fdbb5b1-a4cf-46ff-affa-9eacb7204068}} ),
and mostly confined to a narrow ring with a diameter of {{formula:6dbcacd4-fdcb-46f6-8a72-a2a7c48cea01}}  0.5–1 AU
{{cite:0c6012c7e5ba25800ca5dd6bb25b6680ba0b861b}}. This dust might be a result of collisions between larger
objects at 1 AU or grains lost from icy comets at 80–100 AU in the
outer disk.

Recently, {{cite:f315b3e9036d2b875754223ce57a67f271245c4f}} analyzed high quality Spitzer images at
24, 70, and 160 {{formula:f3a5b17d-24aa-42bd-b991-099b918ce17d}} m. Their results demonstrate that the large-scale
debris consists of a bright ring at 80–200 AU and a smooth `halo' that
extends to {{formula:2bc32954-d1a9-40dd-9c35-ac7e008fc913}}  1000 AU at 160 {{formula:be7650df-fcb8-4f01-97ef-2d8d6a1ff784}} m. The halo has an {{formula:6757977b-3250-4025-9506-c663165b71c3}}  radial
density profile, consistent with a wind of small grains ejected by radiation
pressure. Fits to the radial surface brightness profiles and the spectral
energy distribution suggest the grains in the wind have sizes of
1–50 {{formula:c2b056b3-d42f-4a54-a487-f1c7a36da8be}} m and a total mass of
{{formula:08fdab51-4b66-4ce4-80d6-7efd99f3711d}}  M{{formula:752d6222-48a3-44df-986b-70ede3006398}} . The grains in the bright ring
are larger, with typical sizes of {{formula:b1edfadc-2ecb-430b-a7bd-43536c870a2e}}  240 {{formula:fbd778a1-7dbd-466a-8d0f-497001a0962e}} m, and have a total mass
of {{formula:588394b0-1b4a-40d1-87cb-5d1d36533260}}  M{{formula:97ffeaff-5566-4be2-9181-4588c4bd68b7}}  {{cite:4aa9760d4038a71cbaf4c5cbb9b36ebfaba7985e}}.
For an adopted residence
time of {{formula:90e907a8-23b1-4243-8e06-b76069704d06}}  yr in the wind, the mass in small grains implies
that larger grains in the ring produce smaller dust particles at a rate
of {{formula:e4399e4d-7b4d-4b56-8f8f-6bf76de5c1ae}}  g s{{formula:aaf2ef14-4eda-4aa4-aeb0-5b103b15750f}} .

To check whether our model predictions can match the MIPS data for Vega,
we make a simple comparison with median results from several calculations.
In addition to the observed fluxes at 24, 70, 160, and 850 {{formula:311f9d43-5bdb-428b-9ae8-917aebcaf492}} m
{{cite:f315b3e9036d2b875754223ce57a67f271245c4f}}, we adopt published values for the age {{cite:2525102115cb9dd43c3166d92e6bc0f1546c4f25}},
luminosity {{cite:78dbd31ad07073dae58f3d6d2c2081e09e7b1c9b}}, and mass {{cite:78dbd31ad07073dae58f3d6d2c2081e09e7b1c9b}}
of the central star. {{cite:f315b3e9036d2b875754223ce57a67f271245c4f}} separate the observed fluxes into
contributions from the debris disk and the central star. The first
row of Table REF  lists these results, along with their
derived values for the mass in 1–50 {{formula:74ada8d2-1b8b-49ef-8363-7c7971a7bcf7}} m dust grains and the dust
production rate. The rest of Table REF  lists predictions
for four of our debris disk models around 2–2.5 M{{formula:adc69382-ad1b-4cad-9345-0bf53cf30087}}  stars.

The comparison in Table REF  suggests a reasonable match to
the data. Predictions for the total mass in 1–50 {{formula:138cf562-80d9-4775-aafd-a0f6d5fc63cf}} m dust grains
and the fluxes at 160 {{formula:b6d760df-3830-4e85-82b0-913d52974e83}} m and at 850 {{formula:5847b654-7c4d-4552-9a54-811d790a977f}} m bracket the observed

dust emission at 80–130 AU, close to the observed position of the
bright ring inferred from Spitzer images {{cite:f315b3e9036d2b875754223ce57a67f271245c4f}}. The
mass of 0.1–1 mm particles in this ring, {{formula:cffbe149-4079-4d09-b0ba-229ef2cbc91d}}  M{{formula:03b40ed5-f7dc-4f3c-8b99-f435523b5034}} ,
also agrees with the mass in 240 {{formula:bf476a0f-3431-4274-b0b7-18f824778de1}} m grains derived from the
