and at 70 {{formula:e49b5fb2-f7ae-474e-8982-fadc43981457}} m by a factor of 2–10 and underpredict the dust
production rate by a similar factor.

To understand possible origins for the mismatches between the data and
the models, we consider the evolution of small grains in our calculations.
When the collisional cascade starts removing material from the disk, the
most destructive collisions involve grains with comparable masses. These
collisions gradually erode the parent objects and produce modest amounts
of debris in smaller particles. Because (i) the collision timescale is
much shorter than the timescale for Poynting-Robertson drag and (ii) the
ratio of the radiation force to the gravitational force is
{{formula:0af076c0-5fb4-4ee0-b93d-7b7f5334c2c1}} , erosion continues
until particles reach a size {{formula:0057c22a-67b3-4e7a-a009-1b0538693af0}}  where {{formula:c8c013c6-1513-463a-8fba-01d5b1467ed2}}  0.5–1
{{cite:8920662bb01f946d0044d471e1e44ca1679406ea}}. Particles with {{formula:6e840168-ba5b-4571-a872-b8b35f4dad7e}}  are ejected. For simplicity,
we assume {{formula:14d19f4a-0fa7-4a20-a28e-7840717afecb}}  1 {{formula:18adf867-9de4-45ba-b9cd-48cbb36a063c}} m for all of our calculations.

In this picture for the collisional cascade, the {{cite:f315b3e9036d2b875754223ce57a67f271245c4f}} results
provide a simple solution for the overprediction of the 24–70 {{formula:5effc36b-b298-4804-b8ce-afe385bdac37}} m
fluxes in our calculations. If grains with {{formula:4555b94b-9f12-4bc7-83be-ae151324222c}}  1 {{formula:f7109c77-355e-4199-965b-06052389a24e}} m are in
the wind, our `Vega models' underestimate the mass in the wind and
overestimate the mass left behind in the disk. More mass at larger
distances from the central star lowers the optical depth in the inner
disk, reducing the predicted fluxes at short wavelengths. Thus, increasing
our adopted {{formula:8ea6a2ee-f563-4474-a7a4-9acff6a1d455}}  for Vega models should provide a better match between
observed and predicted fluxes at 24 {{formula:2955c1c5-05e3-4ca9-aa80-ed90f324a02e}} m and at 70 {{formula:49317cd3-95cf-4aaf-bcf9-69bf06d821e6}} m. For an adopted
{{formula:5ce8b588-cee5-48ed-873f-f732cb3ee801}}  = 60 L{{formula:0a8e6aed-8e58-48c9-b799-4a4849bbc39f}} , {{cite:cf43306a729232b383e7c9e12239cd3f9d45740f}} estimated {{formula:b161542f-5068-40cb-a26f-4a2273ff41ee}}  = 14 {{formula:65d3afa1-79b5-4598-92f1-b2b11561a35b}} m. Scaling
this result for our adopted {{formula:c0f7933a-7362-4f61-b517-3c0c7e9eea4f}}  = 37 L{{formula:eade0e65-89bc-4d16-97a5-048fd512badc}} , {{formula:af85fb0d-5c56-445a-ade4-32b79860a449}}  8.5 {{formula:5293851c-d3b8-4d89-bdd8-63e57ed29971}} m.
Several test calculations with {{formula:1a3991c9-7f28-44f3-8bb6-4f65fe68a235}}  10 {{formula:47ba24ac-53f3-4d2f-825d-4666ce53241e}} m yield predicted 24 {{formula:02d57df5-c345-4c57-b4d0-b84fa8557cc4}} m
and 70 {{formula:aadaf87b-747c-4a67-b56a-d281e108a1a1}} m fluxes close to the observed values.

Reconciling the estimated dust production rate with our predictions requires
a more rigorous analysis of dust production and ejection in the Vega debris
disk. To derive the dust production rate, {{cite:f315b3e9036d2b875754223ce57a67f271245c4f}} assume that (i) the
240 {{formula:54582b2f-3a97-4a93-bdc9-74982c367c36}} m grains in the bright ring are bound, with {{formula:c39d1e05-38da-4e20-8276-438a4ed77be2}}  0
and residence times {{formula:1b0e4703-b0e9-48e8-885b-92e3714b6071}}  yr, and (ii) the 1–50 {{formula:dc83561b-5185-4ba6-bf81-d599b3cf0f66}} m grains in the
wind are unbound, with {{formula:b42e5a9e-9655-4550-a9d6-4fccd60f97b8}}  1 and residence times {{formula:51fe039b-0fe1-44fb-95a0-cf12bfce8670}}  yr.
If the collisional cascade proceeds as a gradual erosion of larger objects
into smaller objects, however, we expect a more gradual transition from
grains with {{formula:34d4b107-2434-497e-831f-e10a90f93df1}}  0 to grains with {{formula:d4caf1ae-70dd-44b7-bd51-085250346375}}  1
{{cite:8920662bb01f946d0044d471e1e44ca1679406ea}}, {{cite:f1b6a33095f1cbb469ed913b1ae77430c8f89476}}. Allowing the residence time to change
gradually from the bound 240 {{formula:85bfa9ed-8b58-4c99-9299-fc1faece7dee}} m grains to the unbound 1 {{formula:2a011611-c73f-4a69-b00c-c14252d2d3ba}} m grains
provides a way to lower the apparent dust production rate and to resolve
the mismatch between our models and the observations.

To provide an alternate estimate for the residence time of grains in the Vega
disk, we consider the collision times in the ring and the wind. We adopt the
dust masses derived from the Spitzer images ({{formula:a42b2175-82d7-468d-91d8-f8e94cda7711}}  and {{formula:b3ea4904-99e4-42b0-af27-ee3ee1289293}} ) and
a typical particle size {{formula:80310b7b-5a76-420d-a8aa-d06c651fbc44}} . For a ring at {{formula:070efdba-65c6-4889-8750-92310223750d}}  150 AU
with a width
{{formula:acb15bde-4e99-4fc2-a1cc-d91e5df64749}}  50 AU, the collision time for a single grain is
{{formula:05a4c328-16b4-48ba-94fa-33c2765373e2}}

where {{formula:fb8e16d7-2897-46cd-974c-9baa53e9eaa2}}  is the local orbital period in yr {{cite:45f9bbf4b30879e4a92399c97849dfaa69c91d3a}}, {{cite:e05b94b0abb0e87284463403d1e211fddb97a564}}, {{cite:2ee1f5fbb05af202d278638441fba201dd7de042}}.
Collision times in the wind are similar. For {{formula:4ff45029-6720-4d7f-a79f-2267d5fd31ba}}  yr at 150 AU,
the collision times range from {{formula:b8472d27-1d66-41bb-9a19-ea71345fc699}}  {{formula:4cf705eb-c1f6-470c-a1f6-095c643106cd}}  yr for 1 {{formula:3d824353-62a9-4f17-b39c-9777b0ed8889}} m grains to
{{formula:60996467-92c6-4fc1-912d-a8c3c0329038}}  yr for 240 {{formula:a6e4e848-1908-41f9-801e-fdc6c6e7bfe5}} m grains.

If we assume that the residence times are comparable to the collision times,
we can construct a self-consistent picture for the collisional cascade in the
Vega disk. Collisions in the bright ring gradually erode 200–300 {{formula:be25ce87-ad80-4780-ab69-0ecd8c1d2e5f}} m grains
until they reach sizes {{formula:095b2600-dd07-4672-a30d-9c48df2f737e}}  100 {{formula:56c39802-17c9-481b-86aa-c15e25f29a22}} m, when they become incorporated
into the wind. Collisions in the wind gradually erode the smaller grains until
they reach sizes {{formula:d06604f6-a90b-4f3f-9f9a-ccbb7476f3cc}}  1 {{formula:054b908a-7e70-4ec2-b3c4-fb0419cf2255}} m, when they are ejected rapidly from the system.

As long as the 200–300 {{formula:385f8d39-c08e-4caf-b131-74a859b28446}} m grains are replenished from a reservoir of larger
grains, this cascade can remain in a quasi-steady state over the main sequence
lifetime of Vega. The required mass for the reservoir of larger objects is
{{formula:1407b9c8-127f-4e17-ad30-7ec34307d042}}  100–1000 times the current mass in 240 {{formula:4e4406e7-e253-4741-91c1-8ffd83b6b595}} m grains, {{formula:df932b2c-b1ab-45ba-b3e4-5ab314b5d884}} 
1–5 M{{formula:3b443054-485a-4792-8dfb-ec377cc84f5a}} . This mass is small compared to the initial mass of solid
material in a torus at 80–200 AU in a scaled MMSN, {{formula:bd824af7-bd1b-43bb-a7d1-724749f3eb1c}} 
50–100 M{{formula:4b93a7eb-6e55-4910-98e4-55d8086d61e5}}  (Eq. (REF )). Because the optical depth of
this reservoir is small, it produces a small IR excess compared to the
emission from smaller grains.

This picture relies on two features of the collisional cascade. We need an
approximate equivalence in mass between the large grains in the ring and
the small grains in the wind. The {{cite:f315b3e9036d2b875754223ce57a67f271245c4f}} mass estimates support this
feature. We also need a gradual change in grain lifetime from the
{{formula:5084b89f-300d-444c-9c93-7a36e33fa85a}}  yr collision timescale of the large grains to the {{formula:293142d7-7a8f-43e1-8117-4368781f431b}}  yr
dynamical lifetime of the smallest grains. Otherwise, collisions in the
broad torus cannot occur fast enough to maintain the current smooth structure
of the wind for timescales longer than {{formula:2e3aa3d9-8026-4c69-8826-1c5b49115b4e}}  yr. Current
theoretical analyses support this idea {{cite:8920662bb01f946d0044d471e1e44ca1679406ea}}, {{cite:f1b6a33095f1cbb469ed913b1ae77430c8f89476}}, {{cite:f564fb7f08ddc0c4cced5e8938e90c700423165e}}, {{cite:01eb5920499c3b29f7c9ccbff10a852e4f47759b}}.
Numerical simulations of a collisional cascade with a careful treatment
of the interactions between the radiation field and the small grains
could test this proposal in detail {{cite:01eb5920499c3b29f7c9ccbff10a852e4f47759b}}.

We conclude that our calculations provide a reasonable match to observations
of Vega. If we adopt {{formula:7e67dd58-2ed1-4751-ad24-41ba4878598c}}  10 {{formula:6bf12b73-d3f2-4dce-9a75-5a51ceba432c}} m, the data are consistent with a
standard collisional cascade within a broad torus at 80–200 AU. The cascade
feeds an outflowing wind of small grains with sizes 1–50 {{formula:17b9f3f9-250d-41a5-82c7-cf3852a32829}} m. If the grain
lifetime changes smoothly from {{formula:bba150fa-ff0c-4ce8-895c-62ac1351d394}}  yr for large grains to {{formula:2389137d-a6e5-4c83-b7eb-446c52a09a03}} 
{{formula:87441668-286d-451a-ba88-b5724d0ec1a2}}  yr for small grains, the cascade can maintain the wind
indefinitely.

Since the discovery of the Vega debris disk, IRAS, ISO, and
Spitzer observations have revealed debris around dozens of nearby
A-type stars {{cite:cf43306a729232b383e7c9e12239cd3f9d45740f}}, {{cite:653761372f88cf73944ba32b5464869e0e2056cd}}, {{cite:7616a256c978424eae5a721ae7d84f39a1b29acd}}, {{cite:2525102115cb9dd43c3166d92e6bc0f1546c4f25}}. Like Vega, several of these disks
are resolved and thus provide important information on the radial structure
of the dusty disk {{cite:5a84c91c2c6d88a0f3bf5e2c72352cf852586b70}}, {{cite:d8dc66ac61c877c0dde12c89c2500eb4b8c904e9}}, {{cite:43408897f382a527727c3ac3c3a97ba71d60aff9}}, {{cite:40e1b050f3a5b2cf87eb4d45d8abe38bb64c9685}}, {{cite:0bea0952b722f274f2e75eb3e27b39c37d0785b3}}. Although
most A-type stars with debris disks are unresolved, the sample is large
enough to probe the time evolution of debris around 1.5–3 M{{formula:64e0fb06-f57c-49c6-98af-1f2676ad4d12}}  stars.
We now consider whether our calculations can explain this evolution.

To compare our model predictions with observations, we examine data for
nearby A-type stars from {{cite:7616a256c978424eae5a721ae7d84f39a1b29acd}} and {{cite:2525102115cb9dd43c3166d92e6bc0f1546c4f25}}. {{cite:7616a256c978424eae5a721ae7d84f39a1b29acd}}
combined 24–25 {{formula:53b5e380-3d32-4e96-93d2-6a84c9a80458}} m data from IRAS and ISO with new 24 {{formula:5a00182f-9f61-421f-aa87-3c3e884bf74d}} m
photometry from Spitzer to investigate the decay of planetary debris
disks around 266 A-type stars. {{cite:2525102115cb9dd43c3166d92e6bc0f1546c4f25}} analyze a sample of {{formula:f5748875-9fac-4a99-843d-f972ecd11bb5}}  160
A-type stars with high quality 24 {{formula:b5867569-3d2d-4559-9a7c-d34fb65bd6dd}} m and/or 70 {{formula:9a765181-8a62-4fcd-b311-8c3133f377ef}} m data acquired with
MIPS on Spitzer. The combined sample has 319 (160) stars with 24 {{formula:f501c1a7-a3b1-4d69-a20e-cb8be3fa6129}} m
(70 {{formula:1ec6bb38-06e5-4bd4-bc39-1c1f696cc9b3}} m) observations, spectral types B7–A6, and ages 5–850 Myr.
From the {{cite:f2f57484fd5cf362cc32629f03e70bfe1066f1c7}} table of stellar effective temperatures and spectral
types and the {{cite:85d9408e2887deb2c74d0b747f81c875fc9f6c1a}} stellar evolution tracks,
{{formula:e361344b-1dc2-4d70-8946-1482501e2e4a}}  75% ({{formula:a590215c-d3e5-4c0e-93b7-0eb57bbea360}}  85%) of the stars in the {{cite:7616a256c978424eae5a721ae7d84f39a1b29acd}} {{cite:2525102115cb9dd43c3166d92e6bc0f1546c4f25}}
sample have masses of 1.7–2.5 M{{formula:4c569cf6-9fde-49b2-ae84-61b67166b905}} . Thus, we compare these data with
our results for debris disk evolution around 2 M{{formula:cceebe68-98a5-4cef-a25c-edee76f12e52}}  stars.

The observed 24–70 {{formula:5a5a5a39-edc8-4a63-9068-7246de847088}} m excesses of A-type stars show a clear trend
with the age of the star (Fig. REF –REF ). Although
the statistics are poor, the data suggest a rise in the 24 {{formula:07695b49-566c-47e6-b161-7b812022d462}} m excess
at 5–10 Myr. The larger sample of young stars with 70 {{formula:eaa91813-f020-4748-ba74-f2899817e39f}} m excesses
provides better evidence for this rise. At both wavelengths, the excess
has a broad peak for stars with ages of 10–30 Myr. At later times, the
excess declines with time as {{formula:3a0c0824-dd44-4456-9d78-3b18b6137297}}  with {{formula:418d24cd-89f5-47a1-8280-8041c2ee4085}}  0.5–1
{{cite:750aa339a832ad97d27ecbe47b1c8dced3f128db}}, {{cite:a205301a5c7c83383c1e6dc7ac1e4cd716dd2f75}}, {{cite:7616a256c978424eae5a721ae7d84f39a1b29acd}}, {{cite:89cede9eecacb78d37fe78db71104c330a76cd5f}}.

To improve the statistics for 24 {{formula:49ea81a7-1d16-4fa1-b234-94b6d28c1b01}} m excesses around younger stars,
{{cite:94dc1f0f8296d6b81fc8ea5b7a3645f46ef6211e}} added Spitzer data for many young clusters to the
{{cite:7616a256c978424eae5a721ae7d84f39a1b29acd}} sample. This expanded set of data provides unambiguous
evidence for a rise in the typical 24 {{formula:5139fe50-08a7-422c-8afe-2accf04f7552}} m excess at stellar ages of
5–10 Myr and a robust peak in the excess at stellar ages of 10–15 Myr.
As in Fig. REF , the 24 {{formula:4a885b9d-b5f8-4213-b990-8cb0b568759b}} m excesses for this larger sample
of A-type stars decline with age from {{formula:cf0c414f-b72a-4428-bf38-b2461c5661c9}}  20 Myr to 1 Gyr.

In addition to the long-term time evolution of mid-IR excess, the data
also indicate a large range in the 24–70 {{formula:8b063cc4-2088-4a50-9802-eb2591e0c618}} m excess at fixed stellar
age {{cite:7616a256c978424eae5a721ae7d84f39a1b29acd}}, {{cite:20808febd47df27ee05048002245aabf849bfac2}}, {{cite:2525102115cb9dd43c3166d92e6bc0f1546c4f25}}, {{cite:94dc1f0f8296d6b81fc8ea5b7a3645f46ef6211e}}. Although younger stars are more likely
to have mid-IR excesses than older stars, there are many stars without
excesses at every age. For ages {{formula:36aacefe-f995-4ebe-a7f6-9f4d56510e90}}  200 Myr, stars are equally
likely to have any excess between zero and the maximum excess at that
age. As stars age, they are less likely to have an excess close to the
maximum excess at that age. Thus, the dispersion in the excess declines
with time.

Our calculations provide a good match to the time evolution of the
amplitude of the 24–70 {{formula:c2755d72-93e1-4001-aa4f-62546b81f6ce}} m excesses. At both wavelengths, the
models explain the rise in the amplitude at 5–10 Myr, the maximum
at 10–20 Myr, and the slope of the power-law decline at late times.
For models with {{formula:a59e9219-5844-46e2-932e-bce63422e8ba}}  = 1–3, the predicted excesses also agree with
the maximum observed excesses. Although there are a few stars with
excesses larger than the model predictions, more than 99% of the
A stars in this sample have excesses within the range predicted in
our calculations.

Our calculations also provide a natural explanation for a large range in
the observed 24–70 {{formula:c3807c77-8de2-476e-ab0d-7f3fb7289ec9}} m excesses at fixed stellar age. At 70 {{formula:89418697-6f4c-46d6-8ea7-60c6a6994d2a}} m,
the maximum excess is roughly proportional to the initial disk mass (Eq.
(REF )). Thus, a factor of ten range in initial disk masses yields
nearly a factor of ten range in the maximum excess at 70 {{formula:f378ef74-246d-439c-8404-93a9ff1bb44d}} m. For
stars with ages 10–300 Myr, the Spitzer observations suggest a
factor of {{formula:b9d73a52-d28d-4720-ba17-5e0222dbab10}}  100 range in the 70 {{formula:57ebcecd-cc11-4c31-8e04-e5f38082fe45}} m excess. If this range is
set by the initial disk mass, our models suggest initial disk masses
with {{formula:75415ceb-99c9-4b2d-9076-46a5a55b411c}}  = 0.03–3.

Variations in the initial disk radius can also produce a range in
24–70 {{formula:3414fb78-afca-4947-8dd8-3436abe7138c}} m excesses at fixed stellar age (e.g., Fig.
REF ). For 2 M{{formula:319d4191-16b8-4184-93b6-20a8f3ac1f2a}}  stars
with ages {{formula:85d654d2-995e-44ca-9a08-8dda85c2da25}}  400–800 Myr, our results suggest that a factor of
three variation in the outer disk radius (e.g., 50–150 AU) yields
a factor of two (five) variation in the amplitude of the 24 {{formula:ba64d0ca-4533-4a1d-ad5b-c784186952f5}} m
(70 {{formula:b9856485-39e4-4793-bb59-a17a2ef1cc42}} m) excess. Although the observed range in the amplitude of
the 24 {{formula:c9a2db99-5ab6-4b12-9791-e55f669ab7d4}} m excess for older A stars agrees with this prediction,
the range at 70 {{formula:5769314e-25d9-45e6-929b-7ac6111b9bed}} m is much larger. Thus, variations in the initial
disk radius can explain some of the observed range of excesses at
24–70 {{formula:370959da-74d3-4cb3-b8c0-70068b16e168}} m.

Observations of the youngest stars support a large range in initial
disk masses and disk radii. Submillimeter observations of dusty
disks in the nearby Ophiuchus and Taurus-Auriga star-forming regions
indicate a 2–3 ({{formula:77a72b64-26b8-4225-86f7-f6727af58220}}  1) order of magnitude range in the masses (radii)
of disks surrounding young stars with typical ages of {{formula:3d7a365d-39fa-458c-9ba0-f9059f840a09}}  1 Myr
{{cite:479c2c4bffa1058ac3e136a197a64bac3d9472b9}}, {{cite:af5a247ee499606345d973cb26207fa771f08b27}}, {{cite:f83484ddf4cfa96e8bbff1ab0adf65002df10ffe}}. Our models with {{formula:83d14c75-2828-40f4-80de-3fea37858c03}} 
= 3 have disk masses a little smaller than the maximum dust masses
derived from the submillimeter surveys. Thus, the submillimeter data
imply disks with initial masses {{formula:f60df208-a25f-43d0-9f76-f289ebe94855}}  5 and
initial disk radii 50 AU {{formula:d23ca6a0-4cac-4e0a-8f4c-7729b938b7da}}  1000 AU. Disks
with this range of initial masses and outer radii can produce the
range of 24–70 {{formula:26be9ac1-af75-4c78-bf7e-f121ee84f7bb}} m excesses observed around nearby A-type stars.

Variations in the initial surface density distribution can also lead to a
range in the 24–70 {{formula:14e2b06c-5bcd-4e41-8e67-587d54cde59a}} m excess. In our calculations, we adopted a
`standard' surface density relation with {{formula:1bf72690-7459-4bb3-a039-ddfd96133bed}} .
Compared to this model, disks with shallower (steeper) surface density
distributions have relatively more (less) mass at large semimajor axes.
The outer disk has cooler grains than the inner disk; thus, disks
with shallower (steeper) surface density distributions should produce
more (less) flux at longer wavelengths than our standard models.
Because the relative fluxes at 24 {{formula:529c07e7-0615-4750-b1ca-619868bb537b}} m and at 70 {{formula:0b390d0e-31a7-481a-ad95-8f75d93c889d}} m provide
a measure of the relative disk masses at different semimajor axes,
color indices provide a natural measure of the gradient of the surface
density distribution.

Fig. REF  compares the predicted color evolution for disks
around 2 M{{formula:bd37aed1-9843-4b13-9248-4b99ad8f79bb}}  stars with data from {{cite:2525102115cb9dd43c3166d92e6bc0f1546c4f25}}. Although current
observations do not probe the evolution well at 1–10 Myr, disks
have a large color range, [24]–[70] {{formula:f5686245-d619-4a93-aea5-db1b6889f4bf}}  1–3, for stars with
ages {{formula:d1b36413-9cbc-4735-ac37-012856f15a4c}}  10 Myr. For older stars, the data suggest a slow rise
in the maximum color from [24]–[70] {{formula:d05e85cd-d991-4120-b873-5beb2a878f55}}  3 at 10 Myr to [24]–[70]
{{formula:d4c1d4da-8f88-4249-b679-294749d38364}}  3.5 at {{formula:6d3d3d34-ad6d-46e0-893a-4f04d26c20f5}}  100 Myr. After {{formula:00097f30-1cb7-4fb8-bc9d-6c72c751d513}}  300 Myr, the maximum color
declines. For all stars older than {{formula:a17f9339-0c0f-4480-a395-e59de1c5f579}}  100 Myr, the range in color
is {{formula:3b1100c4-770d-4df2-b414-804845c0dee3}}  3–4 mag.

Our models match the observed color evolution. At all ages, the
predicted colors for calculations with {{formula:3b9c3943-f8a3-4adc-b199-7f7787920ea9}}  = 3 provide a clear
upper envelope to the observed colors. The predicted colors also
explain the slow rise in the maximum observed color for stars with
ages of 10–100 Myr. To explain the full range in observed colors
for 100 Myr to 1 Gyr old stars, we require disks with initial masses
{{formula:22a44f0f-5e1d-4495-baaf-ebfb6e641d0d}}  0.01–3. This range is similar to the range required
for the time evolution of the 24 {{formula:006d5d25-7dac-4816-8ed6-0da8e2aefcfb}} m and 70 {{formula:cea457fd-3edd-43b7-a78b-68a63e4527cc}} m excesses.

The good match to the color observations suggests that the typical
initial surface density distribution is reasonably close to our
adopted {{formula:c7bfcb59-0c5e-48b5-b71f-37001127b6d8}} . For disks with shallower gradients,
we expect redder colors at later times. A few stars lie above our
model predictions; however, most stars have bluer colors than models
with {{formula:3cfb979d-867a-4ca1-89a2-943965260586}}  = 3. Thus, few disks in these samples require shallower surface
density distributions. Disks with steeper surface density distributions
can produce stars with blue colors, [24]–[70] {{formula:16a56098-73d8-4edb-b6d7-aec1b09abf3e}}  1, at late times.
A large sample of A-type stars with [70]–[160] colors and spatially
resolved observations of the radial dust distributions of these stars
would provide a constraint on the initial surface density gradient.

Despite our success in matching these observations, other physical
processes may be needed to explain the full diversity of debris disk
properties for A stars with similar ages and luminosities. In their
analysis of the large debris disk surrounding {{formula:e302cb08-c03a-46f5-bffb-013ce99f1393}}  Oph,
{{cite:0bea0952b722f274f2e75eb3e27b39c37d0785b3}} examine a dozen main sequence stars with A0–A3 spectral
types, ages of 150–400 Myr, and fractional disk luminosities
{{formula:ae46aa61-142d-4e1c-b735-e568bf20b9c0}}  {{formula:ec5f74ab-5848-44f7-a2b9-fd5252fb40ae}}  to {{formula:c585e59a-0264-403f-80f7-6e7c33e2d18f}}  {{cite:2525102115cb9dd43c3166d92e6bc0f1546c4f25}}.
Although all of these stars have dust with {{formula:924c5294-241f-4b60-a5e5-7103b215662f}}  50–100 K,
Fomalhaut has a bright torus of dust with weak or negligible emission
from a wind of small grains, Vega has a bright torus with a luminous
wind of small grains, and {{formula:85b31fc0-0845-48ee-9e09-47d42e4220ca}}  Oph has an extended disk
({{formula:0b9e44e1-a571-459e-8136-9b13fdfdab61}}  500 AU) of dust apparently bound to the star. Some
A0–A3 stars have warm inner disks with dust temperatures {{formula:d08fce7b-719b-4121-987a-dc140e3d688e}}  100 K
to {{formula:50c4d32b-d4fb-46c7-bb45-870a5ba3179e}}  200 K; other A stars have no obvious warm dust emission.
{{cite:0bea0952b722f274f2e75eb3e27b39c37d0785b3}} conclude that collisional cascades in disks with a range
of masses and other processes, such as the formation of giant planets
or recent catastrophic collisions, combine to produce the wide range
of observed properties in this sample.

In principle, our models can explain some of this diversity. The
{{cite:0bea0952b722f274f2e75eb3e27b39c37d0785b3}} sample contains A stars with a factor of five range in
{{formula:e6206feb-8f45-4c8a-bcf7-56f26614de8e}} . Thus, these stars probably have a factor of five range
in the blowout radius {{formula:06bc657f-454a-48df-8834-a9f39b48f82b}}  {{cite:f1b6a33095f1cbb469ed913b1ae77430c8f89476}}, {{cite:cf43306a729232b383e7c9e12239cd3f9d45740f}}.
If the protostellar disks around these stars had properties similar
to those observed in Taurus-Auriga {{cite:f83484ddf4cfa96e8bbff1ab0adf65002df10ffe}}, they
probably had a factor of ten range in initial disk mass, a factor
of three range in initial disk radius, and a 50% range in the slope
of the initial surface density distribution. Coupled with a similar
dispersion in initial conditions for the terrestrial zones of these
stars {{cite:f9076c6c754382bffb5455f1f7bcb6d12936b8a9}}, our results suggest that this range in initial
conditions can produce a broad diversity of debris disks. We have
started a suite of calculations to address this issue. Larger samples
of A stars with resolved disks will provide crucial tests of these
calculations.

Other aspects of planet formation are also important. If the cores
of gas giant planets form before their parent stars reach the main
sequence, we expect gas giants at 20–30 AU around 2–3 M{{formula:be4ac311-b322-4bc8-bc09-4db8c213237d}}  stars
{{cite:2b544fa63a595cf44c0cf68f007a9a3ac68b87e6}}. Gas giants rapidly remove debris in the inner
disk and impose structure in the debris beyond 30 AU
{{cite:a700d67460fa2da1387aff4069c0a49d576ed60c}}, {{cite:bf5a67e603190eab07d2a493e837f970a90f9556}}. Because gas giants are common around
evolved A stars {{cite:468fd35ee3f57480691a12be64d2df6ab935af99}}, gas giants probably play a significant
role in the evolution of debris disks around A stars.

Catastrophic collisions may also produce diversity among A star
debris disks {{cite:7a9eeeba261a83efbda4d5b3ff188b0db08f512c}}, {{cite:f315b3e9036d2b875754223ce57a67f271245c4f}}. Although debris from
complete disruption of colliding planetesimals is unobservable in
our simulations {{cite:f9076c6c754382bffb5455f1f7bcb6d12936b8a9}}, dynamical events similar
to those that produced the Late Heavy Bombardment in the Solar
System probably are visible {{cite:9eb2167708e87d78482ec8ba5f3f02b568c5445e}}. Testing this
idea requires numerical calculations that link the dynamics of
massive planets with the collisional evolution of smaller objects
{{cite:d348ed003b899f9c1950ecc5a70436a8315803bd}}, {{cite:b4821f61d8de2dc75d627ce0a966c0824b1fcb24}}.

We conclude that our debris disk models can explain the overall time
evolution of the IR excesses and IR colors of A-type main sequence
stars at 24 {{formula:71a1c506-e69a-48c1-ab81-f2a0c7349c90}} m and at 70 {{formula:83424398-e843-4418-a91d-9e62630895ff}} m. Our calculations for disks
with {{formula:296770b1-339b-432d-a1f3-f0e3add28158}}  = 1/3 to 3 around 2 M{{formula:0b8c36f0-8f9e-4cd7-b851-fb4e5bd316fc}}  stars fit the overall level of
the excesses and the trends with stellar age. Explaining the full range
of observed IR excesses and IR colors requires a set of disks with
{{formula:a0776708-cfb4-4080-ab16-2cbe69f79704}}  = 0.01–3, as suggested from observations of disks around the
youngest stars. Matching other properties of these stars – including
the relative amount of emission from a warm inner disk, an outflowing
wind of small grains, and a large outer disk – requires calculations
that include a broader range of initial disk radii and gas giant and
terrestrial planet formation at {{formula:173f1210-622f-433b-8f71-e3bf45edcc88}}  30 AU
{{cite:f9076c6c754382bffb5455f1f7bcb6d12936b8a9}}, {{cite:d2b55e89766dd979bb0087bbf11dc00aedfa27e6}}, {{cite:2b544fa63a595cf44c0cf68f007a9a3ac68b87e6}}, {{cite:761587f88ae86288986a126706c64c4520f57d4e}}, {{cite:094550e1f7c926f98aa827f9d7ce252291d1bdab}}.

Although most of the debris disks discovered with IRAS and ISO
have A-type central stars, a few have F-type or G-type central stars
with masses of 1–1.5 M{{formula:286eb28c-2961-4705-a940-10797996424e}}  {{cite:cf43306a729232b383e7c9e12239cd3f9d45740f}}, {{cite:653761372f88cf73944ba32b5464869e0e2056cd}}, {{cite:750aa339a832ad97d27ecbe47b1c8dced3f128db}}, {{cite:35f92704a46f88ff86c81103bb17a9125e1416df}}, {{cite:89cede9eecacb78d37fe78db71104c330a76cd5f}}. More
recent Spitzer observations reveal debris disks around many
solar-type stars {{cite:ec730dc89349d81494e3207e09e0c21833dd1c62}}, {{cite:06b319a8251667a079b756b54b3a0187dc9c6602}}, {{cite:884754eee3d5af011bade93680e5a1758390cf33}}, {{cite:e51dbc9f2514de5ee5354ed875037c5d5ca135ba}}, {{cite:a019f913be7084554f448629b81aac10c6a1e37c}}. Although
several Spitzer programs concentrate on older solar-type stars
as preparation for detailed planet searches, the range of ages is
large enough to provide an initial test of our predictions.

To compare our model predictions with observations, we consider data for
nearby solar-type stars from {{cite:06b319a8251667a079b756b54b3a0187dc9c6602}} and {{cite:a019f913be7084554f448629b81aac10c6a1e37c}}. {{cite:06b319a8251667a079b756b54b3a0187dc9c6602}}
observed {{formula:318ad78d-fa43-49c0-8506-ba7a62fb3da8}}  80 solar-type stars at 24 {{formula:c4c5a8d6-1100-4607-a63c-7011a581adb7}} m and at 70 {{formula:329d3e4d-50bb-4caf-a053-e942d676a0c4}} m using
MIPS on Spitzer. {{cite:a019f913be7084554f448629b81aac10c6a1e37c}} analyze {{formula:d595e4eb-2034-416e-a15b-e74d4651793c}}  30 stars with 70 {{formula:ffdd195b-ddb8-4ffd-a160-e8f5a1daacb7}} m
excesses out of a sample of 328 stars from the Spitzer Legacy Science
Program, “Formation and Evolution of Planetary Systems” {{cite:884754eee3d5af011bade93680e5a1758390cf33}}.
After eliminating K-type and M-type stars from the {{cite:06b319a8251667a079b756b54b3a0187dc9c6602}} study,
the two programs contain {{formula:15b4ccec-c65d-4b6b-8f51-738fb77d686a}}  80 stars with ages of {{formula:15fadcc6-5093-4127-9e3a-b9bf4316b8bb}}  10 Myr to
{{formula:09419b3b-2286-4e53-914b-89d4fc7b1eb5}}  10 Gyr. Most of these stars have masses of 0.8–1.5 M{{formula:5837b918-9512-4cc1-a9d1-5749edd72a5c}} . Thus,
we compare these data with our results for debris disk evolution around
1 M{{formula:7e712ab7-fde2-4c7b-9666-ac0ca13c52e0}}  stars.

The observed 70–160 {{formula:afb81f25-5bc2-42ae-81e0-ed57c1dbb6fa}} m excesses of solar-type stars show trends similar
to those observed in the evolution of A-type stars at 24–70 {{formula:89d58132-8cd7-4bcc-9a05-7915d4440595}} m
(Fig. REF –REF ). Although the statistics for solar-type
stars are poor for the youngest stars, the data suggest a rise in the
70–160 {{formula:804a6e2f-035a-4d75-88df-dfeba8f219ba}} m excess at 10–100 Myr. The maximum in the 70 {{formula:fcf53d99-7091-443d-b24a-736bb84fd281}} m excess
is comparable in magnitude but a factor of {{formula:09799a81-7a6d-4423-88dc-debc4d2c4917}}  10 later in time than
the maximum 70 {{formula:f15ded76-ae9f-48e1-bf2f-1f242f9de2ac}} m excess for A-type stars. At 70 {{formula:bf990d98-15c4-4028-8150-82c28472f27c}} m and at
160 {{formula:9a7da7a5-40b0-47b2-85ae-b1e0a95fbdd8}} m, the excess follows a roughly power-law decline with time
for older stars. Solar-type stars also have a large range in excess at
all ages, with {{formula:13227e03-2233-4db2-a971-802f8c8e22b5}}  1–300 at 100 Myr and
{{formula:5d47faaf-d106-4574-a364-8b394258e8f4}}  1–30 at 1–3 Gyr. For stars with similar
ages, the range in the 70 {{formula:d1f721f6-5e03-40c2-ac45-560db8ac14ea}} m excess is larger for solar-type stars
than for A-type stars.

Our models match the observed trends for the IR excesses of solar-type
stars. At 70 {{formula:20a78d15-8833-4abd-8846-0768ef7eea00}} m, 65%–75% of the observations lie within model
predictions; at 160 {{formula:bd43d4dc-fe35-4400-aea3-6079c6cd969b}} m, more than half of the observations are
within model predictions. For a range of initial disk masses
({{formula:457c59c8-a1da-4ea8-9a46-1db31502c875}}  0.01–3) and outer radii ({{formula:80c87230-5724-4eb2-82dd-14f70d1c9c22}}  70–150 AU),
we predict a large range of excesses at all ages, as observed. These
model also explain the larger 70 {{formula:30caae5c-9aac-44cb-af7f-5c4caf3e91ab}} m excesses observed for solar-type
stars relative to A-type stars, the apparent maximum in the 70–160 {{formula:9135ee3d-ce76-4a13-a625-e7183d7fddc0}} m
excess at 30–100 Myr, and the general power-law decline in the excess
flux for the oldest stars.

Despite this general success, however, the models underpredict the
largest observed excesses. At 70 {{formula:a51176ad-1098-43b3-976d-a2d0d64c3326}} m, the brightest disks are a
factor of 5–10 brighter than disks with {{formula:583809b9-1c1b-437a-aa13-3a9b8867bc4c}}  = 3. At 160 {{formula:17e6cef2-4d37-420e-95ac-6bebd876ac4b}} m,
the brightest systems are 3–5 times brighter than our most luminous
disks. Although the sample of 160 {{formula:35232dc2-02f0-4562-974c-e1144fa6e69f}} m sources is small, our models
underpredict the largest observed fluxes at all ages.

Changing two assumptions in our models yields a better match to the
observed fluxes at 70–160 {{formula:dc38e261-c6ca-41cc-b3e6-57e0afe656b9}} m. For realistic grain properties,
{{cite:8920662bb01f946d0044d471e1e44ca1679406ea}} show that radiation pressure from the Sun cannot eject
small grains from the Solar System. Reducing the minimum stable grain
size from {{formula:a5c13dc2-e137-42ae-a816-15ea3fad9ee0}}  = 1 {{formula:71da86e5-88a2-4599-b2a3-a39652c3a7ca}} m to {{formula:8bbf33c0-a330-428c-8fd8-b0a6c6117dd5}}  = 0.1 {{formula:c1eb08be-e2bf-4e57-8c0c-60b7f3c311b3}} m increases our
predicted 70 {{formula:815233c6-e60e-4aa6-b449-77a1bd034dd7}} m (160 {{formula:74373bb0-ed58-4ec0-8627-914ede641a04}} m) fluxes by a factor of 2–3 (1.5–2).
Submm observations of several debris disks imply {{formula:1b33bbf8-39dd-4ef4-81d2-4b9761c1b258}}  0.6–1
for the slope of the radiative emissivity. If we adopt {{formula:a58bccc8-89b2-4238-9725-87b2eff8295e}} 
instead of {{formula:6181dd9e-e272-4b52-a7c1-eb414be15e63}} , our predicted 70–160 {{formula:204d50a7-abbd-47c9-a868-b991daa637d9}} m fluxes increase
by factors of 2–4. Combining these two modifications increase our
predicted fluxes by a factor of {{formula:72a9783c-d308-4ae7-bf60-c542c3b2a59a}}  5–10 at both wavelengths.

Several observations could check whether these modifications of
our standard model are reasonable.
By analogy with the Spitzer Vega data, detection of an outflowing
wind of small grains in a debris disk around a solar-type star provides
a clean measurement of {{formula:486a7101-dab2-45d7-ba76-cd90eefac297}}  and a better constraint on our predicted IR
excesses. Measurements of {{formula:022ff50b-df85-46b9-9978-3dbfc11152e9}}  for larger samples of debris disks allows
a better assessment of our assumptions for the grain emissivity.

Our calculations provide a robust picture for the formation of planets
and debris disks from a disk of icy planetesimals and set the context
for the evolution of dusty debris in a dynamic system of planets.
The results of this study provide a framework for interpreting
existing observations of debris disks around 1–3 M{{formula:b1573ab5-8002-421e-acac-efd562bb9f45}}  stars and
suggest new observational tests of this picture.

We describe a suite of numerical calculations of planets growing
from ensembles of icy planetesimals at 30–150 AU in disks around
1–3 M{{formula:2bd41325-a0ed-4593-bb68-0b4e49046a9f}}  stars. Using our hybrid multiannulus coagulation code,
we solve for the evolution of sizes and orbits of objects with
radii of {{formula:ac8eb2e6-5502-420c-bff4-fcf33f75d905}}  1 m to {{formula:048eb70b-a8d0-4dce-ac3c-971994582629}}  1000 km over the main sequence
lifetime of the central star. These results allow us to constrain
the growth of planets as a function of disk mass, stellar mass, and
semimajor axis.

Debris disk formation is coincident with the formation of a planetary
system. All calculations of icy planet formation at 30–150 AU lead
to a collisional cascade which produces copious amounts of dust on
timescales of 5–30 Myr. This dust is observable throughout the
lifetime of the central star. Because we consider a broad range of
input parameters, we derive the time evolution of (i) dust produced
in the collisional cascade and (ii) the IR and submm emission from
this dust as a function of disk mass, stellar mass, and time.

We divide the rest of this section into
(i) theoretical considerations,
(ii) observable consequences, and
(iii) observational tests.
The theoretical considerations build on the highlights of icy planet
formation in §3.4. Observable consequences of the calculations
follow from the discussion in §4. The observational tests of
the models are described in §5.

Icy planet formation at 30–150 AU is self-limiting. Starting with
a swarm of {{formula:17ee6e8d-b686-47e2-80a5-a51b564dfe6b}}  1 km planetesimals, runaway growth produces a set
of 100–500 km protoplanets. As the protoplanets grow, they stir up
leftover planetesimals along their orbits. When the leftovers reach high
{{formula:22c992c9-bbd7-4296-b731-f2e942c62db7}} , collisions produce debris instead of mergers. Because protoplanets
cannot accrete leftovers rapidly, a cascade of destructive collisions
grinds the leftovers to dust. Poynting-Robertson drag and radiation
pressure then remove the dust from the disk.

The maximum sizes of icy planets at 30–150 AU are remarkably
independent of initial disk mass, stellar mass, and stellar age.
For disks with {{formula:addb1fda-d1b4-4d80-a030-c73e75731f19}}  = 1/3 to 3 around 1–3 M{{formula:84c97804-acab-4216-911d-1d24ac994313}}  stars with ages
{{formula:c725bc59-2981-419b-bfaa-0a3ac991d4bb}} , the typical planet has {{formula:483b5100-4c4a-49e2-b48a-e1d1eff64730}}  1750 km
and {{formula:09bc50ff-ba4b-43df-b143-acf7421f42ef}}  M{{formula:a33908dd-b171-4769-a184-7091b4e6c654}} . These objects contain {{formula:9cdbcfa1-0259-420b-ac05-6cd94f020f76}} 
3%–4% of the initial disk mass. Although
this result is also independent of the fragmentation parameters, the
finite main sequence lifetimes of 1–3 M{{formula:200a46df-edd7-45ad-b889-36a9d624d8f7}}  stars limits the formation
of many large planets in the outer disk. Thus, the inner disk produces
many more Pluto-mass planets than the outer disk (Tables REF 
and REF ).

For stars close to the main sequence turnoff, stellar lifetimes and
the collisional cascade limit the mass in solid objects at 30–150 AU.
In the inner disk, the collisional cascade removes most of the leftover
planetesimals before the central star evolves off the main sequence.
Thus, the typical mass in small objects is {{formula:b90b10bf-b3a8-47c8-8b4a-470d58500aee}}  10% of the initial
mass at 30–40 AU. In the outer disk, smaller collision rates produce
a slower cascade. Thus, the central star evolves off the main sequence
with {{formula:133f76dd-be89-4d6e-bfc2-f7c7938a28c7}}  50% of the initial mass remaining in 1–10 km planetesimals
at 125–150 AU.

The collisional cascade produces copious amounts of dust. Dust
begins to form during the transition from runaway to oligarchic growth
({{formula:66304f80-5c97-412b-a3ae-0fb366c90cf7}}  = 5–10 Myr), peaks when the first objects reach their maximum sizes
({{formula:882a64f9-d39f-45c8-9322-6154f50f9ebb}}  = 10–30 Myr), and then slowly declines {{formula:54916113-dc9d-4d5e-8748-c9ddc20c7bb1}}  30–50 Myr).
The peak mass in 0.001–1 mm (0.001–1 m) particles is {{formula:5d0c1b05-ae81-4323-a725-b87013a066e9}}  1–2 lunar
masses ({{formula:a2efcb2c-4526-4cbe-9b8b-b35ad5e6ab31}}  1 M{{formula:e7c56ae2-b1d1-42ce-ba6c-e3b18fa85d2f}} ). Disks with initial masses {{formula:6ea4f7ab-2dc4-42f8-b228-99ccaecdba88}}  = 1/3 to 3
reach these peak masses when the age of the star is {{formula:c101ce24-4c94-4404-87a7-c8fe9e4e8167}}  10% to 20%
of its main sequence lifetime. Because the timescale to form dust
is short ({{formula:a1565077-fccd-4429-bdcb-8f9bec20b56a}}  10–20 Myr), stars are surrounded by large disks
of debris at 30–150 AU throughout their main sequence lifetimes.

Radiative processes remove large amounts of mass from debris disks.
Radiation pressure produces a radial wind of small particles containing
{{formula:8fccc830-a834-45e1-91d0-ade3538e63a4}}  60% to 70% of the mass removed from the disk. Poynting-Robertson
drag pulls the rest of the lost mass into the inner disk. Because radiation
pressure is more important than Poynting-Robertson drag when collision rates
are large, we expect more wind (inner disk) emission earlier (later) in
the evolution.

We derive clear observational consequences of the collisional cascade.

The dusty debris from the collisional cascade is directly
observable. For disks around 1–3 M{{formula:ab83091d-d12a-49cb-a60e-719368020858}}  stars, the maximum fractional
dust luminosity of {{formula:d9c7b618-55ee-4507-9f47-c3556da4ee95}}  is comparable
to the maximum dust luminosities of known debris disks
{{cite:cf43306a729232b383e7c9e12239cd3f9d45740f}}, {{cite:7616a256c978424eae5a721ae7d84f39a1b29acd}}, {{cite:2525102115cb9dd43c3166d92e6bc0f1546c4f25}}, {{cite:89cede9eecacb78d37fe78db71104c330a76cd5f}}. The dust temperature at the inner edge of
a 30–150 AU disk scales with the temperature of the central star;
thus, the predicted 24 {{formula:0ac5433b-1ff0-4c77-a04d-71e07ac48baf}} m excess is very sensitive to the stellar
mass. At 70 {{formula:698aad9c-cef3-49a9-a107-e123a03dd09b}} m, the predicted excesses scale roughly linearly
with disk mass and stellar mass. The predicted 160–850 {{formula:8131b520-a16d-4461-9e43-8df9c7a58aa1}} m excesses
depend on the disk mass but are nearly independent of the stellar mass.

For systems with little or no emission from terrestrial dust
([5.8]–[8] {{formula:94f37b1d-fee5-40e9-b5ba-7c1a4b562567}}  0.1), mid-IR color-color diagrams clearly
distinguish debris disks around stars of different masses. In a
[8]–[24] vs [24]–[70] diagram, 2–3 M{{formula:916abaca-2ee0-40a0-9f55-835006fa8574}}  (1–2 M{{formula:49782c46-5f53-4f3d-a675-66c2991e1086}} )
stars have red (blue) [8]–[24] and blue (red) [24]–[70]
(Fig REF ). In both cases, the color scales with the
initial disk mass (Fig REF ). Optical colors and spectra
generally provide good estimates for stellar mass; thus, these
diagrams provide good tests of our model predictions.

We compare our predictions with observations of A-type stars and
solar-type stars.

For A-type stars, our calculations are the first to explain the
observed rise and fall of debris disk fluxes at 24 {{formula:9da87747-e257-45d2-ab41-48dc3942cf4c}} m
{{cite:94dc1f0f8296d6b81fc8ea5b7a3645f46ef6211e}}, {{cite:510f5d7dcd2fd7a8c64e27949bc196e3406db98e}}. In our picture, the rise
in debris disk emission corresponds to the transition from runaway
growth – when mergers of small planetesimals produce larger
protoplanets – to oligarchic growth – when the collisional cascade
begins to grind leftover planetesimals into dust. When oligarchs in
the inner disk are close to their maximum sizes of {{formula:6992d0b4-da9c-4f8d-a5da-157d0af83e7d}}  1750 km,
the collisional cascade produces a maximum in debris disk emission.
For a wide range of initial conditions, this maximum occurs at 10–20 Myr.
As the collisional cascade moves out through the disk, smaller collision
rates produce less dust which emits at lower temperatures. Thus, the
24 {{formula:b5bd1c75-04fc-4dfd-b314-4a463f2ca92c}} m excess falls with time. The predicted rate of decline,
{{formula:0fd97998-3ce2-4b19-b299-ecbf876c3f72}}  with {{formula:e4bbaf5f-6c87-4dfb-8a14-e4e5c401323f}}  0.6–0.8, is close to the observed rate
{{cite:a205301a5c7c83383c1e6dc7ac1e4cd716dd2f75}}, {{cite:7616a256c978424eae5a721ae7d84f39a1b29acd}}, {{cite:89cede9eecacb78d37fe78db71104c330a76cd5f}}.

At longer wavelengths, the maximum excess is larger and lasts
longer than at 24 {{formula:0a61378e-c2bb-4e13-8fc3-a9205ee6db95}} m. Predicted mid-IR colors also increase
slowly with time. Although larger samples of A-type stars with 8 {{formula:bd332d8d-19cc-4dc9-b125-0e0b39b6e7c9}} m
photometry would provide a better test of our models, current data
for the 70 {{formula:c6fe9164-2ddd-405b-864f-45ece2a1d793}} m excess and the evolution of the [24]–[70] color
agree with our predictions (Fig. REF –REF ). For
2–3 M{{formula:f996dd26-d5a1-4e1e-a0f7-0c2a9f81d162}}  stars near the main-sequence turnoff, our calculations
also yield a clear maximum in the 850 {{formula:32aab7f7-2357-424e-9489-2555087d3d76}} m flux. Large surveys, such
as the proposed JCMT Legacy Survey {{cite:84794352958bd76c21e5ffd5b48f42322cbcbb82}} and submm observations
with ALMA, Herschel and SOFIA, can test this prediction.

For solar-type stars, our models match observations of most sources.
The predicted evolution of the 70–160 {{formula:1c3346e6-dc53-4c73-bcfc-d67e37fb7e09}} m excesses follows the
observed rise at 10–100 Myr, the peak at {{formula:1c68dd2d-df96-4224-92ea-38e63e1247ac}}  30–100 Myr, and
the decline at {{formula:e623643c-9f61-44c9-988a-439befcd89e3}}  300 Myr. Although {{formula:8a76a253-f7a1-4008-a6c1-e8fd1e20bd3e}}  70% (55%) of
observed debris disks have fluxes that lie within model predictions,
our models underpredict fluxes for the brightest sources by a factor of
5–10. Fluxes for models with {{formula:c02ee5e6-2524-41af-84e5-43cc516bee11}}  0.1 {{formula:e68918b1-6854-4bc4-aaac-c19310b9f010}} m and {{formula:3f7c00e3-cfc5-4e88-a4db-7795c6ae2284}} 
0.7 provide better matches to these observations. To guide our choices
for {{formula:5876ad0d-6824-4302-aa56-06d90d0b8a7a}}  and {{formula:364e1220-1e42-4bbe-a59a-6dd1af9e69e9}} , we require spatially resolved images and submm
fluxes for these objects.

For 1–3 M{{formula:5127f37a-27fc-4052-a6a4-f6f8d16e5524}}  stars with ages {{formula:5c4495df-e9a4-4360-8afa-a3d1ab4e7e35}}  0.1–1 Gyr, current data
suggest that solar-type stars have a larger range of far-IR excesses
than A-type stars. In our models, faster debris disk evolution around
A-type stars produces a smaller dispersion in far-IR excesses and
colors for stars with ages of 100 Myr to 1 Gyr. Larger samples of
debris disks can test this prediction in more detail.

We also consider observations of Vega, the prototypical debris disk.
If we adopt models with a blowout radius {{formula:aa8b57f7-dde0-4463-9ad6-1f7286c315ea}}  = 10 {{formula:732965bc-b770-4cdc-a89a-7487366c9b31}} m, we can
match observations
with a standard collisional cascade within a broad torus at 80–200 AU.
If the torus contains {{formula:f9da35c2-9887-466b-ad77-eab2895c1e44}}  1–5 M{{formula:41ae142e-73c4-4cdf-8e4d-ac5de72db6b7}}  in large objects with
{{formula:080edea5-6772-4b8b-b61e-f269f2b704b1}}  1 cm, the cascade can generate (i) the observed ensemble
of grains with {{formula:3b789106-0687-41b5-b6a8-f4b4d46296ff}}  200–300 {{formula:16aa1c9f-1788-4698-a43c-1c46b5d59a7e}} m within the torus and (ii) an
outflowing wind of small grains with {{formula:52c6cd0d-3c09-4ccc-bb1f-db9492a4b168}}  1–50 {{formula:975d41c7-e232-4d0b-97da-2351bfb6a19f}} m.
This conclusion differs from {{cite:2525102115cb9dd43c3166d92e6bc0f1546c4f25}}, who postulate a recent
catastrophic collision between two large objects as the source of
the dusty Vega wind. Although the complete destruction of two large
icy objects can produce a massive outflowing wind, our results
suggest that the dusty wind is short-lived and cannot be rapidly
replenished by the observed population of larger objects. We show
that a steady-state collisional cascade can explain the Spitzer
data {{cite:f9076c6c754382bffb5455f1f7bcb6d12936b8a9}}. If our interpretation is correct,
sensitive observations at 1–10 mm should detect our proposed
reservoir of larger objects.

Matching other observations of debris disks requires more realism in our
planet formation calculations. Adding binary companions and giant planets
provides ways to modify the evolution of the collisional cascade and
to impose structure on rings and tori {{cite:a700d67460fa2da1387aff4069c0a49d576ed60c}}, {{cite:bf5a67e603190eab07d2a493e837f970a90f9556}}, {{cite:cf8b411b2438f5b1dbd88022403251d7beb549f2}}.
Extending the coagulation calculations to smaller sizes allows studies
of the formation of winds and other large structures. Although these
calculations have been prohibitively expensive in computing time, rapid
advances in computing technology will make these additions possible in
the next few years.

Based on the results described here and in {{cite:34b2cc4693695ca9f2a682d190e35e7ab035e5d5}}, we conclude
that debris disks are the inevitable outcome of icy planet formation
in a disk of solid objects. The basic structures produced by this
model – broad tori and narrow rings of dust that propagate out
through the disk {{cite:34b2cc4693695ca9f2a682d190e35e7ab035e5d5}} – are consistent with observations
{{cite:461c441bdfd15bd1e3d5091da4d192147d956651}}, {{cite:43408897f382a527727c3ac3c3a97ba71d60aff9}}, {{cite:2525102115cb9dd43c3166d92e6bc0f1546c4f25}}, {{cite:0c9a6e2592ec88211418a707b0587224e481bf41}}. The model also explains the
time evolution of mid-IR colors and fluxes for debris disks around
A-type and solar-type stars.

Resource metadata plays a pivotal role in the functionality and interoperability of digital information repositories. However, in spite of its value, high quality metadata is difficult to come by {{cite:6c4b8a74af1efebffecff7faf0a4f8d4b3acabe7}}. {{cite:58d4cd3ff2e747b878c1f7b90b53e0d13b1ccedc}} demonstrates that although as many as 15 possible metadata properties can theoretically be included in the widely used Dublin Core standardThe Dublin Core 1.1 specification is available at: http://dublincore.org/documents/1999/07/02/dces/, few are frequently used in collections whose metadata are generally created by the author's themselvesThe most frequently used are creator, identifier, title, date, and type.. The problem of poor and incomplete metadata is expected to worsen as repositories are applied to materials collected beyond the traditional, centralized methods of publication and start to obtain data from web pages, blogs, personal multimedia collections, and collaborative tagging environments.

Metadata is a costly resource to create, maintain, and/or recover manually. There has therefore been significant research on automated metadata generation (e.g. by extracting metadata from the content of resources). Natural language processing {{cite:48a920401084ed18d7eff6a0f5d04a0d588258f3}} and document image analysis techniques {{cite:95d64b6dbedc607b4eb226fbe41952dfdd2db1cd}}, {{cite:79dca905080ff4219b9d29335aed632645180f5b}}, {{cite:addb8a052498155708a7d1f7c2159195ab1e4847}}, {{cite:58ef1e38042992ffe9cba17c2d998f2cf5ba3b28}} may extract keywords, subject categories, author, and citations (e.g. CiteSeerCiteSeer available at: http://citeseer.ist.psu.edu/) from manuscripts. Furthermore, in {{cite:8c6b1c1adda288b30af5a8776d81cd580ca59645}}, two metadata generators are demonstrated that successfully harvest and extract metadata from existing resource source and content. Such content-based techniques are much less efficient for multimedia resources, e.g. video, music, images, and datasets. Reliable content analysis for such data is still an active research area and existing methods generally yield little content-related metadata. In addition, content-based approaches can be prohibitively expensive in computational terms {{cite:d911c31d06da6306902c107e5c9116b637217d93}}.

For the reasons outlined above, methods for the generation of metadata that do not rely on resource content have generated considerable interest. The recent growth in applications of “folksonomies" (i.e. community-based “tagging" {{cite:b2cc8b495b7c2fdc76ea5155c5a4f751577766d2}}, {{cite:4578dbb90ea24ba470a5172012076f43cce212d8}}), has been, to some extent, inspired by the shortcomings of existing metadata generation methods. Unfortunately, human tagging only works well in situations where the number of participants greatly exceeds the number of resources to be tagged and where there is no requirement for controlled vocabularies or standardized metadata formats.

In this article, we propose a system for automated metadata generation that starts from a common scenario: a heterogeneous repository contains resources for which varying degrees of metadata are available. Some resources have been imbued with rich, vetted metadata, whereas others have not. However, if it can be assumed that resources that are “similar" (e.g. similar in publication venue, authorship, date, citations, etc.) are more likely to have shared metadata, then the problem of metadata generation can be reformulated as one of extrapolating metadata from metadata-rich to related, but metadata-poor resources. This article's experiment focuses on identifying which aspects of metadata similarity are best used to extrapolate resource metadata in a bibliographic dataset.

As a case in point, {{cite:6dc91b96bcb1697c0ed28c884a7af1ce81959611}} describes a method to support the annotation of personal photograph collections. Once a user has annotated a photograph its metadata is automatically transferred to photographs taken at similar times and locations. For example, a user photographs a group of friends at 3:45PM. Another photograph is made at 3:47PM. Since the second photograph was taken only two minutes after the first, it is likely that it depicts a similar scene. The system therefore transfers metadata from photograph 1 to photograph 2. Similarly, {{cite:f96588c612f1bed2194798449dc8144a60a0c085}} proposes a method of web page metadata propagation using co-citation networks. The general idea is that if two web pages cite other web pages in common, then the probability that they share similar metadata is higher. The user can later correct and augment any transferred metadata.

The mentioned systems are strongly related to collaborative filtering {{cite:b0c2087fbbb87953fc561d384b7554ff610779ea}}. Collaborative filtering systems are commonly employed in online retail systems to recommend items of interest to individual users. Using the principle that similar users are more likely to appreciate similar items, users are recommended items that are missing from their profiles but occur in the profiles of similar users. The collaborative filtering process can thus be regarded as an instance of metadata propagation. If users are considered resources and their profiles are considered “resource metadata", it can be said that collaborative filtering systems “recommend" metadata from one resource to another based on resource similarity.

A generalization of the above metadata propagation systems can be made in terms of the following elements:

A mechanism to generate resource relations, i.e. assess their similarity.

The determination of a metadata-rich subset of the repository's collection that can serve as a reference set.

A means of propagating metadata from the metadata-rich reference set to a metadata-poor subset of the collection using the established resource relations as a substrate.

Such systems for the generation of metadata can be said to operate on a “Robin Hood" principle; they take from metadata-rich resources and give to metadata-poor resources, with the exception that metadata is not a zero-sum resource. This mode of operation has a number of desirable properties. First, it reduces the need for the costly generation of metadata; metadata is automatically extrapolated from an existing metadata-rich reference collection to a metadata-poor subset. Second, resource relations can be defined independent of content and metadata extrapolation can thus be implemented for wide range of heterogeneous resources, e.g. audio, video, and images.

This article outlines a proposal for a metadata propagation system designed for scholarly repositories that takes advantage of the multiple means by which two resources can be related (e.g. co-citation, citation, co-author, co-keyword, etc.). Figure REF  presents the outline of the proposed system's components and processing stages. First, resource metadata is extracted from the collection of a repository. Second, an associative multi-relational network (i.e. a directed labeled graph) of resource relations is derived from a subset of the available metadata. Third, a metadata-rich subset of the collection is selected to serve as a reference data set. Fourth, and finally, metadata is propagated (i.e. extrapolated) from the metadata-rich reference set to all other metadata-poor resources over the associative network of resources after which the repository is updated. Human validation can vet the results of the metadata extrapolation before insertion into the repository occurs.
{{figure:0dcafde9-177b-4c70-94ec-5d6ae2cc5d9a}}

It is important to emphasize that this system requires the existence of some preliminary metadata both for the construction of resource relations and for metadata propagation. Furthermore, the quality or accuracy of the preliminary metadata is important in ensuring successful results (i.e. to avoid a “garbage in, garbage out" scenario). However, the metadata being propagated can be different from the metadata used to generate resource relations. For instance, in the manuscript domain, the propagation of keyword metadata may be most efficient along resource relations derived from citation metadata. Therefore, two aspects affect the efficiency of metadata propagation: the type of resource relations and the algorithm used to propagate metadata. It is important to note that no new metadata values are created in model proposed in this article. While it is important for resources to maintain metadata, this method only propagates pre-existing metadata values and thus, does not increase the discriminatory aspects that metadata should and generally provides. While like resources should have similar metadata, variations should also exist to make sure that a resource's metadata accentuates the unique characteristics of the resource.

This paper will first discuss two algorithms to define sets of resource relations and represent these relations in terms of associative networks. It will then formally define a metadata propagation algorithm which can operate on the basis of the generated resource relations. Finally, the proposed metadata generation system is validated using a modified version of the KDD Cup 2003 High-Energy Physics bibliographic dataset (hep-th 2003)hep-th 2003 available at: http://www.cs.cornell.edu/projects/kddcup/datasets.html. While it is theoretically possible for this method to work on other resource types (e.g. video, audio, etc.) as it doesn't require an analysis of the content of the resources, only their metadata; it is only speculated that the results of such a method would be viable in these other, non-tested, domains.

The remainder of this section will describe two associative network construction algorithms. One is based on occurrence metadata where a resource is considered similar to another if there is a direct reference from one resource to the other (e.g. a direct citation). The other algorithm is based on co-occurrence metadata and thus, considers two resources to be similar if they share similar metadata. That is, two resources are deemed similar if the same metadata values occur in both their properties (i.e. same authors, same keywords, same publication venue, etc.). Depending on how the repository represents its metdata some property types will be direct reference properties and others will have to be infered through indirect, co-occurence algorithms.

Reconstructing the metadata for a metadata-poor collection of resources is dependent not only on the associative network data structure, but also upon the use of a metadata propagation algorithm. The algorithm chosen is a derivative of the particle-swarm algorithm {{cite:0fc36c236f0c23307785f02f30afb7c963cc9968}}. Particle-swarm algorithms are a discrete form of the spreading activation algorithms {{cite:5ad91e68289f5bd1bcb255ce18d23107c9b809c1}}, {{cite:e8b14af809a7de7846c2abd5b950d3443135f7fb}}, {{cite:74dade5b0e4da572290b43308486f4eebf3171df}}, {{cite:8da6c6972ae0cac4c8eedf24834df3ce5936488d}}, {{cite:6747a01c6a0a37e5fdd70f97a5a9bb0402ffdcba}}. Because particles are indivisible entities, it is easy to represent metadata properties as being encapsulated inside a particle. These metadata particles are then propagated over the edges of the associative network. Upon reaching a resource node that is missing a particular property type, the particle recommends its property value to the visited resource. This section will formally describe the metadata propagation algorithm before discussing the results of an experiement using a bibliographic dataset.

Propagating metadata particles through an associative network of type {{formula:4d148b16-bd88-4073-88e3-8d4c26736ee9}}

This section will present the results of the proposed metadata generation system when attempting to reconstruct an artificially atrophied bibliographic dataset. By artificially reducing the amount of metadata in the full bibliographic dataset, it is possible to simulate a metadata-poor environment and at the same time still be able to validate the results of the metadata propagation algorithm. The section is outlined as follows. First, the dataset used for this experiment is described. Second, a short review of the validation metrics (precision, recall, and F-score) is presented. Third, the various system parameters are discussed. Finally, the results of the experiment are presented as a validation of the systems use for manuscript-based digital library repositories. Further research into other domains besides manuscripts will demonstrate the validity of this method for other resource types.

The dataset used to validate the proposed system is a modified version of the hep-th 2003 bibliographic dataset for high energy physics and theory {{cite:47360405d83a4e24cd126765d77924d7ea733ab8}}.The details of how the hep-th dataset was created can be found in the disseminated README (http://kdl.cs.umass.edu/data/hepth/hepth-README.txt) of the data set and a few specifics are quoted here: “Object and link properties such as title, authors, journal (if published), and various dates were extracted from the abstract files with additional date information coming from the slacdates citation tarball. Because institutions were often not presented in a consistent format, the email domain of the submitter (if available) was used as a surrogate for institution. Because many authors had no associated email address, domain information is not available for all authors. Consolidation was performed on journal names, domains, and author names. A nominal amount of hand-cleaning to correct spelling or formatting problems was also performed." A modified version of the hep-th dataset, as used in {{cite:229a46601637907ccf559b7bcde6cf5ceaecda46}}, is represented as a semantic network containing manuscripts (29,014), authors (12,755), journals (267), organizations (963), keywords (40), and publication date in year/season pairs (60). These nodes are then connected according to the following semantics:

For the purposes of this experiment, the semantic network from {{cite:229a46601637907ccf559b7bcde6cf5ceaecda46}} was transformed into a list of manuscripts and their associated metadata property name/value pairs. These manuscript properites include: authors, date of publication, citations, keywords, publishing journal, and organizations. Of the 29,014 manuscript nodes, different occurrence and co-occurrence algorithms were used to construct the following associative networks:

citation: manuscript {{formula:be5cf32d-6c89-4f58-ab18-6a62d169c784}}  maintains an edge to manuscript {{formula:5e5854dc-b0dd-4b5d-941f-ad5c1055b249}}  if {{formula:9de33a6b-f2b2-4dab-ab49-c835b1af98be}}  cites {{formula:2fcbbee6-c3b2-4a4f-a8af-b40034e287fc}}  (27,240 edges)

co-author: manuscripts maintain an edge if they share authors (724,406 edges)

co-citation: manuscripts maintain an edge if they share citations (23,089,616 edges)

co-keyword: manuscripts maintain an edge if they share keywords (12,418,172 edges)

co-organization: manuscript maintain an edge if they share organizations (33,947,083 edges)

Though not explored empirically, it is worth noting that link prediction algorithms can be employed to resolve issues relating to edge sparsity in the network. In particular, the methods proposed in {{cite:801b8ed74d248ed856e92be9e99cb69b2f382e7f}} and {{cite:481242739565f1d0f908296a1637c95240d63c6d}} are such algorithms.

Recall, Eq. REF , on the other hand, is defined as the proportion of relevant property values received to the total amount of relevant property values possible. For example, if resource {{formula:e3ec2a93-acbd-40f6-8b09-60c9f9b9635f}}  previously (before artificial atrophy) had the property value keyword={{formula:2548607e-0f40-4109-9e8d-cc114e650bdd}} swarm{{formula:feff7745-3f79-4cd4-a191-063f94247b1d}}  and is recommended the property value keyword={{formula:aa4eaae3-3ee8-4f87-93d5-25e1eacde28e}} swarm{{formula:b87d0a27-e132-4b2c-9154-39aa3e1db9e4}} , then there is a 100% recall. On the other hand, if resource {{formula:944bb275-0300-4161-a19e-ebc571efa3a6}}  previously had the property values keyword={{formula:84114353-b048-4bf8-b670-ffab4b0200e6}} swarm, network{{formula:f3c89006-a6f0-4192-9eda-d9cb78c68227}}  and is recommended the property value keyword={{formula:ad4a0ceb-22ab-4cd4-a4dc-c1eb3ca2d20e}} swarm{{formula:9545bd31-2845-4577-a642-65a92b30295f}} , then there is a 50% recall, whereas its precision is 100% in both cases.
{{formula:b9328c00-cd62-4c7a-8654-1836235ddd29}}

Precision and recall tend to be inversely related, {{formula:4525835f-beae-42c2-bb70-969bfeb19651}} . This inverse relationship is understood best when examining the extreme cases. If every possible property value was provided to a resource ({{formula:3387f183-c579-487e-ad46-47cc54318b88}} ), and that resource originally only had one property value ({{formula:bdb9f38e-6b66-4adb-9e05-8630f06bdb58}} ) then the recall would be 100% while the precision would be near 0%. At the opposite extreme, if a resource previously had every possible property value in its original metadata ({{formula:047e0f1f-c5f6-4279-8ee5-cd4a474a172e}} ) and was recommend only one property value ({{formula:9e88b0d1-53d7-4980-bc82-fb696020bd8b}} ), then the precision would be 100%, but the recall would be near 0%. While, in some systems, precision and recall can be inversely related, it is the goal of information retrieval systems that are validated according to this criterion to achieve both high precision and recall values.

Finally, F-score, Eq. REF , can be used to combine precision and recall into a single measure. Note that different associative networks will perform differently for different property types. For instance, co-citation networks will, intuitively, preform better at propagating keyword values than co-organization networks. Therefore, the F-score measure will be represented as {{formula:86f14ffb-3abd-420d-9624-1c4e70a5a410}}  in order to express the F-score of a network created from metadata properties of type {{formula:54da50c6-d04b-4364-b438-32d5ae974fce}}  propagating property values of type {{formula:485ab8d1-8bc6-48fd-9df8-16842f6c149b}} . Precision and recall can be represented in a similar fashion though the results of the experiment to follow are expressed according to the F-score measure only.

The experiment was set up to determine various F-scores, {{formula:85b2d6f6-fd63-4c5f-990e-28858868be28}} , where {{formula:21ab1be6-f3dd-4875-8937-093e1dc4e2f2}}  and {{formula:07a6e8f9-682c-477f-91aa-ab1e222fc0b9}} . This means that for every type of associative network generated, an F-score for each metadata property type was determined. Since the hep-th 2003 bibliographic dataset is a metadata-rich dataset, it was necessary to destroy a percentage of the metadata to test whether or not the metadata generation algorithm could reconstruct the property values for the selected metadata-poor resources. Therefore, the tunable parameter, density, {{formula:fc97bda2-555a-4df0-b189-a0cb2d65c9b0}} , was created. The density of the network metadata ranges from 1% of the network resources containing metadata to 99% of the resources. Given the percentage parameter, resources were randomly selected for atrophy before the metadata propagation algorithm was run.

With the potential for 99% of the network containing metadata, the propagation of metadata to the lacking 1% would be overwhelming (a high recall with a low precision). In order to allow nodes to regulate the amount of metadata property values they accept, a second parameter exists. The percentile parameter, {{formula:a741b863-3fca-4149-89b4-bc56c7e78e47}} , determines the energy threshold for property value recommendations. Since each {{formula:72fc0246-93de-4d14-8b1c-adeafdbdc8a5}}  entry has an associated energy value (recommendation influence), a range from 0{{formula:bf0cd070-97c5-481c-9873-14e8823c9105}}  percentile, meaning all provided property values are accepted to 100{{formula:6e7325f6-4af1-436f-8689-661d91c85676}}  percentile, meaning only the top energy property value is accepted, is used. Determining the F-score for the various experimental parameters

The general expected trend is that as the density of the network increases, the recall increases and the precision decreases. With more property values being propagated, any metadata-poor record, on average, will receive more recommendations than are needed. For instance, a manuscript only has one publishing journal, therefore a recommendation of 100 journals is going to yield a very low precision ({{formula:0a802be7-f513-45da-b990-93983145c6f7}} ). To balance this effect, a percentile increase will tend to increase the precision of the algorithm at the expense of recall. When only the highest energy recommendations are accepted, the probability of rejecting a useful recommendation increases. In the case of journal propagation, if only the 100{{formula:51ccacc0-9505-4462-b9f0-e3c1b5ad890a}}  percentile recommendation is accepted, then only the highest energy recommendation is accepted. If this journal recommendation is the correct publishing venue, then there is 100% recall and precision. If not, then there is 0% recall and precision. Depending on the amount of values needed to fill a particular property, different {{formula:cd497320-5a3c-4264-a5b4-523f13b1e42d}}  values will be most suitable than others.

This paper has provided a preliminary exploration of metadata generation in terms of metadata property propagation within an associative network of repository resources. Further research in this area may prove useful for other network types such as those generated from other metadata properties. For instance, it may be of interest to study the effect of this algorithm on usage networks {{cite:468a23a878b132724286a69804c9d8374e3227f1}}. Usage metadata, unlike citation and journal metadata, is applicable to every accessible resource. It would be interesting to see what co-usage means for a particular genera of resources by determining which metadata properties these networks are best at propagating.

A variety of propagation algorithms may also be explored. It is assumed that a particle will take only edges of a particular {{formula:69034a93-9efc-465a-822a-5a926b5ed2be}}  type for the duration of their life-span. Different path types might be an important aspect of increasing the precision and recall performance of this method. For instance, keyword metadata that first propagates over co-authorship edges and then over co-citation edges might provide better results. Methods to implement such propagation algorithms have been presented in {{cite:0fc36c236f0c23307785f02f30afb7c963cc9968}}, {{cite:ac83c19a43bc3812eb92d333a562fe90717a74f2}}. Also, different edge types can be merged such that all co-keyword and co-authorship edges are collapsed to form a single edge.

What has been presented in this study is the results of this algorithm without the intervention of any human components (besides the initial creation of metadata through the hep-th dataset creation process). Future work that studies this method with the inclusion of humans that help to validate and “clean" the recommended metadata would be telling of how much this method is able to speed up the process of generating accurate and reliable metadata for metadata-poor resources. Such an analysis is left to future research.

Finally, multiplicative effects due to particle interaction may effect the results of the algorithm. For instance, if two particles, {{formula:259b42d2-baa5-450b-b757-10dec3ad9808}}  and {{formula:6bc0533a-75fe-4e38-811f-39afda2f9096}} , meet at a particular node, {{formula:ce269697-9b00-45cc-853f-a1ecda243696}} , and {{formula:b85f1c22-1d44-44b3-ae8c-cc1e2f6946f8}}  and {{formula:ad79b342-7582-4f30-9ed8-c6bf27d05b3a}}  have similar metadata then the footprint they leave at {{formula:eabf6d95-a9d8-4b7e-a89b-774502603579}}  should be more noticeable. Because two different metadata sources are supplying the same property values, there is an increased probability of that recommended metadata value being correct. Currently, only a summation is being provided. It may be interesting to multiply this summation by the number of unique particles that provided energy for a particular recommended metadata value. The variations of this preliminary framework will be explored in future work.

Automatic metadata generation is becoming an increasingly important field of research as digital library repositories become more prevalent and move into the arena of less strongly controlled, decentralized collections (e.g. arXiv and CiteSeer). The creation and maintenance of high-quality, detailed metadata is hampered on numerous levels. Manual metadata creation methods are costly. Recent efforts to leverage the collective power of social tagging (i.e. “folksonomies") may address some of the shortcomings of the manual creation of metadata and result in viable models for online resources that do not require strongly controlled vocabularies and metadata ontologies. However, it is doubtful that “folksonomies" can be generalized to situations that require vetted, well-standardized metadata. The automated creation of metadata on the basis of content-analysis is a promising alternative to the manual creation of metadata. It is conceivably more efficient in situations where textual data is available and allows for more formal control of the type and nature of metadata that is extracted. However, it can be unreliable for non-text resources, yield low-quality metadata and can be computationally expensive.

This article proposed another possible component of the metadata generation toolkit which may complement and support the above mentioned approaches. Instead of creating new metadata, metadata is propagated from a metadata-rich subset of the collection to similar, but metadata-poor subsets. The substrate for this extrapolation is an associative network of resource relations created from other available metadata. Metadata propagation may provide a computationally feasible means of generating large amounts of metadata for heterogeneous resources which can later be fine-tuned by manual intervention or cross-validation with content-based methods. The article finally provided experimental results using the High-Energy Physics bibliographic data set (hep-th 2003). Human intervention may play an important role in fine-tuning the metadata propagation algorithm. The results of this experiment are promising and there still exists a range of potential modifications to this basic framework that may lead to even better results.

In the standard model of quantum computing {{cite:327616c49487f50abe45354e1205fa9b6b522ff8}}, the computation proceeds by coherently performing unitary dynamics on a simple initial state of a quantum system before being read out by a sequence of local measurements. By contrast, the one-way model of quantum computing {{cite:287a5221b5cdeb84f1a7dd8a0f8244f4d7fa6ac9}} eliminates the need for coherent quantum evolution, substituting instead a highly entangled, but easily prepared initial state as the resource for the computation. The typical resource state used is the cluster state {{cite:c173e7a5c0bd2fcb0068bf0f435acda581b86aa3}}, whose preparation consists of, for example, coupling a system of qubits with a nearest-neighbor Ising interaction. The computation proceeds by a sequence of local measurements on the cluster state and the basis chosen at each step determines the computation. In this way, a cluster state is like a quantum breadboard on which the quantum circuit is inscribed via measurements.

Although cluster states were originally defined using qubits, they generalize to {{formula:d5989742-60dd-43f3-b858-45c542ee19dc}} -level quantum systems {{cite:7fcd3ca28128ce5be99393489e0b85da694b2fb9}} and continuous variables {{cite:59fd25ba963318806c7a60e6c217fa1096ca86de}}, {{cite:f9655cf632110e8644de5b3faff2ddc7a232b91e}}. Recently, Ref. {{cite:4efe9dd016c2d263d418ae82099bd3cb8553ffa5}} proposed a method for efficiently generating continuous-variable cluster states (CVCS). The method relies on pumping an optical cavity containing a special nonlinear medium at certain carefully chosen frequencies. The resulting CVCS is encoded in the quadratures of the photons that emerge from the cavity.

The method of CVCS generation proposed in {{cite:4efe9dd016c2d263d418ae82099bd3cb8553ffa5}} required, on grounds of experimental and theoretical tractability, the existence of certain families of matrices. The required matrices are weighing matrices, defined as matrices {{formula:b147c5d1-f5e8-464f-9cfb-938c291ba23f}}  whose entries are in {{formula:b92d73d8-6f03-4040-8ec5-3c42718393af}}  and satisfy {{formula:d5891b62-0eef-4f96-b4b5-6b620779f33d}} , where {{formula:6c0720a8-f7fb-4b09-a559-4fe7be98f72a}}  is called the weight. The weighing matrices were obliged to have Hankel form, meaning that the skew-diagonals of the matrix were all constant, and any skew-diagonal with support on the main diagonal must be identically 0. A matrix with vanishing main diagonal is said to be hollow. As we show later, when viewing the matrices as adjacency matrices for an associated graph, this is implied when the graph is connected and bipartite.

In this article, we investigate the mathematical structure behind the construction in {{cite:4efe9dd016c2d263d418ae82099bd3cb8553ffa5}} and begin to classify the associated matrices. The discussion is organized as follows. In S:physics we give a brief glimpse of the physics which motivates the restrictions given in the previous paragraph. We begin the mathematical discussion in S:ag, where we discuss anticirculant graphs, and S:awm, where we discuss anticirculant weighing matrices, a special case of the Hankel weighing matrices. In S:2reg, we complete the rather trivial classification of the case of weight 2, while S:4reg provides several examples about the case of weight 4. We discuss a number of open problems in S:openproblems, and conclude in S:conc.

For completeness, we mention one further elaboration that is possible for this scheme. If the photons' polarization, transverse, or spatial degrees of freedom are taken into account, then the Hamiltonian E:Hamiltonian can be modified by adding additional indices for these modes. If these additional modes are all frequency-degenerate, then an additional sum over these degenerate modes appears in E:Hamiltonian, which allows for the symmetric intercoupling between the degenerate degrees of freedom. If such an interaction could be simultaneously phasematched by the nonlinear medium inside the cavity, then one is naturally lead to consider block-Hankel matrices, where the size of the blocks is equal to the number of degenerate degrees of freedom. We leave the consideration of block-Hankel hollow weighing matrices to future work.

Since there is no general classification of weighing matrices, characterizing graphs of Hankel weighing matrices seems to be out of reach. This could be however done for graphs of degree 4 and 9, on the basis of present knowledge on {{formula:d4a6afcf-30a2-472b-8737-06b8e9fb234c}}  and {{formula:3ebada2b-1957-4fef-bfde-668b53de2673}}  (see {{cite:d2b81348ac8204edd98e7fd48d8bb1df5c9ba744}}).

We have seen that there are examples of Hankel weighing matrices which are not anticirculant. A way to study the relation between these matrices and anticirculant ones, would be to prove that the graphs of Hankel weighing matrices are always isomorphic to graphs of {{formula:f1f125b5-a07c-4699-96d3-b7290f902bfa}} , except for some special cases which will include the examples in proposition REF .
