A Hamiltonian cycle in a graph is an ordered set of sequentially adjacent vertices, in which every vertex of the graph appears exactly once. Graphs with Hamiltonian cycles are said to be Hamiltonian. Alspach and Zhang {{cite:23331cfdeb1acc1bf9b321884f681030ecb73bf7}} conjectured that a connected Cayley graph {{formula:2861b017-0d38-45fa-995f-f397d0e45869}}  is Hamiltonian whenever {{formula:b41dad51-c21f-4a9f-bf1b-a6f38a52efc4}}  is a set of reflections. According to this conjecture, any connected anticirculant graph is Hamiltonian whenever it is loopless. Additionally, Gutin et al.  {{cite:277f0406c3fc7217d6eea449d5b4ffc473ba8b53}} conjectured that graphs of unitary matrices are Hamiltonian if connected. According to these conjectures the graphs of Hankel weighing matrices are Hamiltonian if connected. This is the case for the graphs considered here. In Figure REF  are drawn the graphs {{formula:1bb5c92d-9485-4a4f-8aab-5e93c85e4aac}}  and {{formula:9c17e54d-f301-4679-9f48-6674a17810f9}} . The highlighted edges represent Hamiltonian cycles. Perhaps the physical picture that motivates our study could provide some insight toward proving these conjectures.

We have seen that graphs of the form {{formula:67564a15-6a2b-4b87-aebd-d4329fbe44a8}}  are graphs of unitary matrices. The quantum dynamics induced by these matrices is trivial because of symmetry. However symmetry can be broken with the action of a diagonal matrix without altering the zero pattern of the unitary. This suggests the possibility of constructing unitaries with a nontrivial dynamics whose graph is a undirected Cayley graph of the dihedral group.

Sections  and  make extensive use of the following trick. Begin with a circulant weighing matrix, then reverse the columns. If the resulting graph has loops, one can create a loopless graph by the “interlacing” trick. In fact the interlaced graph will again be connected if the original graph was connected but not bipartite. Can one classify the Hankel and anticirculant weighing matrices which cannot be obtained by this trick?

We have demonstrated connections between an approach to quantum computation with optical modes and the existence of certain weighing matrices with Hankel structure. Because the degree of the graph associated to a matrix corresponds to the experimental resources required to implement the graph as a CVCS, it is important to characterize which graphs with small degree have adjacency matrices with Hankel structure. We proved some general theorems about such matrices, classified completely the case of degree 2, and provided some examples with degree 4. We also raised some interesting open problems that might help shed some light on which graphs can be implemented in a single OPO using the scheme in Ref. {{cite:4efe9dd016c2d263d418ae82099bd3cb8553ffa5}}, {{cite:d056802759dcadf80d8c2aabd03c3bbbca179c4e}}.

Brown dwarfs are very low-mass stars
whose masses (M {{formula:64f99e1b-828b-478b-97fd-b0262aa47ac5}}  0.075 M{{formula:61ef22c9-f13b-4d69-b6c5-50a42d5ca501}} ) are insufficient to sustain
the core hydrogen fusion reactions that balance radiative energy losses {{cite:9170716755d473826ac14964d0cb62589d891daf}}, {{cite:b0e347f5821f2ba817708876b63ac1737f51ce25}}. Supported from further gravitational contraction
by electron degeneracy pressure, evolved brown dwarfs continually cool
and dim over time as they radiate away their initial
contraction energy, ultimately
achieving photospheric conditions that can be similar to those of giant planets.
The first examples of brown dwarfs were identified as recently as
1995 {{cite:de68a42af154d46551cbd5081711c27bd091bcf8}}, {{cite:66fde91d92b0cb6e4cbf3d3040e441f68fea2442}}.
Today, there are hundreds known in nearly
all Galactic environments, identified largely
in wide-field, red and near-infrared imaging surveys such as 2MASS, DENIS, SDSS and UKIDSS.
The known population of brown dwarfs encompasses
the late-type M (T{{formula:5ac32b02-a2ac-4232-97ed-c0d068ae90f0}}  {{formula:cdc1eeb3-7f2c-49eb-97ae-8edf2c214c77}}  2500–3500 K), L (T{{formula:0c85d405-28eb-42c1-b463-7777d23a99d1}}  {{formula:68a51351-611e-4314-8e3f-1bd3f99e4bdd}}  1400–2500 K) and T spectral classes (T{{formula:a95c8f59-8337-44ea-9f94-46377d600b15}}  {{formula:9ec1983a-b84b-4d50-93dc-f1d0f8e2aee2}}  600–1400 K; e.g., {{cite:045b038305520c015c66e2d5ba41916514e2841a}}),
while efforts are currently underway to find even colder
members of the putative Y dwarf class (see review by {{cite:c67fe98c0781d0ccd8539d07697a7a83b38240bc}}).

Because brown dwarfs cool over time, their spectral properties are inherently time-dependent,
making them potentially useful chronometers for Galactic studies (much like white dwarfs;
see contributions by M. Salaris, J. Kalirai, S. Catalán and H. Richer).
However, the primary observables of a brown dwarf—temperature, luminosity and spectral type—depend on both mass and age (and weakly on metallicity). This degeneracy complicates characterizations of individual sources and mixed
populations. Unfortunately, traditional stellar age-dating methods do not appear to be applicable
for brown dwarfs.
Magnetic activity metrics, such as the frequency and strength
of optical or X-ray non-thermal emission, appear to be largely age-invariant
(e.g., {{cite:18a25446d9ae74722d4c146d7c34f2bffeb4d778}}) and quiescent emission drops off
precipitously in the early L dwarfs as cool photospheres are decoupled from
field lines
Interestingly, radio emission does not drop off for cooler brown
dwarfs, and may even
increase relative to bolometric flux, although there are currently few detections (e.g., {{cite:ba1b89bdaea13a0f790140f3e77d01038e5e37e2}}).
(e.g., {{cite:deca82c2edcdd355781249dc1b59f6e8caba56bf}}; see contribution by A. West). Long-term angular momentum loss in brown
dwarfs is far more muted than in stars, and there is no clear rotation-activity
relation for L dwarfs (e.g., {{cite:cad07166edd7c0643f6e849b4fff28057e5868f8}}).
Exploitation of the cooling properties of brown dwarfs is therefore a favorable approach
for determining their ages.

In this contribution, I review five methods currently employed to age-date brown dwarfs and summarize
their applicability, inherent limitations and current (typical) precisions.
Table 1 provides a summary of the methods discussed in detail below.
{{table:67942bf9-1a5d-4406-b397-f7379833015d}}

The most straightforward way to age-date an individual brown dwarf is to borrow
from its environment, a tactic that is suitable for members of coeval
clusters/associations and companions to age-dated stars.
Brown dwarfs are well-sampled
down to and below the deuterium fusing mass limit (M {{formula:c8a349ce-636d-43f4-bab2-0cb3319d7cb6}}  0.013 M{{formula:d0fbbffc-95bf-4633-b5e8-9575ac78911e}} )
in the youngest nearby clusters ({{formula:948f7e90-0ecc-489d-8b26-ecbb263678db}}  {{formula:8c2f00e5-7217-4422-877c-a1eb14475eda}}  5 Myr), as their
luminosities are greater at early ages. Brown dwarfs have
also been identified in somewhat older (10–50 Myr)“loose associations” in the vicinity
of the Sun ({{formula:9cfa10b6-30cb-4031-897f-5c96275e3bde}}  {{formula:9cbdbdfb-ef9b-4aea-befe-84be9eb2f8c5}}  50–100 pc; e.g., {{cite:15f44987c00c2b2c90a1607b6160c901c1aec91a}}).
For older and more distant clusters ({{formula:83b41c4b-48c1-487a-a353-8178d9b31b89}}  {{formula:690b614b-3bd5-4319-b3ff-87fa70b66e4b}}  1 kpc),
decreasing surface temperatures and compact radii exacerbate the sensitivity
issues that plague low-mass stellar studies (see contribution by G. Piotto). There are as yet
no known brown dwarfs in globular clusters, despite detection of the end
of the stellar main sequence in systems such as NGC 6397 {{cite:c3aec005bae16b8b016b152ed6e95e913ebbba61}}.

For brown dwarfs in young clusters,
numerous studies have examined age-related trends in
colors (e.g., {{cite:ed91b8da3b41f6438d06892edbbf3ee46a47aada}}),
spectral characteristics (e.g., {{cite:6d02497190066bfb3e6db4becc621e12240d8bfe}}),
accretion timescales (e.g., {{cite:5824d928b0c3153c36288041e9f25861d4c851ec}}) and
circum(sub)stellar disk evolution (e.g., {{cite:06ee4a9220fefb3f0be20346894f41b1319014a5}}). These
have been coarsely quantified, and appear to be most useful at very
young ages ({{formula:f6f71487-1f38-401e-93b1-b41140900d04}}  10 Myr).
Surface properties and luminosities are highly variable at these ages
due to sensitivity to formation conditions
(e.g., {{cite:c5cc0a11710490811486e6b9d14804e54b1b53bd}}), ongoing accretion,
complex magnetic effects (e.g., {{cite:fc93e941df80ffc048a92610918a627d5cad904c}})
and age spreads within a cluster (see contribution by R. Jeffries).
Hence, while brown dwarfs in clusters with ages
spanning {{formula:d04cab8f-1ad5-4f29-8829-12127be65e27}} 1–650 Myr are now well-documented, with age uncertainties
as good as 10% (for the LDB technique; see {{formula:2752efcf-bf12-4728-b9ad-906588d5f8b6}}  3), useful predictive trends are probably
limited to ages of {{formula:0e4883ac-4a31-445b-9a11-524283ca5db6}} 10 Myr.

Known brown dwarf companions to main sequence stars now number a few dozen,
spanning a wide range of separation, age and composition. Many of these systems are widely-separated so that their brown dwarf
companions can be directly studied.
Age uncertainties for companion brown dwarfs depend on stellar dating methods which are generally
more uncertain (50–100%; e.g., {{cite:2846bd411a46d3033c7ace28d4b8d255ace1785e}}) than cluster ages. Searches for substellar companions to more precisely age-dated
white dwarfs (e.g. {{cite:83e6d0a5494a6f0fdbad6697a9c46cf831bf1a6a}}, {{cite:c27d7df5faca8aba6723804766afa5a4e49bba75}}) and subgiants {{cite:b8139efc3091db6b2604210afb1c5ed65573ba4f}} have so far met with limited success.
Nevertheless, brown dwarf companions to age-dated stars serve as important benchmarks for calibrating
other age-dating methods at late ages ({{formula:c75a3202-9e01-42fa-92f1-9c09a435267b}} 500 Myr) and are fundamental
for testing evolutionary models (see contribution by T. Dupuy).

Lithium is fused at a lower temperature
than hydrogen (2.5{{formula:cf67f965-09e2-493d-b267-4b03c1ec73e8}} 10{{formula:891d6978-1c0c-4d95-921f-01f3ef3a86f9}}  K), resulting in a somewhat lower fusing mass limit
(0.065 M{{formula:dbed2bf3-07ce-4e0b-a1e9-b6f2b17b6542}} ; {{cite:e56827c6774e756dc66db9a31d4182ddfe03b275}}).
Because the interiors of low mass stars and brown dwarfs are fully convective at early ages, an
object with a mass above this limit will fully deplete its initial reservoir of lithium within {{formula:1e5696d9-60b2-4638-a668-65e4af396991}} 200 Myr.
Hence, any system older than this
which exhibits Li I absorption has a mass less than 0.065 M{{formula:0be468ff-5122-4aa7-93dc-3031536f4187}} 
and is therefore a brown dwarf (e.g., {{cite:0c902710e5720aec64c89f9b33a6ff410227a8fb}}). With a mass limit, one can use evolutionary models to determine an age limit.

In the age range {{formula:b02712a0-f638-44bc-a613-fab77a625628}} 10–200 Myr, the degree of lithium depletion in low-mass stars
and brown dwarfs
is itself mass-dependent, occurring earlier in more massive stars which first achieve
the necessary core temperatures. Hence, over this range the age of an individual source can be
precisely constrained if its mass is known. A more practical approach, however, is to
ascertain the age of a group of coeval low-mass objects based on which sources do or do not
exhibit Li I absorption; this is the lithium depletion boundary (LDB) technique. Different
evolutionary models yield remarkably similar predictions for the location of the LDB over a broad
range of ages {{cite:941cd1870230b9e4d007f12acad1b516f7fd9d17}}, and the boundary itself is readily identifiable in color-magnitude
diagrams. As such, this technique has been used to age-date several nearby young clusters and
associations (e.g., {{cite:5f4c473f4a626eb7b813da038e19762f25362cdb}}, {{cite:0aa86035ed3570d1faf6a667580310e96f3752cd}}, {{cite:a539d773f3285dc40c56bb63d2d2755c693ea5b3}}, {{cite:d0ed153c67c33b36fcac16e67b9643f6e70c7998}}). LDB studies have also provided independent
confirmation of other cluster-dating methods such as isochrone fitting {{cite:a539d773f3285dc40c56bb63d2d2755c693ea5b3}}.
A variant of the LDB technique for coeval binary systems has been proposed by {{cite:17984f83a2310cd48d75b477084a8897b2300087}}, in which a system that exhibits Li I absorption in the secondary but not
in the primary can have both lower and upper age limits assigned to it (note that the presence/absence of Li I in both components simply sets a single upper/lower age limit). This technique requires resolved optical spectroscopy of both components and can be pursued only for
a few (rare) wide low-mass pairs (e.g., Burgasser et al., in prep.)
or using high spatial-resolution spectroscopy (e.g. {{cite:09db6dfd8019c882d6da74c45a9487139c06e08b}}).
No single brown dwarf pair straddling the LDB has yet been identified.

Despite its utility, the detection of LI I absorption in brown dwarf spectra has
limitations. The 6708 Å line lies in an relatively faint spectral region for cool L-type dwarfs, so sensitive spectral observations on large telescopes are typically required to
detect (or convincingly rule out) this feature. For optically-brighter
M-type brown dwarfs,
high-resolution observations are generally required to distinguish Li I absorption from overlapping
molecular absorption features. Young brown dwarfs ({{formula:87369e06-cec4-46cc-8511-286c1e16ef36}}  50 Myr)
with low surface gravities show weakened alkali line absorption (see {{formula:df33d6ef-3020-4acf-809e-f839464296be}}  5),
including Li I, making it again necessary to obtain sensitive, high-resolution
observations {{cite:15f44987c00c2b2c90a1607b6160c901c1aec91a}}. For brown dwarfs cooler than {{formula:e0c2aa9c-6148-4794-8b6d-b3243dc501a3}} 1500 K
(i.e., the T dwarfs), lithium is chemically
depleted in the photosphere through its conversion to LiCl, LiF or LiOH {{cite:58bb262fbbae7790bd0028d0996a7cd72afdc9fb}}. As such, practical age constraints using Li I
can only be made for systems younger than {{formula:b8192f04-3fd9-413e-9e72-26db95a07286}} 2 Gyr.

One way of breaking the mass/age/luminosity degeneracy for an individual brown dwarf is to explicitly
measure its mass. This is feasible for sufficiently tight brown dwarf binaries for which
radial velocity (RV) and/or astrometric orbits can be measured.
Of the {{formula:471d5d70-d747-492e-ae15-cb4dfaffff09}} 100 very low mass (M{{formula:8825957a-72d7-4064-b48f-6f5aaef250b8}} ,M{{formula:118ffeec-35f0-4d75-8310-777071641376}}  {{formula:277e3ba9-d0c6-4be8-8cb3-67474716ee3a}}  0.1 M{{formula:d7a93909-538f-44be-bc30-c0a2ce0d7166}} ) binary systems
now known, only a handful have sufficiently short periods that
large portions of their RV orbits (e.g., {{cite:3276bbbf97869dab5fdb15b9e9df52657a3a0017}}, {{cite:c7bfad3510bff5eb96a2cf2f245271ecd9fb9a5c}}), astrometric orbits (e.g., {{cite:721acb6bec080741ddde47fb2014535f5f9f233f}}, {{cite:7c70a9a1320171dff4648f21bd781f14ab62f793}}, {{cite:2846bd411a46d3033c7ace28d4b8d255ace1785e}}, {{cite:0377f4370fd61c9c849ac197234b3251f9f62f2c}}), or both {{cite:c8a43d5ec0aa6efd5166aec66d3879bcf804451e}}, {{cite:dd6ac857f8d2eaa2bbdde7c9d44d4fae1f764b50}} have been measured. With measurable total system masses or mass functions, individual masses can be
estimated from relative photometry or directly
determined from recoil motion in both components (e.g., {{cite:dd6ac857f8d2eaa2bbdde7c9d44d4fae1f764b50}}). The individual masses and component
luminosities can then be compared to evolutionary models to determine ages.

{{cite:2846bd411a46d3033c7ace28d4b8d255ace1785e}} have suggested that such “mass standards” provide more precise constraints on the
physical properties (including ages) of brown dwarfs as compared to “age standards”, namely companions to
main sequence stars. Orbital masses can currently be constrained to
roughly 5–10% precision, translating into 10–20% uncertainties in ages based
on evolutionary tracks (versus 50–100% for main-sequence stars).
More importantly, brown dwarf binaries with
mass measurements and independent
age determinations—i.e., companions to age-dated stars and cluster members—can provide
specific tests of the evolutionary models themselves. Further details are provided
in the contribution by T. Dupuy.

Only 10–20% of brown dwarfs are found to be multiple (e.g., {{cite:a5df37702be0d633adf9193596aff83aa045974d}}) and few of these are suitable for orbital mass measurements. A proxy for mass
is surface gravity, which can be determined directly from a brown dwarf's spectrum.
For T{{formula:12945e63-1d1d-4b71-92bb-c086e3e7853e}}  {{formula:3e0e9a33-5c43-4263-ba80-c41744f6f551}}  2500 K and ages greater than {{formula:e7003958-c71b-4674-894d-889923c54698}} 50 Myr, evolutionary
models predict that brown dwarf surface gravities ({{formula:983f31c0-79bc-4a6e-b183-c2d3cac3746b}} ) are roughly proportional to mass due to
near-constant radii (roughly equal to Jupiter's radius).
Surface gravity is also proportional to photospheric pressure ({{formula:1774890f-c2b5-4da2-806e-965469cc9dfa}} , where {{formula:04bac7cc-a336-4032-bb7b-0da2cfbbea8d}}  is the Rosseland mean opacity), which in turn influences the chemistry, line broadening and (in some cases) opacities of absorbing species in the photosphere.
Hence, “gravity-sensitive” features in a brown dwarf's spectrum can be used to
infer its mass and, through evolutionary models, its age.

Examples of gravity-sensitive features include the optical and near-infrared VO bands and alkali lines in late-type M and L dwarfs, all of which evolve considerably between field dwarfs ({{formula:5c27fffc-a158-4d81-928a-ebfb41ea60cc}}  {{formula:4d75de0e-f6b4-4195-b64b-dc36e5c65f0e}}  5 cgs),
young cluster dwarfs ({{formula:5baa503d-6acc-463d-aac5-5eec1dbd2022}}  {{formula:df5280d6-0fb9-45b4-bd56-1f8aaac999d0}}  3–4) and giant stars ({{formula:299ecd57-baeb-4dd2-8425-03cf43c969cc}}  {{formula:0399bb94-a77e-4ece-baab-ae6dea3fa669}}  0; e.g., {{cite:7cb432a13dad80258d2e40c9b1f6e3ece5cb02a5}}).
Enhanced VO absorption and weakened alkali line absorption is a characteristic trait
of young brown dwarf spectra
(e.g., {{cite:1e48b99dc7210ed177e47a4792d5d8ef3eda78bb}}, {{cite:6d02497190066bfb3e6db4becc621e12240d8bfe}}).
Alkali features in particular are useful for cooler brown dwarfs
as VO condenses out of the photosphere.
Quantitative analyses of these features have been used to distinguish “young” ({{formula:a720b495-2700-4a1b-8b10-d84be1425304}} 10 Myr) from “very young” sources thus far ({{formula:1d2c7f0f-06cb-450b-af24-ffbc8339012a}} 5 Myr; e.g., {{cite:5a84340daf406b78cc57c565eb2957d6412eee28}}).
More robust metrics await larger and more fully-characterized samples.

Another important surface gravity diagnostic is collision-induced H{{formula:49551b4d-f93b-47db-90e6-fafacae2f3ae}} 
absorption, a smooth opacity source spanning a
broad swath of the infrared (e.g., {{cite:afc3d5d9c9c573ee07db1e51b9ee08c3ed51d55e}}, {{cite:d1b92e235fd75633b3c87ec59f7ec7fd790b67e5}}).
H{{formula:2cfc85d0-bdb0-4efd-a452-d90313ac9b98}}  absorption is weakened in the low-pressure atmospheres of
young cluster brown dwarfs, resulting in reddened near-infrared spectral energy
distributions and colors; in particular, a characteristic, triangular-shaped H-band (1.7 {{formula:b107606c-59d7-45c9-95b6-820e8f52daea}} m)
flux peak (e.g., {{cite:8938441f76702b631038ba7406c3d7dafc5e9f79}}, {{cite:94fa0a9bdbfacbf9f2936eea314c41eb0a96ec8f}}).
The proximity of many young and reddened brown dwarfs ({{formula:d9be8165-2b83-4a7c-a2b8-c02ed2149c7a}}  100 pc) rules out ISM absorption as a primary source for this reddening. {{cite:ed91b8da3b41f6438d06892edbbf3ee46a47aada}} have exploited this trend by using a
proper-motion selected sample of nearby young cluster candidate members to infer an
age/color/luminosity relation for brown dwarfs younger than 0.7 Gyr, with a stated accuracy
of {{formula:f3ebfc4d-a305-4f14-a2a1-333cc5f0fe50}} 0.2 dex in log(age), or about 60% fractional uncertainty.
Kinematically older low-mass stars and brown dwarfs in the Galactic disk
(e.g., {{cite:e3fe24ea687207311e5436dba1fce66849a255e1}}) and halo populations (e.g., {{cite:44db74ce2c0dd3749e181d72a0ccb860b458ab01}})
exhibit unusually blue near-infrared colors due to enhanced H{{formula:debf9409-4643-4e24-b976-5e9097d4b5be}}  absorption.
However, differences in metallicities and condensate cloud properties can
muddle surface gravity determinations in these sources by modulating the
photospheric pressure through opacity effects (changing {{formula:13a02eb4-676f-4b32-a200-5c6bf331d9c1}} ; e.g.,
{{cite:222cadeda2d6ac8db4d95a02d2edea30d13ebdbc}}, {{cite:ab18f4ec587740f08fca03c911945240f1a05e85}}).

The use of H{{formula:b1d66821-12a9-4e6d-b603-69947c7d8c1e}}  absorption as a surface gravity indicator is particularly useful
for T dwarfs, as H{{formula:510390c7-8de2-4bdb-88a8-5a9d81e96890}}  dominates the {{formula:59abd69a-ef41-4d62-bc44-3abb29156e08}} -band (2.1 {{formula:c991450c-6e31-43d7-9ccb-5c52d78067c7}} m) opacity
and significantly influences near-infrared colors (e.g., {{cite:3bdd225db4615ac9ad78165b1411ebfb531d31dc}}, {{cite:fb904cf0510d6538fedb57c6e5b1a50ef27e40ff}}).
Several groups now employ this feature to estimate the atmospheric properties of individual T dwarfs
(e.g., {{cite:fa3f3ecd85cf85725332230852882a6c058d4c55}}, {{cite:12ead5c950b15313f6e769542abf6eb0cabd7378}}, {{cite:cee7c9390c13ccf67f3505af3d326101e6acdc8b}}), typically through the use of
spectral indices that separately sample surface gravity (e.g., the {{formula:515e6a12-16ea-411d-8480-fd61c681161d}} -band) and temperature variations (e.g., H{{formula:600de8c8-f583-47d2-ae09-cd1a51e49132}} O or CH{{formula:ec9f440c-a99a-4630-a371-842749b5154b}}  bands). These indices are compared
to atmospheric models calibrated by one or more benchmarks (e.g., a companion to a precisely age-dated star), and evolutionary models are used to determine individual masses and ages.
Typical uncertainties of {{formula:3ce39b49-b2d8-4397-a8ee-5a8491979e26}}  {{formula:6e91887e-b2f7-46ff-b051-40820dacb9e7}} 0.3 dex translate into 50-100% uncertainties in age, comparable to uncertainties for main
sequence stars.
Again, variations in metallicity can mimic variations in surface gravity, although a third
diagnostic such as luminosity can break this degeneracy (e.g., {{cite:b16905bfccd94d3f197e429c18a97ecfd46ea187}}).
As atmosphere models improve in fidelity, parameters are increasingly inferred
from direct fits to spectral data, with comparable uncertainties
(e.g., {{cite:125cf6b83f37683cd2efaa44b03329a0f05861cd}}, {{cite:95c527e9dd383c3b9384e3c1f677d1c0ba3a0b66}}).

When a sufficiently large enough sample of brown dwarfs is assembled, one can
apply standard kinematic analyses, building from the assumption
that gravitational perturbations lead to increased velocity
dispersions with time (e.g., {{cite:45b401854a0556b283c238cf6d2af8798400eb2d}}; see
contribution by B. Nordström). Velocity dispersions are typically characterized
by a time-dependent power-law form, i.e., {{formula:48dffa4d-5320-4c36-ad4f-bec08e63aeab}}  (e.g., {{cite:8fb7ac33a1c932c035b8564e81f91ba15476884e}}, {{cite:c83d50408c3c76e24240731902d1a8b6f62cf2c0}}). Other statistics, such as Galactic scale height, can also be tied to age through kinematic simulations (e.g., {{cite:7379c0aae43d1f93f369586783ae0e57713c5f31}}) to calibrate
secondary age diagnostics such as magnetic activity (see contribution by A. West).

Samples of very low mass stars and
brown dwarfs have only recently become large enough that kinematic studies are feasible.
The largest samples (over 800 sources) have been based on proper motion measurements (e.g., {{cite:9bfff3eff401ec10ee218a7575b39b5ace603584}}, {{cite:fe2be62e654beaa432a642cd3f50ec7f64acd666}}, {{cite:e3fe24ea687207311e5436dba1fce66849a255e1}}). For field dwarfs,
dispersion in tangential velocities for both magnitude- and volume-limited samples indicate a mean age
in the range 2–8 Gyr, largely invariant with spectral type. This is consistent with the ages of
more massive field stars and population synthesis models
(e.g., {{cite:50d0c770caa6dbbeb117db60504776a19868feae}}). However, when field samples are broken down by color {{cite:e3fe24ea687207311e5436dba1fce66849a255e1}} or presence of magnetic activity {{cite:9bfff3eff401ec10ee218a7575b39b5ace603584}}, distinct age groupings are inferred, indicating that both very old (i.e., thick disk or halo) and very young (i.e., thin disk or young association) brown dwarf populations coexist in the immediate vicinity of the Sun. Indeed, one of the major results from these studies is the identification of widely-dispersed brown dwarf members of nearby, young moving groups such as the Hyades (e.g., {{cite:7d024ae4d580c44f3c9d11b9d20e8de8645aa174}}).

With only two dimensions of motion measured, proper motion samples may produce biased dispersion measurements depending on the area of sky covered by a sample. Full 3D velocities require
RV measurements which are more expensive and have thus far been obtained only for a small fraction of the known brown dwarf population
(e.g., {{cite:03cefbadc7680d0fc54e83cf925cdca62cb4eae0}}, {{cite:886389898c0b0539adef63b7be76ad691db4a0e3}}).
A seminal study by {{cite:6f355ffcb088afea907edb558a61d99574838b18}} of
21 nearby, late-type dwarfs with parallax, proper motion and RV measurements found
considerably smaller 3D velocity dispersions for L and T dwarfs than GKM stars, suggesting that local brown dwarfs
are young ({{formula:e91906e3-3a01-4ac2-a819-66fd8fe3f508}}  0.5–4 Gyr). The discrepancy between this result
and the proper motion studies may be attributable to small number statistics and/or contamination
by young moving groups; {{formula:ec7cde93-98b0-4583-81d3-37ef885b97a9}} 40% of the brown dwarfs in the {{cite:6f355ffcb088afea907edb558a61d99574838b18}} sample appear
to be associated with the Hyades. Resolving this discrepancy requires
larger RV samples, which has the side benefit of potentially uncovering RV variables
that can be used as mass standards (e.g., {{cite:03cefbadc7680d0fc54e83cf925cdca62cb4eae0}}).

With several methods for age-dating brown dwarfs over a broad range of phase space now
available,
opportunities to use these objects as chronometers for various
Galactic studies look to be increasingly promising; e.g., age-dating
planetary systems, examining cluster age spreads,
testing Galactic disk dynamical heating models, and direct measures of the
substellar mass function and birthrate in the field and other populations. However, there are areas where improvements
in uncertainties are needed and basic assumptions tested. Surface gravity determinations
in particular require better constraints, since these
enable age-dating of individual sources. In the short term, improvements
in spectral models can help in this endeavor; however, a sufficiently sampled grid of
benchmark sources
may obviate the need for models entirely.
Benchmarks should increasingly arise from mass standards, for which
age constraints are more precise; these additionally provide
necessary tests of evolutionary models upon which most of the age-dating
techniques hinge. Improved angular resolution and sensitivity
with {{formula:c355ace2-97f7-441c-892b-5b9952550f3e}}  and the next generation of large ({{formula:ea7f78cb-378b-4c98-acd2-38b0a459a0c8}} m) telescopes
will increase resolved binary sample sizes by expanding the volume in which they
can be found and monitored. These facilities will also aid searches for
substellar cluster members in old open field and globular clusters and, perhaps more
importantly, mass standards in these clusters to facilitate more stringent tests of evolutionary models
(T. Dupuy, priv. comm.).
Finally, a larger, more complete sample of brown dwarfs with precise RV measurements
will both improve our statistical constraints on the age of the local brown dwarf
population (and subpopulations) while additionally aiding in the search for mass standards.

Isomorphism problems over various mathematical structures have been a
source of intriguing problems in complexity theory (see {{cite:3a07d78e50794e558b03b07fc7026011bb5dc573}}).
The most important problem of this domain is the well-known graph
isomorphism problem. Though the complexity characterization of the
general version of this problem is still unknown, there have been
various interesting special cases of the problem which are known to
have polynomial time algorithms {{cite:1dc727c28afde709407f1a08746370ba7d1c883c}}, {{cite:5b51d63e485ee5b2afaa7b09ff6e9f4b0d0c3114}}. In this paper we
talk about isomorphism problem associated with matroids.

A matroid {{formula:2e6b8948-9bb4-40a1-862d-776238bd3fd7}}  is a combinatorial object defined over a finite set {{formula:f3077218-cd30-4798-8a71-f2637db31816}} 
(of size {{formula:bc73b66f-e513-4e50-933e-ac312d0e57d0}} ) called the ground set, equipped with a non-empty
family {{formula:355ad943-78bc-4612-a189-e7f2df51ff2b}}  of subsets of {{formula:a505c5a5-e4bf-4cb3-af7e-a8b6121d8d84}}  (containing the empty subset) which is
closed under taking of subsets and satisfies the exchange axiom
: for any {{formula:3d618616-3feb-4bba-a9f1-f1008b6a9e1f}}  such that {{formula:07e168c7-c4a7-42a2-b7ad-7fdea1bfdaf1}} , {{formula:ee39b1b2-f668-4492-ae32-0cf9ca4fb7bc}} , {{formula:5e9af4e3-993e-45c3-a1ec-9a360d96f71b}} . The sets in {{formula:d1ab7285-d317-4fd0-a470-e1b29cb51373}}  are
called independent sets. The rank of the matroid is the size of
the maximal independent set.
This provides useful abstractions of many concepts in combinatorics
and linear algebra {{cite:0721587bcaf63864ad285d784672cc85666e5c77}}. The theory of matroids is a well
studied area of combinatorics {{cite:7e69a4b5ad5c22677aa5e3a8a793965af8cb3a9f}}. We study the problem
of testing isomorphism between two given matroids.

Two matroids {{formula:6fd9fd0e-7a1e-4cc9-acfd-139f78093039}}  and {{formula:1597b594-e9dc-43b6-a071-93cdd73168d4}}  are said to be isomorphic if there is a
bijection between the elements of the ground set which maps
independent sets to independent sets, (or equivalently circuits to
circuits, or bases to bases, see section ). Quite
naturally, the representation of the input matroids is important in
deciding the complexity of the algorithmic problem.

There are several equivalent representations of a matroid. For
example, enumerating the maximal independent sets (called bases) or
the minimal dependent sets (called circuits) also defines the matroid.
These representations, although can be exponential in the size of the
ground set, indeed exist for every matroid, by definition. With this
enumerative representation, Mayhew {{cite:a71b0441cb7867118c964b16682186c6aa37fb3d}} studied the matroid
isomorphism problem, and shows that the problem is equivalent to graph
isomorphism problem. However, a natural question is whether the
problem is difficult when the representation of the matroid is
more implicit?. In a black-box setting, one can also consider the input
representation in the form of an oracle or a black-box, where the
oracle answers whether a given set is independent or not.

More implicit (and efficient) representation of matroids have been
studied. One natural way is to identify the given matroid with matroids defined over combinatorial or algebraic
objects which have implicit descriptions. A general framework in this
direction is the representation of a matroid over a field. A matroid {{formula:cb985151-b69f-416c-a5f1-571f35600aac}}  of rank {{formula:cf42b685-fb12-4d76-a532-8c1813bf0d6f}}  is said to be representable over a
field {{formula:8865f422-b29f-41dd-b33e-e19a04276995}}  if there is a map, {{formula:9c0700d2-4801-4282-8bac-2b5d96b947e4}}  such that, {{formula:372fe4a0-0392-4487-beca-f66ade2bfe3b}} , {{formula:572eb40e-cfc9-4426-a2a5-bdb32e465fb9}}  is linearly independent over {{formula:5d47783d-92b3-48b3-b47b-f1a9118de14f}}  as a vector
space. However, there are matroids which do not admit linear
representations over any field. (For example, the Vamós Matroid, See
Proposition 6.1.10, {{cite:7e69a4b5ad5c22677aa5e3a8a793965af8cb3a9f}}.). In contrast, there are
matroids (called regular matroids) which admit linear representations
over all fields.

Another natural representation for a matroid is over graphs. For any
graph {{formula:a58dbd5a-3d53-4a6a-b2dd-b9b9129072c7}} , we can associate a matroid {{formula:5d38bf07-1aef-4a18-b0a1-c2d79a60104f}}  as follows: the set of
edges of {{formula:0c25bf10-180c-44e7-b51f-466921a57c63}}  is the ground set, and the acyclic subgraphs of the given
graph form the independent sets. A matroid {{formula:9f1b71cd-7b05-4947-baa9-3aee4e4d2364}}  is called a graphic
matroid (also called polygon matroid or cyclic matroid) if it is
isomorphic to {{formula:142ca55d-ec56-4769-97fb-bdba05aed492}}  for some graph {{formula:8122ace4-2b0a-4811-8571-73ec5e70ae98}} . It is known that graphic
matroids are linear. Indeed, the incidence matrix of the graph will
give a representation over {{formula:eb18fd33-256f-4c15-8fad-e59ffbb8f8cf}} . There are linear matroids which are
not graphic. (See {{cite:7e69a4b5ad5c22677aa5e3a8a793965af8cb3a9f}} for more details.)

The above definitions themselves highlight the importance of testing
isomorphism between two given matroids.
We study the isomorphism problem for the case of linear matroids (Linear
Matroid Isomorphism problem ({{formula:781dc024-102e-4560-ba43-8e2c09d10ede}}  and graphic matroids (Graphic
Matroid Isomorphism problem ({{formula:01404fc7-8297-45de-a6f0-31b872e98ba8}} )).

From a complexity perspective, the general case of the problem is in
{{formula:eb33a2a1-da7e-498b-b139-574c766d3d0e}} . However, it is not even clear a priori if the problem is
in {{formula:6c3114ed-b02d-4ba6-9c42-adb5162fea9c}}  even in the above restricted cases where there are implicit
representations. But we note that for the case of graphic matroids the
problem admits an {{formula:3b69a019-5565-485c-8e87-04397f3bae6e}}  algorithm. Hence an intriguing question is
about the comparison of this problem to the well studied graph
isomorphism problem.

At an intuitive level, in the graph isomorphism problem we ask for a
map between the vertices that preserves the adjacency relations,
whereas in the case of graphic matroid isomorphism, we ask for maps
between the edges such that the set of cycles (or spanning trees) in
the graph are preserved. As an example, in the case of trees, any
permutation gives a 2-isomorphism, where as computing the isomorphism
between trees is known to be {{formula:4b8690f0-5e9f-4ef3-a948-ad05f5a831b0}} -complete. This indicates that the
reduction between the problems cannot be obtained by a local
replacement of edges with gadgets, and has to consider the global
structure.

An important result in this direction, due to Whitney
(see {{cite:3c914c97d96e5e5c4c3112e1786360572ddc7b94}}), says that in the case of 3-connected graphs, the
graphs are isomorphic if and only if the corresponding matroids are
isomorphic (see section ). Thus the problem of testing
isomorphism of graphs and the corresponding graphic matroids are
equivalent for the case of 3-connected graphs are equivalent. Despite
this similarity between the problems, to the best of our knowledge,
there has not been a systematic study of {{formula:383ee9b5-7cd5-411a-9461-0f837984dea7}}  and its relationships
to graph isomorphism problem ({{formula:c85c0085-269f-4543-8680-f9d3bbbd0493}} ). This immediately gives a
motivation to study the isomorphism problem for 3-connected graphs.
In particular, from the recent results on graph isomorphism problem
for these classes of graphs {{cite:857f1548c154222c61430f5d77dac3435df03c10}}, {{cite:3b3330a8d49d7032921126fdd468c95bc33a3748}}, it follows that
graphic matroid isomorphism problem for 3-connected planar graphs
{{formula:d86af8ec-7796-4654-b719-79ce589621b2}} -complete.

In this context we study the general, linear and graphic matroid
isomorphism problems. Our main contributions in the paper are as
follows:

Matroid isomorphism problem is easily seen to be in
{{formula:f2c08949-c5a9-4ca9-940a-c1c3a2b35fc6}} . In the case of linear matroids where the field is
also a part of the input we observe that the problem is
{{formula:8237f394-89f5-49c6-aadc-19e85f91f261}} -hard (Proposition REF ), and is unlikely to
be {{formula:87b859d1-82ec-4c4d-aaef-619a773c3540}} -complete (Proposition REF ). We also
observe that when the rank of the matroid is bounded, linear matroid
isomorphism, and matroid isomorphism are both equivalent to {{formula:c453b4a4-bc98-43f8-893f-968deb00515e}} 
(Theorem REF )We note that, although not
explicitly stated, the equivalence of bounded rank matroid
isomorphism and and graph isomorphism also follows from the
results of Mayhew {{cite:a71b0441cb7867118c964b16682186c6aa37fb3d}}. However, it is not immediately
clear if the GI-hard instances are linearly representable.
Our proofs are different and extends this to linear matroids.

We develop tools to handle colouring of ground set elements in
the context of isomorphism problem. We show that coloured version of
the linear matroid isomorphism and graphic matroid isomorphisms are
as hard as the general version
(Lemma REF , REF ). As an immediate
application of this, we show that the automorphism problems for
graphic matroids and linear matroids are polynomial time Turing
equivalent to the corresponding isomorphism problems. In this
context, we also give a polynomial time membership test algorithm
for the automorphism group of a graphic matroid
(Theorem REF ).

We give a polynomial time Turing reduction from graphic matroid
isomorphism problem to the graph isomorphism problem by developing
an edge colouring scheme which algorithmically uses a decomposition
given by {{cite:b1cdb4de9cb33b785b477ece96f955cc6efd6a62}} (and {{cite:9c13e8a20b0732dc38783dc73882b43cc1fbb32f}}) and reduce the graphic
matroid (Theorem REF ). Our reduction, in particular implies
that the graphic matroid isomorphism testing for planar graphs can
be done in deterministic polynomial time
(Corollary REF ).

Finally, we give a reduction from bounded rank matroid
isomorphism problem to graphic matroid isomorphism
(Theorem REF ), thus showing that all the above
problems are poly-time equivalent.

Let us first look into the case of 3-connected graphs. A separating
pair is a pair of vertices whose deletion leaves the graph
disconnected. A 3-connected

In {{cite:b1cdb4de9cb33b785b477ece96f955cc6efd6a62}}, Hopcroft and Tarjan proved that every 2-connected
graph can be decomposed uniquely into a tree of 3-connected
components, bonds or polygons.Cunningham et al.  {{cite:9c13e8a20b0732dc38783dc73882b43cc1fbb32f}}

and {{formula:8265e63b-977e-4e79-88a9-661ad366d93a}}  are the virtual edges. However, it is unclear if this
can be turned into a reduction from {{formula:fdefc712-8100-417d-80f5-6dddcfff8f75}}  to {{formula:92eeab3d-e73e-49dd-8e24-13a4e2ec3095}}  using edge/vertex
colouring.
Moreover,  {{cite:b1cdb4de9cb33b785b477ece96f955cc6efd6a62}} showed that this decomposition can
be computed in polynomial time. The idea is to then find the
isomorphism classes of these 3-connected components using queries to
{{formula:79e0b7fc-b4b8-4d69-9ff0-ea05a1213802}}  (see theorem REF ), and then colour the tree
nodes with the corresponding isomorphism class, and then compute a
coloured tree isomorphism between the two trees produced from the two
graphs.

A first mind block is that these isomorphisms between the 3-connected
components need not map separating pairs to separating pairs. We
overcome this by colouring the separating pairs (in fact the edge
between them), with a canonical label of the two sub trees which the
corresponding edge connects. To support this, we observe the
following. There may be many isomorphisms between two 3-connected
components which preserves the colours of the separating
pairs. However, the order in which the vertices are mapped within a
separating pair is irrelevant, since any order will be canonical up to
a twist operation with respect to the separating pair.

So with the new colouring, the isomorphism between 3-connected
components maps a separating pair to a separating pair, if and only if
the two pairs of sub trees are isomorphic. However, even if this is the
case, the coloured sub trees need not be isomorphic. This creates a
simultaneity problem of colouring of the 3-connected components and
the tree nodes and thus a second mind block.

We overcome this by colouring again using the code for coloured
sub trees, and then finding the new isomorphism classes between the
3-connected components. This process is iterated till the colours
stabilize on the tree as well as on the individual separating pairs
(since there are only linear number of 3-connected components). Once
this is ensured, we can recover the 2-isomorphism of the original
graph by weaving the isomorphism of the 3-connected components guided
by the tree adjacency relationship. In addition, if two 3-connected
components are indeed isomorphic in the correctly aligned way, the
above colouring scheme, at any point, does not distinguish between
them.

Now we convert this idea into an algorithm and a formal proof.

We use the algorithm of Hopcroft and Tarjan {{cite:b1cdb4de9cb33b785b477ece96f955cc6efd6a62}} to compute
the set of 3-connected components of a 2-connected graph in polynomial
time. We will now describe some details of the algorithm which we will
exploit.

We studied the matroid isomorphism problem under various input
representations and restriction on the rank of the matroid. We proved
that graph isomorphism,
graphic matroid isomorphism and bounded rank version of matroid isomorphism
are all polynomial time equivalent.

In addition, we find it interesting that in the bounded rank case,
{{formula:67e88915-6dab-467c-86b3-9ecc39083464}}  and {{formula:73a9eab3-bef5-4755-b312-be18f0212e9c}}  are equivalent, though there exist matroids of
bounded rank which are not representable over any field. Some of the
open questions that we see are as follows:

isomorphism problem. For example, it will be interesting to prove a

is over fields of size at least {{formula:fd9e4674-c05f-4b5d-8f5f-4ad51bcf12f1}}  and at most {{formula:5f94f549-04f2-4d28-969a-d2893ccbca5c}} , where

Can we use the colouring technique of linear matroid isomorphism
to reduce the general instances of linear matroid isomorphism to
isomorphism testing of “simpler components” of the matroid?

Can we make the reduction from {{formula:3a57d6cb-005e-4e6a-8cb9-22de9d9fdbb8}}  to {{formula:14b40ab7-67b3-4493-8c98-b150b4fc9983}}  many-one? Can we
improve the complexity of this reduction in the general case?

A problem of testing if a given matroid is uniform, is clearly as a
special case of the matroid isomorphism problem, where one of the
matroid is uniform. The problem is known to be {{formula:a6b862db-b4da-43b1-9337-afb2844a2026}} -complete as
shown below.

Proposition D.1 Given a representable matroid of rank {{formula:75e0a298-a6bc-41ff-8332-51a70cde6ac1}}  (input is a {{formula:5490b42f-f5c6-4d48-b076-14ee309b2be5}} 
matrix {{formula:f7bc62af-97c7-4fae-b1bd-3192daf2d74a}} ), the problem of checking if the matroid is uniform is
{{formula:666ce6e7-4655-4416-b59c-53894e1feca3}} -complete. In other words, testing if the matroid {{formula:3bdf8683-d76e-4c37-9c9b-35af9fe2509f}} 
represented by columns of {{formula:dac02a02-3d0e-45c7-bf6a-370074d3c64b}}  is isomorphic to {{formula:b6a17178-3f78-4f17-b8dd-708d4ccba636}}  is
{{formula:b04bf7a2-115d-407a-ad65-b159cc636167}} -complete.

This proof is due to Oxley and Welsh {{cite:063e12550d55c0c5b5514e789607eea9a3a6e823}}. We make it more
explicit. A set of {{formula:df6fc63d-eb35-4a90-8343-6c216aa9fd70}}  points in {{formula:6e59dc77-1297-4669-9d88-2be8dcc4ca58}}  dimensions is linearly
degenerate if there is a set of {{formula:96667bdc-0384-4a8f-bbd6-9740dc5bb98c}}  points which is linearly
dependent. In other words, the set of {{formula:30d820bf-6cf5-4554-99ba-e70f989a43cf}}  points is said to be in
general position if all subsets of size {{formula:80eaf8ff-3747-49c6-809e-5843dd45f998}}  are linearly
independent. Khanchiyan {{cite:70bc757cd87110ae2440646fa3b920a338b2faf5}}
proved that given {{formula:af499c1e-19ca-48b2-82f8-02479f81be0a}}  points
testing if they are in general position is {{formula:71b82bb0-8fd1-4964-bf84-8a9897a3f6c2}} -hard. Now notice
that this exactly answers the question of testing if the matroid
is uniform.
